For some sets (e.g., the rationals) we can explicitly describe a well-ordering (by identifying \(\mathbb{Q}\) with a subset of \(\mathbb{Z}\times \mathbb{N}\) and then well-ordering that). But \(\mathsf{AC}\) also guarantees a well-order of the reals, and if you try to ‘write down’ such a well-order, you will quickly run into difficulties.







Remark 10.1 (Further reading). For more on the history and the controversy surrounding the Axiom of Choice, see G.H. Moore: Zermelo’s Axiom of Choice, Springer. 1982.




We will need the Axiom of Choice in many places. In the next section, we will use it to develop the theory of cardinal numbers. Some axioms that are considered in descriptive set theory (such as the Axiom of Determinacy, \(\mathsf{AD}\)) contradict \(\mathsf{AC}\). It is therefore important to keep track of where exactly we use the Axiom of Choice.
For some applications, it suffices to use weaker forms of \(\mathsf{AC}\).






NoteAxiom of Countable Choice (\(\mathsf{AC}_\omega\))



\[
\forall n \in \mathbb{N}\; A_n \ne \emptyset \quad \Rightarrow \quad  \exists f \; \forall n \in \omega \;  f(n) \in A_n
\]








NoteAxiom of Dependent Choice (\(\mathsf{DC}\))



If \(R\) is a binary relation on a set \(A\), \(a_0 \in A\), and \(\forall x \in A \exists y \in A \; xRy\), then \[
\exists f : \mathbb{N}\longrightarrow A  \text{ with }  \; f(0) = a_0  \; \wedge  \;\forall n \in \mathbb{N}\; f(n) R f(n+1).
\]









Proposition 10.1 
\(\mathsf{AC}\) implies \(\mathsf{DC}\) and \(\mathsf{DC}\) implies \(\mathsf{AC}_\omega\).




Both implications are strict, in the sense that there are mathematical universes in which the weaker axiom holds and the stronger fails.
The axiom \(\mathsf{AC}_{\omega}\) is sufficient to prove, for example, the following:

Every infinite set contains a countably infinite subset.
A countable union of countable sets is countable.

\(\mathsf{DC}\) and \(\mathsf{AC}_\omega\) therefore play an important role in the foundations of analysis and measure theory.

title: Cardinals
text: Cardinals

title: Cardinals
text:
Cardinality
Cardinal numbers capture the notion of the cardinality of a set. We measure the cardinality of a set relative to other sets by saying sets \(a,b\) have the same cardinality if there exists a bijection between them.
We use the following notation: \[\begin{align*}
a \sim b \quad & : \Leftrightarrow \quad \text{ there exists a bijection } a \leftrightarrow b \\
a \preceq b \quad & : \Leftrightarrow \quad \text{ there exists an injection } a \hookrightarrow b \\
a \prec b \quad & : \Leftrightarrow \quad a \preceq b \; \wedge \; a \nsim b
\end{align*}\]
It is straightforward to show \(\sim\) is an equivalence relation and that \(\preceq\) is transitive. \(\preceq\) is obviously also reflexive. Relations that are reflexive and transitive are called preorders. If we mod out by \(\sim\), do we get a partial order? In other words, do we have antisymmetry in the form \[
a \preceq b \; \wedge \; b \preceq a \quad \overset{?}{\Rightarrow} \quad a \sim b.
\] This follows pretty easily if we use the Axiom of Choice (in form of the well-ordering principle \(\mathsf{WO}\)), but it is one of the few fundamental results in the theory of cardinality one can prove without using Choice.







Theorem 11.1 (Cantor-Schröder-Bernstein Theorem) 
Let \(a\) and \(b\) be sets. If there is an injection from \(a\) to \(b\) and an injection from \(b\) to \(a\), then there exists a bijection between \(a\) and \(b\).











Exercise 11.1 (Warmup) Find a bijection between \([0,1)\) and \([0,1]\).











NoteProof






Proof. Let \(X_0 = X\setminus g(Y)\), \(Y_0 = Y \setminus f(X)\). Let \(X_1 = g(Y)\setminus g(f(X))\), \(Y_1 = f(X) \setminus f(g(Y))\). Note that there is a bijection between \(X_0 \cup X_1\) and \(Y_0 \cup Y_1\) by letting \[
\varphi(x) = \begin{cases}
  f(x) & \text{ if } x \in X_0, \\
  g^{-1}(x) & \text{ if } x \in X_1.
\end{cases}
\] Iterate this process with new \(X : = g(f(X))\) and \(Y := f(g(Y))\). This gives rise to sequences of pairwise disjoint sets \(X_0, X_1, X_2, \dots\) and \(Y_0, Y_1, Y_2, \dots\), together with a bijection \[
\varphi: \bigcup_{i \in \omega}  X_i \leftrightarrow \bigcup_{i \in \omega} Y_i.
\] We now define \[
h(x) = \begin{cases}
  \varphi(x) & \text{ if } x \in \bigcup_{i \in \omega}  X_i, \\
  f(x) & \text{ if } x \in X\setminus \bigcup_{i \in \omega}  X_i.
\end{cases}
\] It is clear that \(h\) is one-to-one. Suppose \(y \in Y \setminus \bigcup_{i \in \omega} Y_i\) is not in \(f(X\setminus \bigcup_{i \in \omega}  X_i)\). But then, by definition of \(\varphi\), \(y\) is not in \(f(Y)\), which would imply \(y \in Y_0\), contradiction. Hence \(h\) is onto.




The next result shows that this order is linear. To prove it, we have to use Choice.







Theorem 11.2 (Hartogs) 
For any sets \(a,b\), \[
a \preceq b \; \vee \; b \preceq a.
\]










NoteProof






Proof. By the well-ordering principle \(\mathsf{WO}\), there exist ordinals \(\alpha, \beta\) such that \(a \sim \alpha\) and \(b \sim \beta\). Since any two ordinals are comparable by \(<\), \(\alpha \subseteq \beta\) or \(\beta \subseteq \alpha\), which easily yields the theorem.




Cantor’s famous result shows that for every set there exists one with greater cardinality. In particular, the order \(\preceq\) is infinite. Given a set \(a\), we denote its power set by \(\mathcal{P}(a)\), \[
\mathcal{P}(a) = \{ b \colon b \subseteq a \}.
\]







Theorem 11.3 (Cantor’s Theorem) 
For every set \(a\), \[
a \prec \mathcal{P}(a).
\]










NoteProof






Proof. \(x \mapsto \{x\}\) is an injection from \(a\) to \(\mathcal{P}(a)\), hence \(a \preceq \mathcal{P}(a)\). Now assume \(a \sim \mathcal{P}(a)\) via a bijection \(f\). We use a diagonal argument (as for the case \(a = \mathbb{N}\)) to derive a contradiction. Let \(d: = \{x \in a\colon x \notin f(x) \}\). As \(f\) is onto, there exists \(b \in a\) with \(f(b) = d\). But then \[
b \in d \; \Leftrightarrow \; b \notin f(b) \; \Leftrightarrow \; b \notin d,
\] contradiction.

title: Cardinals
text:
Cardinal numbers
As with ordinals, we would like to choose a system of representatives for the equivalence classes under \(\sim\). Theorem 11.2 suggests to use ordinals (which we can compare using the well-ordering of ordinals). We therefore assume the Axiom of Choice (so every set has a well-ordering). One issue that remains is that a set can have well-orderings of different lengths (as we saw in the case of the natural numbers \(\mathbb{N}\)). But since the ordinals are well-ordered, we can choose the least one of the same cardinality.







Definition 11.1 
The cardinality \(|a|\) of a set \(a\) is defined as \[
|a| = \min \{ \alpha \in \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\colon \alpha \sim a \}.
\]











Remark 11.1. We have to be careful what we are taking a minimum over, since there could be a lot (i.e. “more than a set” many ordinals equinumeral to \(a\).) We can avoid this by first using \(\mathsf{AC}\) to find one ordinal \(\beta \sim a\), and then taking the minimum ordinals \(\leq \beta\). As we will see later, the latter will always be a set.











Lemma 11.1  

\(a \sim b \quad \iff \quad |a| = |b|\)
\(a \preceq b \quad \iff \quad |a| \leq |b|\)
\(a \prec b \quad \iff \quad |a| < |b|\)





An ordinal \({}\kappa\) is a cardinal if it is the cardinality of some set. Equivalently, \({}\kappa\) is a cardinal if \[
\forall \beta < \kappa \; \beta \prec \kappa.
\] We usually use Greek letters from the middle of the alphabet, \(\kappa, \mu, \nu, \dots\) to denote cardinals.
Given a cardinal \({}\kappa\), we let \(\kappa^+\) be the cardinal successor of \({}\kappa\), i.e.  \[
\kappa^+ = \text{ least cardinal } \nu \text{ with }  \kappa \prec \nu.
\] By Theorem 11.3 (and the Axiom of Choice), we have







Remark 11.2. The fact that \(\kappa^+ \preceq |\mathcal{P}(\kappa)|\) also ensures in the definition of \(\kappa^+\) we are taking the minimum over a set.




\[
  \kappa \prec \kappa^+ \preceq |\mathcal{P}(\kappa)|,
\] and as ordinals, \[
  \kappa < \kappa^+ \leq |\mathcal{P}(\kappa)|.
\]
All finite ordinals \[
0, 1, 2, 3, \dots
\] are cardinals. The first infinite cardinal is \({}\omega\), the cardinality of all countably infinite sets.
We can use ordinals to enumerate all infinite cardinals. This gives the aleph-sequence.
\[\begin{align*}
  \aleph_0 &  \; := \; \omega\\
  \aleph_{\alpha+1}  & \; := \; \aleph^+_\alpha \\
  \aleph_\lambda  &\;  := \; \sup \{ \aleph_\beta \colon \beta < \lambda \}
\end{align*}\]







Exercise 11.2 Show that the supremum of a set of cardinals is a cardinal. (In particular, \(\aleph_\lambda\) in the definition above is a cardinal.)




As in the case of ordinals, cardinals of the form \(\aleph_{\alpha+1}\) are called successor cardinals, whereas alephs whose index is a limit ordinal are called limit cardinals.







Proposition 11.1 
Every cardinal is an aleph, i.e. for every cardinal \({}\kappa\) there exists an ordinal \(\alpha\) such that \(\kappa = \aleph_\alpha\).










NoteProof (Sketch)






Proof (Sketch). The mapping \(\alpha \mapsto \aleph_\alpha\) is stricly increasing. It follows that \(\kappa \leq \aleph_\kappa\) and hence \(\kappa < \aleph_{\kappa+1}\). Choose \({}\alpha\) minimal such that \(\kappa < \aleph_\alpha\). A simple case distinction yields that \({}\alpha\) must be a successor ordinal, \(\alpha = \beta+1\). It then follows from \(\aleph_{\beta+1} = \aleph_\beta^+\) that \(\kappa = \aleph_\beta\).




While every cardinal is an ordinal, not every ordinal is a cardinal. For example \[
\aleph_0 = \omega = |\omega +1| = | \omega +2|= \ldots = |\omega+ \omega| = | \mathbb{Z}| =  |\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}| = | \mathbb{Q}|.
\]
The next cardinal is \[
  \aleph_1 = \aleph_0^+ = \omega_1 = \{\alpha \in \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\colon \alpha \text{ countable}\}.
\] Between \(\aleph_0\) and \(\aleph_1\) are uncountably many ordinals, all of which are countable. The ordinal \(\omega_1\) will play an important role when we close sets under countably infinite operations (like the Borel sets).
We know the set of reals is uncountable, so at this time we are able to conclude \[\begin{equation*}
|\mathbb{R}|\ge \aleph_1, \quad
|\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R})| \ge \aleph_2, \ldots
\end{equation*}\]

title: Cardinals
text:
Operations on cardinals
What can we say about the cardinality of unions, products, etc.?







Exercise 11.3 Show that \(|\mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{R}| = |\mathbb{R}|\).




This is an instance of a more general result. We can define arithmetic operation on cardinals by looking at the cardinalities of the corresponding set theoretic operations.
\[\begin{align*}
\kappa + \lambda \quad & = \quad  |(\kappa  \times \{0\}) \cup (\lambda  \times \{1\})| & \qquad (\text{disjoint union}) \\
\kappa \cdot \lambda \quad & =  \quad  |\kappa  \times \lambda | & \qquad (\text{product})\\
\kappa^{\lambda} \quad & = \quad   |\{f \colon f: \lambda \to \kappa \}| & \qquad (\text{exponentiation})
\end{align*}\]







Exercise 11.4 Verify that for finite cardinalities, the operations defined above agree with the usual arithmetic operations on natural numbers.




It turns out for infinite cardinals, \(+\) and \(\cdot\) are trivial. This is mostly due to the fact that there is a nice (canonical) well-ordering of \(\mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\times\mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\).

The canonical well-ordering of ordinal pairs
We define a bijection \(F: \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\times \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\leftrightarrow \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\). As a first step, we define the lexicographic order \(<_{\mathop{\mathrm{lex}}}\) on \(\mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\times \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\): \[\begin{equation*}
(\alpha, \beta) <_{\mathop{\mathrm{lex}}} (\gamma, \delta) \quad : \iff \quad \alpha < \gamma \, \vee \, ( \alpha = \gamma \, \wedge \beta < \delta).
\end{equation*}\]
This is a linear order in which every non-empty subset has a minimal element, but we have to be careful since in this order all pairs of the form \((0,\xi)\), \(\xi \in \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\), precede \((1,0)\). And we saw that there is no set of the form \(\{(0,\xi) \colon  \xi \in \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\}\). Gödel modified this order by presorting according to the maximum of the pair: \[\begin{align}
(\alpha, \beta) <_g (\gamma, \delta) \; : \iff \; & \max(\alpha,\beta) <  \max(\gamma,\delta)  \\
  & \qquad \vee \; (\max(\alpha,\beta) =  \max(\gamma,\delta)  \: \wedge \: (\alpha, \beta) <_{\mathop{\mathrm{lex}}} (\gamma, \delta)).
\end{align}\] This yields a linear order in which every element has only a set of predecessors. Moreover, the minimality condition is still satisfied: Let \(A \subseteq \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\times \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\) be non-empty. We find the least element of \(A\) by - first finding the least \(\gamma_0 \in \{ \max(\alpha,\beta) \colon  (\alpha,\beta)\in A\}\), - then finding the least \(\alpha_0 \in \{\alpha \colon \exists \beta \;( (\alpha,\beta)\in A \wedge  \max(\alpha,\beta) = \gamma_0) \}\), - and finally finding the least \(\beta_0 \in \{\beta \colon (\alpha_0,\beta) \in A \wedge \max(\alpha_0,\beta) = \gamma_0 \}\).
It is straightforward to verify that \((\alpha_0, \beta_0)\) is the smallest element of \(A\) with respect to \(<_g\).
Enumerating pairs of ordinals along \(<_g\) now yields and order isomorphism \(F: \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\times \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\to \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\), \[  
(\alpha, \beta) <_g (\gamma, \delta) \; \iff \;  F(\alpha, \beta) < F(\gamma, \delta).
\] Note that \(f(\alpha) := F(\alpha\times \alpha)\) is a strictly increasing map on ordinals, and hence \(F(\alpha) \geq \alpha\). Further note that \[
\alpha \times \alpha = \{(\beta,\gamma) \colon (\beta,\gamma) <_g (0,\alpha) \},
\] hence \(\alpha\times\alpha\) is a \(<_g\)-initial segment.
An important application of the well-ordering of \(\mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\times \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\) is the following theorem.







Theorem 11.4 (Hessenberg’s Theorem) 
Let \({\kappa}\) be an infinite cardinal. Then \[
  \kappa \cdot \kappa = \kappa.
\]










NoteProof






Proof. Show that for any infinite cardinal \({}\kappa\), the restriction of the mapping \(F\) to \(\kappa \times \kappa\), \(F\mid_{\kappa\times\kappa}\), is a bijection between \(\kappa \times \kappa\) and \({}\kappa\). In other words, show that \(F(\kappa\times\kappa)=\kappa\).
It is straightforward to verify this for \(\kappa = \aleph_0\).
Now assume it does not hold for a larger cardinal. Since every infinite cardinal is of the form \(\kappa = \aleph_\alpha\), choose \(\alpha > 0\) minimal such that \(F(\aleph_\alpha \times \aleph_\alpha) \neq \aleph_\alpha\).
Note that since for any \(\beta\), \(F(\beta,\beta) \geq \beta\), we must have \(F(\aleph_\alpha, \aleph_\alpha) > \aleph_\alpha\).
Since \(F\) is a bijection, there exist ordinals \(\beta, \gamma < \aleph_\alpha\) such that \(F(\beta, \gamma) = \aleph_\alpha\). If we put \(\delta = \max\{\beta,\gamma\}+1\), we have \(\omega \leq \delta < \aleph_\alpha\) (since \(\aleph_\alpha\) has to be a limit ordinal).
Since \((\beta, \gamma) <_g (\delta, \delta)\), it follows that \(F(\delta \times \delta) > \aleph_\alpha\) and thus \(F(\delta\times \delta) \supseteq \aleph_\alpha\). The latter implies \(|\delta \times \delta| \geq \aleph_\alpha\). But \(|\delta\times\delta| = |\delta|\cdot |\delta|\) and by minimality of \(\alpha\), \(|\delta|\cdot |\delta| = |\delta| < \aleph_\alpha\), contradiction.











Corollary 11.1 
If \(\kappa, \lambda\) are infinite cardinals, then \[\begin{equation*}
\kappa  + \lambda = \kappa \cdot \lambda = \max\{\kappa, \lambda\}.
\end{equation*}\]










NoteProof






Proof. If \(\kappa\) is infinite, we have, by simple monotonicity arguments, \[\begin{equation*}
\kappa \le \kappa  + \kappa \le \kappa \cdot \kappa = \kappa, \quad  \text{hence}  \; \kappa  + \kappa = \kappa \cdot \kappa = \kappa.
\end{equation*}\]
If, say, \(0< \kappa \leq \lambda\) with \(\lambda\) infinite, the above implies \[\begin{align}
\lambda \le \kappa  + \lambda \le \lambda + \lambda = \lambda, & \quad \text{ and thus }  \;\kappa  + \lambda= \lambda = \max\{\kappa,\lambda\},\\
\lambda \le \kappa  \cdot \lambda \le \lambda \cdot \lambda = \lambda, & \quad  \text{ and thus }  \; \kappa  \cdot \lambda = \lambda = \max\{\kappa,\lambda\}.
\end{align}\]

title: Cardinals
section: The cardinality of \(\mathbb{R}\) and related sets
text:
The cardinality of \(\mathbb{R}\) and related sets
While, as we just saw, addition and multiplication are trivial for infinite cardinals, determining the simplest transfinite power, \(2^{\aleph_0}\), already leads to unsolvable problems. \(2^{\aleph_0}\) plays an important role since it is the cardinality of the continuum.







Proposition 11.2 
\[|\mathbb{R}| = |\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})| = 2^{\aleph_0}.\]










TipHint





Use, for example:

Dedekind cuts
every real number has an infinite binary expansion
subsets can be identified with their characteristic function

The Theorem 11.1 makes life easier here.



We can draw some conclusions:

With \(|\mathbb{R}| = 2^{ \aleph_0}\) we also get \(|\mathbb{R}^n |\) = \((2^{ \aleph_0})^n = 2^{\aleph_0},\) by Hessenberg’s Theorem. It even holds that (exercise!) \[\begin{equation*}
|\{s \colon \mathbb{N}\to  \mathbb{R}\}|  =  (2^{ \aleph_0})^{\aleph_0} = 2^{ \aleph_0 \cdot \aleph_0} = 2^{ \aleph_0}.
\end{equation*}\] That is, there are as many countable sequences of real numbers as there are real numbers.
Since every continuous real-valued function on \(\mathbb{R}\) is determined by its values on \(\mathbb{Q}\), we have \[
|\{f:\mathbb{R}\to \mathbb{R}\text{ continuous } \}| = |\{f:\mathbb{Q}\to \mathbb{R}\}| = (2^{ \aleph_0})^{\aleph_0} =  2^{ \aleph_0}.
\]
We obtain a higher cardinality by passing to the power set of the real numbers or to the set of all real-valued functions on \(\mathbb{R}\): \[\begin{equation*}
|\{f:\mathbb{R}\to \mathbb{R}\}| = |\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R})| =  2^{2^{ \aleph_0}} > 2^{ \aleph_0}.
\end{equation*}\]







ImportantContinuum Hypothesis (\(\mathsf{CH}\) – cardinal version)



\[
2^{\aleph_0} = \aleph_1
\]


\(\mathsf{CH}\) asserts that the cardinality of \(\mathbb{R}\) is the next biggest cardinal after \(\omega = \aleph_0\) (the cardinality of all countably infinite sets).

title: Models of Set Theory
text:
Models of Set Theory
You may have noticed that, when introducing the axioms of \(\mathsf{ZFC}\), we never really answered the question “What is a set?” Instead, we developed a formal theory of axioms for a binary relation that somehow describe “how sets work”, that is, how we can obtain sets from given ones using well-known operations like power set and union.
We have then seen how we can develop a lot of standard mathematical objects (like \(\mathbb{N}\), \(\mathbb{R}\)) and techniques (like induction and definition by recursion) inside this formal system. In fact, most of mathematics can be developed formally inside this system. Almost all proofs you find in any standard math book are proofs that can be formalized in \(\mathsf{ZFC}\). It is very tedious to do this for us humans, but there is little doubt it can be done, and in fact, looking at the recent work on proof assistants (like Coq or Lean), many parts of mathematics have been formalized (albeit not directly in \(\mathsf{ZFC}\)).
This expressiveness gives \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) its foundational importance, but it is also the cause for much confusion for someone who first studies set theory.
From a pedagogical point of view, in what follows it is helpful to assume a “Platonist” perspective of mathematics, and set theory in particular, namely that sets and the relations between exist independently (and outside) of the \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) axioms. The set of real numbers exists, and our development of \(\mathbb{R}\) inside \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) is just a formal way to describe them. From this perspective, the axioms of \(\mathsf{ZF}\) (\(\mathsf{AC}\) is a little different) are just obvious truths about sets, just like the Peano axioms are obvious truths about natural numbers.
Among other things, this perspective allows us to treat \(\mathsf{ZF}\) just like any other mathematical theory, like group theory or the theory of algebraically closed fields. In particular, we can think about models of set theory the way we would think about models of group theory, in the sense of model theory.
A model would simply be a set \(M\) together with a binary relation \(E\) on \(S\) such that
\[
    (M,E) \models \mathsf{ZF},
\]
that is, all axioms hold when interpreted in \((M,E)\). Note that we use “set” in this context not in the formal sense, but in the “meta”-sense (the Platonist world of sets).
Working in the meta-theory (“that what is mathematically true”), we know by Gödel’s completeness theorem that
if \(\mathsf{ZF}\) is consistent, then it has a model.
This model should be seen as a set-theoretic universe: Its elements can be seen as sets, and the interpretation \(E\) of the \(\in\)-symbol will tell us how these sets are connected via the element-relation.
Note that \(E\) does not have to be the actual element relation on a set (of sets), but just some binary relation so that the axioms are satisfied.
In the meta-world, there are, of course, sets other than \(M\), but that does not matter here, since all we are interested in is giving some universe in which our axioms hold. (Timothy Chow has suggested that set theory should rather be called “universe theory. He is right in the sense that what axiomatic set theory does is to define such universes of sets, rather than what a set is.)
In the meta-theory, we can then follow the usual techniques to show provability or non-provability results.
If we want to prove that \(\mathsf{CH}\) is consistent with \(\mathsf{ZF}\) (assuming \(\mathsf{ZF}\) is consistent), we need to find a model in which both hold.
One difficulty in working with models of set theory is that they can look very different depending on whether you look at a model “from the inside” or “from the outside”.
To illustrate this, assume \(\mathsf{ZF}\) is consistent. Then, by the Löwenheim-Skolem theorem, there exists a countable model for \(\mathsf{ZF}\). Yet it is a theorem of \(\mathsf{ZF}\) that there exists an uncountable set. This is often referred to as Skolem’s paradox, although it is not really an antinomy.
If we break this down a bit, we see that the apparent paradox is really just a matter of perspective (inside or outside). Assume \((M,E)\) is a countable model of \(\mathsf{ZF}\). Then there exists \(x \in M\) such that there is no injection from \(x\) to the natural numbers. Since \(M\) is countable, \(x\) can have at most countably many elements. So why is this not a contradiction? We should really read the statement above as
there is no injection in \(M\) from \(x\) to \(M\)’s version of the natural numbers.
In other words, even though \(x\) is countable from the outside, \(x\) appears uncountable inside \(M\) since a mapping witnessing its countability does not exist in \(M\).
This is a first warning sign that models of \(\mathsf{ZF}\) can behave in very unexpected ways. For another example, recall the axiom of Foundation asserts that the \(\in\)-relation is well-founded. But again, this means only “from the inside”.
Since, as mentioned above, the model \((M^*,E^*)\) satisfies Foundation, the set \(\{c_n \colon n \in \mathbb{N}\}\) is actually not in the model (and neither can be any other set with an infinite descending \(\in\)-chain).

title: Models of Set Theory
text:
Mostowski collapse
If we restrict ourselves to models on which the \(E\)-relation is actually well-founded (i.e. from the outside), then interestingly these models look, in a way, “natural”: They can be assumed to be the \(\in\)-relation on a set. Such models are also called standard.
Given a set theoretic structure \((M,E)\) (not necessarily a model of \(\mathsf{ZF}\)), for each \(x \in M\) let \[\begin{equation*}
    \operatorname{ext}_E(x) = \{ y \in X \colon y\, E \, x \}
\end{equation*}\]
If \(E\) behaves “set-like”, then it will respect the axiom of Extensionality, i.e. two sets are identical if and only if they have the same elements. Therefore we say that \(E\) is extensional if \[\begin{equation*}
    x,z \in X, \; x\neq z \quad \text{ implies } \quad \operatorname{ext}_E(x) \neq \operatorname{ext}_E(z).
\end{equation*}\]
Furthermore, as stated above, we want to exclude infinite descending \(E\)-chains. Recall we say that \(E\) is well-founded if

every non-empty set \(Y \subseteq X\) has an \(E\)-minimal element.








Theorem 12.1 (Mostowski collapse) 
If \(E\) is an extensional and well-founded relation on a set \(X\), then there exists a transitive set \(S\) and a bijection \(\pi: X \to S\) such that \[\begin{equation*}
    x \, E \, y \iff \pi(x) \in \pi(y) \quad \text{ for all $ x,y \in X$}.      
\end{equation*}\] Moreover, \(S\) and \({}\pi\) are unique.










NoteProof






Proof. We construct \({}\pi\) and \(S = \operatorname{im}(\pi)\) by recursion on \(E\), which is possible since it is well-founded.
For each \(x \in X\), let \[\begin{equation*}
    \pi(x) = \{\pi(y) \colon y \, E \, x \},
\end{equation*}\] and set \(S = \operatorname{ran}(\pi)\).
The injectivity of \({}\pi\) follows from the extensionality of \({}\pi\) by induction along \(E\):
Suppose we have shown \[\begin{equation*}
\forall z \; (z E x \to \forall y  \in X (\pi(z) = \pi(y) \to z = y)).
\end{equation*}\] and we have to show that it holds for \(x\). Assume \(\pi(x) = \pi(y)\) for some \(y \in X\). Then \[\begin{align*}
cEx &\Rightarrow& \pi(c) \in \pi(x) = \pi(y) &\\
&\Rightarrow& \pi(c) = \pi(z) & \qquad \text{ for some } zEy\\
&\Rightarrow& c=z & \qquad  (\text{by ind. hyp., since } cEx)\\
&\Rightarrow& cEy &.
\end{align*}\] Similarly, we get \(cEy \Rightarrow cEx\), hence \(x=y\) as desired due to the extensionality of \(E\). Finally we have \[\begin{align*}
\pi(x) \in \pi(y) & \Rightarrow & \pi(x) = \pi(c) & \qquad \text{ for some } cEy \\
&\Rightarrow& x = c & \qquad \text{ (since ${}\pi$ is injective)}\\
&\Rightarrow& xEy &
\end{align*}\] Thus \({}\pi\) is an isomorphism.
To see the uniqueness of \({}\pi\) and \(S\), assume \(\rho\), \(T\) are such that the statement of the theorem is satisfied. Then \(\pi \circ \rho^{-1}\) is an isomorphism between \((T, \in)\) and \((S,\in)\). Now apply the following lemma.











Lemma 12.1 
Suppose \(X,Y\) are sets, and \({}\theta\) is an isomorphism between \((X,\in)\) and \((Y,\in)\). Then \(X=Y\) and \(\theta(x) = x\) for all \(x \in X\).










NoteProof






Proof. By induction on the well-founded relation \(\in\). Assume that \(\theta(z)=z\) for all \(z \in x\) and let \(y = \theta(x)\).
We have \(x \subseteq y\) because if \(z \in x\), then \(z = \theta(z) \in \theta(x) = y\).
We also have \(y \subseteq x\): Let \(t \in y\). Since \(y \in Y\), there is \(z \in X\) with \(\theta(z) = t\). Since \(\theta(z) \in y\) and \(y = \theta(x)\), we have \(z \in x\), and thus \(t = \theta(z) = z \in x\).
Hence \(x = y\), and this also implies \(\theta(x) = x\).











Corollary 12.1 
If \(E\) is a well-order on a set \(X\), then \((X,E)\) is isomorphic to \((\alpha, \in)\) for a unique ordinal \(\alpha\).










NoteProof






Proof. Every linear order is extensional. Hence we can apply the Mostowski Collapse. It is easy to see that the resulting set is an ordinal.

title: Models of Set Theory
text:
Absoluteness and transitive models
Even if we consider well-founded standard models, interpreting set-theoretic statements in them can still lead to very different results, even for very simple formulas.







Example 12.1 
Consider \(M = \{0, \{\{0\}\}\}\) and let \(\varphi \equiv \{\{0\}\} \subseteq 0\). Clearly \({}\varphi\) is not true from the “outside”. But what if we look at it from “inside” \(M\)? \(x \subseteq y\) means \(\forall z (z \in x \to z \in y)\). Inside \(M\) this means every set \(z\) in \(M\) that is an element of \(x\) is also an element of \(y\). But in \(M\), there is no element \(z \in \{\{0\}\}\), \(\{0\}\) is not an element of \(M\). Therefore, \[
    (M, \in) \models \{\{0\}\} \subseteq 0.
\]




In the example above, the set \(M\) is not transitive, which allowed it to “hide” its elements. It turns out that if we require our model to be transitive, the truth of simple formulas cannot vary between the “inside” and the “outside” perspective. We call such properties absolute.
Given a formula \({}\varphi\) and some class \(M\), we can relativize \({}\varphi\) with respect to \(M\) essentially by restricting all quantifiers in \({}\varphi\) to range over \(M\), i.e. \(\exists x\) becomes \(\exists x \in M\) and \(\forall x\) becomes \(\forall x \in M\). Note that classes are defined by formulas, so the resulting formula, which we denote by \(\varphi^M\), is still a formula of set theory.







Definition 12.1 
We say a formula \(\varphi(x_0, \ldots, x_n)\) is absolute for a class \(M\) if for all \(a_0, \ldots, a_n \in M\) \[
    \varphi^M(a_0, \ldots, a_n) \text{ holds} \iff  \varphi(a_0, \ldots, a_n) \text{ holds}.
\]











Exercise 12.1 If \(M\) is transitive, then for all \({}\varphi\), \[
    (M, \in) \models \varphi \; \iff \; \varphi^M \text{ holds}.
\]











Definition 12.2 
A formula \({}\varphi\) is \(\Delta_0\) if it has no quantifiers or every quantifier of \({}\varphi\) is of the form \(\exists x \in y\) or \(\forall x \in y\) (i.e. every quantifier is bounded).











Lemma 12.2 
If \(M\) is transitive and \({}\varphi\) is \(\Delta_0\), then \({}\varphi\) is absolute for \(M\).










NoteProof






Proof. Clearly \(x=y\) and \(x\in y\) are absolute for any \(M\). It is also not hard to see that if \({}\varphi\) and \({}\psi\) are absolute for \(M\), then so are \(\neg \varphi\) and \(\varphi \wedge \psi\). Hence all quantifier free formulas are absolute.
Finally, if \({}\varphi\) is absolute for \(M\), so is \(\psi \equiv \exists x \in y \: \varphi\): If \(\psi^M(y,\bar{z})\) holds for \(y,\bar{z} \in M\), then we have \([\exists x (x \in y \: \wedge \: \varphi(x,y,\bar{z}))]^M\), i.e., \(\exists x \in M(x \in y \: \wedge \: \varphi^M(x,y,\bar{z}))\). Since \(\varphi^M(x,y,\bar{z})\) if and only if \(\varphi(x,y,\bar{z})\), it follows that \(\exists x\in y \varphi(x,y,\bar{z})\), i.e. \({}\psi\).
Conversely, if for \(y,\bar{z} \in M\), \(\exists x\in y \varphi(x,y,\bar{z})\), then since \(M\) is transitive, \(x\) belongs to \(M\), and since \(\varphi(x,y,\bar{z})\) if and only \(\varphi^M(x,y,\bar{z})\), we have \(\exists x \in M \, (x \in y \: \wedge \: \varphi^M(x,y,\bar{z}) )\) and so \(\psi^M(y,\bar{z})\).











Proposition 12.2 
Over \(\mathsf{ZF}\), the following properties can be expressed via \(\Delta_0\)-formulas and hence are absolute for any transitive class \(M\):

\(x = \emptyset\), \(x=y\), \(x \subseteq y\), \(z = x \cap y\), \(z = x \cup y\), \(x = \bigcap y\), \(x = \bigcup y\), \(z = \{x,y\}\), \(z =(x,y)\), \(z= x \times y\)
\(r\) is a relation, \(f\) is a function, \(x = \operatorname{dom}(f)\), \(y = \operatorname{ran}(f)\)
\(<\) is a linear order on \(x\), \(x\) is an ordinal, \(x\) is a limit ordinal, \(x=\omega\)





We leave the proof as an exercise.
We can extend the previous absoluteness result to a slightly larger family of formulas.







Definition 12.3 
A formula \({}\varphi\) is

\(\Sigma_1\) if it is of the form \(\exists x_1 \dots \exists x_m \: \psi\) for a \(\Delta_0\)-formula \(\psi\),
\(\Pi_1\) if it is of the form \(\forall x_1 \dots \forall x_m \: \psi\) for a \(\Delta_0\)-formula \(\psi\).

Given a set of formulas \(T\) and formula \({}\varphi\), we say \({}\varphi\) is \(\Delta_1^{T}\) if there exists a \(\Sigma_1\)-formula \(\psi_\exists\) and a \(\Pi_1\)-formula \(\psi_\forall\) such that \[
    T \vdash \varphi \leftrightarrow \psi_\exists \quad \text{ and } T \vdash \varphi \leftrightarrow \psi_\forall.
\]











Proposition 12.3 
If \(M\) is transitive and for all \(\sigma \in T\), \(\sigma^M\) holds, then any \(\Delta_1^T\)-formula is absolute for \(M\)

title: Models of Set Theory
section: Levels of the von Neumann hierarchy as models
text:
Levels of the von Neumann hierarchy as models
The absoluteness property of “simple” formulas can be put to use to identify many “almost” models of \(\mathsf{ZF}\) among the levels \(V_\alpha\) of the von Neumann hierarchy. Since each \(V_\alpha\) is transitive, we can check an axiom in \(V_\alpha\) by checking its relativization: all quantifiers range over \(V_\alpha\).
Recall that the rank of a set \(x\) is \[
    \operatorname{rank}(x) = \min\{\alpha \colon x \in V_{\alpha+1}\}.
\]

The hereditarily finite sets \(V_\omega\)







Lemma 12.3 
Each \(V_\alpha\) is transitive.










NoteProof






Proof. By induction on \({}\alpha\). \(V_0 = \emptyset\) is trivially transitive. Suppose \(V_\alpha\) is transitive. We first note that \(V_\alpha \subseteq V_{\alpha+1}\): \[
    z \in V_\alpha \; \overset{V_\alpha \text{ trans.}}{\Longrightarrow} \; z \subseteq V_\alpha \; \Longrightarrow \; z \in \mathcal{P}(V_\alpha) = V_{\alpha+1}.
\] Now \[
    x \in V_{\alpha+1} \; \Rightarrow \; x \in \mathcal{P}(V_\alpha) \; \Rightarrow \; x \subseteq V_\alpha \; \Rightarrow \; x \subseteq V_{\alpha+1}.
\] Limit stages are fine, since a union of transitive sets is transitive.











Lemma 12.4 
\(x \in V_\omega\) if and only if \(x \subseteq V_\omega\) and \(x\) is finite.










NoteProof






Proof. (\(\Rightarrow\)) Since \(V_\omega\) is transitive (Lemma 12.3), \(x \in V_\omega\) implies \(x \subseteq V_\omega\). Moreover, \(x \in V_n\) for some \(n < \omega\). By induction on \(n\), each \(V_n\) is finite (\(|V_{n+1}| = 2^{|V_n|}\)), and since \(V_n\) is transitive, \(x \subseteq V_n\), so \(x\) is finite.
(\(\Leftarrow\)) Let \(x \subseteq V_\omega\) be finite. If \(x = \emptyset\), then \(x \in V_1\). Otherwise, each \(y \in x\) has finite rank, so we can let \[
    M = \max\{\operatorname{rank}(y) \colon y \in x\} < \omega.
\] Then \(y \in V_{M+1}\) for all \(y \in x\), i.e. \(x \subseteq V_{M+1}\). Hence \(x \in V_{M+2} \subseteq V_\omega\).




Because of this lemma, the elements of \(V_\omega\) are also called the hereditarily finite sets.







Theorem 12.2 
\((V_\omega, \in) \models \mathsf{ZF}- \mathsf{Infinity}\).










NoteProof






Proof. We go through the axioms one by one.
Extensionality: The axiom reads \[
    \forall z \, (z \in x \leftrightarrow z \in y) \to x = y,
\] but in \(V_\omega\) we have to read this as “\(\forall z \in V_\omega\)”. So let \(x,y \in V_\omega\). If \(z \in x \in V_\omega\), then by transitivity \(z \in V_\omega\). So if \(x\) and \(y\) have the same elements in \(V_\omega\), they have the same elements, and thus \(x = y\). In other words, Extensionality follows directly from transitivity.
(Without transitivity, Extensionality can fail: in \(M = \{\emptyset, \mathbb{R}\}\), the sets \(\emptyset \neq \mathbb{R}\) have the same elements in \(M\), namely none. The same happens for \(\{\emptyset, \mathbb{C}\}\).)
Foundation: Every non-empty set has an \(\in\)-minimal element. Let \(x \in V_\omega\), \(x \neq \emptyset\). Choose \(y \in x\) of minimal rank. If \(z \in y\), then \(\operatorname{rank}(z) < \operatorname{rank}(y)\), so \(z \notin x\). Hence \(y\) is \(\in\)-minimal in \(x\) (and \(y \in V_\omega\) by transitivity).
Comprehension: This follows from Lemma 12.4. Let \(a \in V_\omega\) and let \({}\varphi\) be a formula (possibly with parameters from \(V_\omega\)). Then \[
    z = \{ v \in a \colon \varphi^{V_\omega}(v) \}
\] (\(\varphi\) is evaluated in \(V_\omega\)) is a subset of \(a\). Since \(a \in V_n\) for some \(n < \omega\), by transitivity \(a \subseteq V_n\), so \(z \subseteq V_n\) and hence \(z \in \mathcal{P}(V_n) = V_{n+1} \subseteq V_\omega\).
Pairing: If \(x, y \in V_\omega\), then \(\{x,y\}\) is a finite subset of \(V_\omega\), hence in \(V_\omega\) by Lemma 12.4.
Union: Let \(a \in V_\omega\). Then \(\bigcup a\) is a finite union of finite sets and hence finite. Moreover, \[
    \textstyle \bigcup a = \{z \in V_\omega \colon \exists y \in a \; (z \in y)\},
\] since \(a \in V_\omega\) implies, by transitivity, that every \(z \in \bigcup a\) is in \(V_\omega\), i.e. \(\bigcup a \subseteq V_\omega\). By Lemma 12.4, \(\bigcup a \in V_\omega\).
Power Set: If \(x \in V_\omega\), then \(x \in V_n\) for some \(n < \omega\), so \(x \subseteq V_n\) and \[
    \mathcal{P}(x) \subseteq \mathcal{P}(V_n) = V_{n+1} \; \Rightarrow \; \mathcal{P}(x) \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(V_n)) = V_{n+2} \subseteq V_\omega.
\] (Alternatively, \(\mathcal{P}(x)\) is a finite subset of \(V_\omega\), so apply Lemma 12.4.)
Replacement: Suppose \({}\varphi\) defines (in \(V_\omega\)) a function \(f_\varphi: a \to V_\omega\), where \(a \in V_\omega\). Since \(a\) is finite, \(f_\varphi[a]\) is a finite subset of \(V_\omega\), hence, by Lemma 12.4, \(f_\varphi[a] \in V_\omega\).




On the other hand, Infinity fails in \(V_\omega\), since every element of \(V_\omega\) is finite, while any inductive set is infinite.


Beyond \(V_\omega\)






TipQuestion



Where are \(\mathbb{Q}\), \(\mathbb{R}\), \(\mathbb{C}\), … “located” in the von Neumann hierarchy?









Proposition 12.4 
For every ordinal \({}\alpha\),

\(\operatorname{rank}(\alpha) = \alpha\),
\(\mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\cap V_\alpha = \alpha\).





We can represent a rational number as a signed pair of mutually prime natural numbers \(\geq 1\), that is, as \[
    \langle i, \langle m,n \rangle \rangle,
\] where \(i\) codes the sign (with some fixed set representing \(0\)). Each such triple is in \(V_\omega\), by the Pairing argument above. Therefore, \[
    \mathbb{Q}\subseteq V_\omega \quad \leadsto \quad \mathbb{Q}\in V_{\omega+1}.
\]
The real numbers \(\mathbb{R}\) are the set of all Dedekind cuts. A Dedekind cut is a subset of \(\mathbb{Q}\), hence an element of \(\mathcal{P}(V_\omega) = V_{\omega+1}\). So all cuts are elements of \(V_{\omega+1}\), i.e. \(\mathbb{R}\subseteq V_{\omega+1}\), and therefore \[
    \mathbb{R}\in V_{\omega+2}.
\]
Finally, \(\mathbb{C}= \mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{R}\). An ordered pair \(\langle x,y \rangle = \{\{x\},\{x,y\}\}\) of elements of \(V_{\omega+1}\) is in \(V_{\omega+3}\), so \[
    \mathbb{C}\in V_{\omega+4}.
\]
Continuing like this, it seems that “elementary mathematics” lives in \(V_{\omega+\omega}\).






TipQuestion



Which axioms does \(V_{\omega+\omega}\) satisfy?


Replacement fails in \(V_{\omega+\omega}\): The function \(f: n \mapsto \omega + n\) is definable in \(V_{\omega+\omega}\) and has domain \(\omega \in V_{\omega+\omega}\). But its range \(\{\omega + n \colon n < \omega\}\) has rank \(\omega+\omega\) (by Proposition 12.4), so it is not an element of \(V_{\omega+\omega}\).
The other axioms, however, all hold, as the next theorem shows.


Limit levels
Let \(\mathsf{ZC}\) denote \(\mathsf{ZFC}- \mathsf{Replacement}\) (Zermelo set theory with Choice).







Theorem 12.3 
If \(\alpha > \omega\) is a limit ordinal, then \((V_\alpha, \in) \models \mathsf{ZC}\), i.e. \((V_\alpha, \in) \models \mathsf{ZFC}- \mathsf{Replacement}\).










NoteProof






Proof. We verify a few axioms and leave the rest as an exercise.
Extensionality: The relativized version of this axiom is \[
    \forall a,b \in V_\alpha \, ( \forall x\in V_\alpha (x \in a  \leftrightarrow x \in b)  \to a=b)
\] This simply states that the \(\in\)-relation (as a binary relation) is extensional on \(V_\alpha\) (as defined above). It is easy to see that for every transitive set, the \(\in\)-relation is extensional.
Power Set: We have seen that \(\subseteq\) is absolute for transitive classes. Therefore, the relativized version of the Power Set axiom becomes \[
\forall a \in V_\alpha\, \exists y \in V_\alpha \forall z \in V_\alpha (z \in y \leftrightarrow z \subseteq a)
\] This means we only need to have those subsets in the power set that are in \(V_\alpha\). In other words, we need to verify \[
\forall a \in V_\alpha\, ( \mathcal{P}(a) \cap V_\alpha \in V_\alpha)
\] If \(a \in V_\alpha\), then \(a \in V_\beta\) for some \(\beta < \alpha\), since \({}\alpha\) is limit. Since \(V_\beta\) is transitive, \(a \subseteq V_\beta\) and thus \(\mathcal{P}(a)\subseteq \mathcal{P}(V_\beta) = V_{\beta+1}\), which in turn yields \(\mathcal{P}(a) \in V_{\beta+2}\)
If \(b \in \mathcal{P}(a) \cap V_\alpha\), then \(b \in V_{\beta+2}\). Therefore, \(\mathcal{P}(a) \cap V_\alpha \subseteq V_{\beta+2}\). It follows that \(\mathcal{P}(a) \cap V_\alpha \in V_{\beta+3} \subseteq V_\alpha\), as desired.
Infinity: We have seen that \(x = \omega\) is absolute for transitive classes. Hence \(V_\alpha\) will satisfy the Axiom of Infinity if \(\omega \in V_\alpha\). But this is true since we assume \(\alpha > \omega\).




How about \(V_{\omega_1}\)? Perhaps the failure of Replacement in \(V_{\omega+\omega}\) is due to \(\omega+\omega\) being “too small”. But Replacement fails in \(V_{\omega_1}\), too. Consider the formula \[
    \varphi(x,y) \; \iff \; x \subseteq \omega\times\omega \; \wedge \; x \text{ is a well-order} \; \wedge \; y = \operatorname{type}(x).
\] The set \[
    A = \{ x \colon x \subseteq \omega\times\omega, \; x \text{ is a well-order} \}
\] exists in \(V_{\omega_1}\) (it is a subset of \(\mathcal{P}(\omega\times\omega) \subseteq V_{\omega+1}\)). All the relevant notions are absolute for \(V_{\omega_1}\) (for example, the isomorphism between \(x\) and \(\operatorname{type}(x)\) is a subset of \(\omega \times \operatorname{type}(x)\) and hence in \(V_{\omega_1}\)), so \({}\varphi\) defines, in \(V_{\omega_1}\), a function \[
    f: A \to V_{\omega_1}, \quad \operatorname{ran}(f) = \omega_1,
\] since every countable ordinal is the order type of some well-order on a subset of \({}\omega\). But \(\operatorname{rank}(\omega_1) = \omega_1\), so \(\operatorname{ran}(f)\) does not exist in \(V_{\omega_1}\). Hence Replacement fails.
What is the problem with Replacement? The axiom says that if \({}\varphi\) defines a function, then the image of any set under this function is a set. Relativized to some \(M\), this means we need to find a set in \(M\) that contains the image. Here we run into a cardinality problem. The cardinality of \(V_\alpha\) can be much bigger than the cardinality of \({}\alpha\). For example, \(\mathcal{P}(\omega) \in V_{\omega+\omega}\) but \(\omega+\omega\) is countable. We could have a function that maps \(\mathcal{P}(\omega)\) to sets of rank cofinal in \(\omega+\omega\), which implies that the image cannot be in \(V_{\omega+\omega}\).
For \(V_\alpha\) to be a model, we would need \({}\alpha\) to be “unreachable” by such mappings. This gives rise to the notion of inaccessible cardinals, which we will introduce in the next section.

title: Cofinality and Inaccessible Cardinals
text: Cofinality and Inaccessible Cardinals

title: Cofinality and Inaccessible Cardinals
text:
Cofinality
Recall two basic facts about cardinalities:

Finite unions of finite sets are finite.
Countable unions of countable sets are countable (using \(\mathsf{AC}\)).

This means it is “hard” to reach the cardinals \(\aleph_0\) and \(\aleph_1\) “from below”: you cannot obtain a set of size \(\aleph_0\) by putting together a few small pieces, and similarly for \(\aleph_1\). The notion of cofinality quantifies “how hard” it is to reach an ordinal from below.
Throughout this section, \({}\alpha\) denotes a limit ordinal (following Kunen, Def. I.13.10, we define cofinality only for limit ordinals).







Definition 13.1 
A set \(X \subseteq \alpha\) is cofinal in \({}\alpha\) if \[
    \forall \gamma < \alpha \; \exists \xi \in X \;\; \gamma < \xi.
\] Equivalently, \[
    \alpha = \bigcup_{\xi \in X} \xi = \sup X.
\]











Definition 13.2 
The cofinality of \({}\alpha\) is \[
    \operatorname{cf}(\alpha) = \text{least ordinal } \beta \text{ such that there exists } f: \beta \to \alpha \text{ with } \operatorname{ran}(f) \text{ cofinal in } \alpha.
\] We call such an \(f\) a cofinal map.




We can always assume that a cofinal map \(f: \operatorname{cf}(\alpha) \to \alpha\) is strictly increasing: if necessary, we can “thin it out”.







Lemma 13.1 
There exists a strictly increasing cofinal map \(g: \operatorname{cf}(\alpha) \to \alpha\).










NoteProof






Proof. Let \(f: \operatorname{cf}(\alpha) \to \alpha\) be cofinal. Define \(g\) by recursion: \[
    g(\eta) = \max\left\{ f(\eta), \; \sup\{g(\zeta)+1 \colon \zeta < \eta\} \right\}.
\] We have to check that \(g(\eta) < \alpha\). If \(\sup\{g(\zeta)+1 \colon \zeta < \eta\} = \alpha\), then \(g\mid_{\eta}\) would be a cofinal map from \(\eta < \operatorname{cf}(\alpha)\) into \({}\alpha\) (here we use that \({}\alpha\) is a limit), contradicting the minimality of \(\operatorname{cf}(\alpha)\). By construction, \(g\) is strictly increasing, and \(g(\eta) \geq f(\eta)\) implies that \(g\) is cofinal.











Example 13.1 


\(\operatorname{cf}(\omega) = \omega\)
\(\operatorname{cf}(\omega+\omega) = \omega\), via \(n \mapsto \omega + n\)
\(\operatorname{cf}(\omega\cdot\omega) = \omega\), via \(n \mapsto \omega \cdot n\)












Proposition 13.1 
For any limit ordinal \({}\alpha\),

\(\operatorname{cf}(\alpha) \leq \alpha\),
\(\operatorname{cf}(\alpha)\) is a cardinal,
\(\operatorname{cf}(\operatorname{cf}(\alpha)) = \operatorname{cf}(\alpha)\).











NoteProof






Proof. 

The identity map \(\alpha \to \alpha\) is cofinal.
Let \(\beta = \operatorname{cf}(\alpha)\) and suppose \(|\beta| < \beta\). Let \(h: |\beta| \to \beta\) be a bijection and \(f: \beta \to \alpha\) cofinal. Then \(f \circ h: |\beta| \to \alpha\) has the same range as \(f\) and hence is cofinal, contradicting the minimality of \({}\beta\).
By (1), \(\operatorname{cf}(\operatorname{cf}(\alpha)) \leq \operatorname{cf}(\alpha)\). For the other inequality, let \(f: \operatorname{cf}(\alpha) \to \alpha\) be strictly increasing and cofinal (Lemma 13.1), and let \(g: \delta \to \operatorname{cf}(\alpha)\) be cofinal. Then \(f \circ g: \delta \to \alpha\) is cofinal: given \(\gamma < \alpha\), pick \(\eta\) with \(f(\eta) > \gamma\), and \(\zeta < \delta\) with \(g(\zeta) > \eta\). Then \(f(g(\zeta)) > f(\eta) > \gamma\). Hence \(\delta \geq \operatorname{cf}(\alpha)\).

title: Cofinality and Inaccessible Cardinals
text:
Regular and singular cardinals
Recall the enumeration of all infinite cardinals by means of the \(\aleph\)-sequence:
\[\begin{equation*}
\aleph_0 = \omega, \quad \aleph_{\alpha+1} = \aleph_\alpha^+, \quad  \aleph_\lambda = \sup \{ \aleph_\xi \colon \xi<\lambda\} \; \text{ for limit } \lambda.
\end{equation*}\]
Here \(\kappa^+\) is the least cardinal \(> \kappa\). Some cardinals are limits of short sequences of smaller cardinals – for example, \[\begin{equation*}
    \aleph_\omega = \lim_n \aleph_n
\end{equation*}\] is uncountable, but a limit of a countable sequence of smaller cardinals.







Definition 13.3 
Let \({}\kappa\) be an infinite cardinal. \({}\kappa\) is

regular if \(\operatorname{cf}(\kappa) = \kappa\),
singular if \(\operatorname{cf}(\kappa) < \kappa\).





In other words, a regular cardinal \({}\kappa\) cannot be reached by less than \({}\kappa\)-many steps: \[\begin{equation*}
\operatorname{reg}(\kappa) \iff \forall \alpha < \kappa \;  \forall f \;( f: \alpha \to \kappa \;  \to \; \sup_{\xi < \alpha} f(\xi) < \kappa).
\end{equation*}\]







Example 13.2 


\(\aleph_0\) is regular.
\(\aleph_1\) is regular.
\(\aleph_\omega\) is singular, with \(\operatorname{cf}(\aleph_\omega) = \omega\), as witnessed by the cofinal sequence \(\aleph_0, \aleph_1, \aleph_2, \ldots \to \aleph_\omega\).





The regularity of \(\aleph_1\) is an instance of a general fact.







Proposition 13.2 
(\(\mathsf{AC}\)) Every infinite successor cardinal is regular.










NoteProof






Proof. Suppose \(\delta = \operatorname{cf}(\aleph_{\alpha+1}) < \aleph_{\alpha+1}\). Then there exists a cofinal \(f: \delta \to \aleph_{\alpha+1}\), so \[
    \aleph_{\alpha+1} = \bigcup_{\gamma < \delta} f(\gamma).
\] Now \(|\delta| < \aleph_{\alpha+1}\), and \(|f(\gamma)| < \aleph_{\alpha+1}\) for all \(\gamma < \delta\). Hence \(|\delta| \leq \aleph_\alpha\) and \(|f(\gamma)| \leq \aleph_\alpha\) for all \(\gamma < \delta\). This implies \[
    |\aleph_{\alpha+1}| = \left|\bigcup_{\gamma<\delta} f(\gamma)\right| \leq \aleph_\alpha \cdot \aleph_\alpha = \aleph_\alpha,
\] a consequence of Hessenberg’s Theorem (see the notes on Cardinals). This is a contradiction.




On the other hand, \[\begin{equation*}
\aleph_\omega,  \aleph_{\omega+\omega}, \aleph_{\aleph_{\omega}}, \aleph_{\aleph_{\aleph_\omega}}, \ldots
\end{equation*}\] are all singular. This follows from the following result, which reduces the cofinality of \(\aleph_\lambda\) to that of its index.







Proposition 13.3 
If \({}\lambda\) is a limit ordinal, then \(\operatorname{cf}(\aleph_\lambda) = \operatorname{cf}(\lambda)\).










NoteProof






Proof. (\(\leq\)) Let \(f: \gamma \to \lambda\) be cofinal. Then \[
\hat{f}: \gamma \to \aleph_\lambda, \quad \beta \mapsto \aleph_{f(\beta)}
\] is cofinal in \(\aleph_\lambda\): If \(\eta < \aleph_\lambda\), then \(\eta < \aleph_\xi\) for some \(\xi < \lambda\). Pick \(\beta\) with \(f(\beta) > \xi\). Then \(\aleph_{f(\beta)} > \aleph_\xi > \eta\).
(\(\geq\)) Let \(f: \gamma \to \aleph_\lambda\) be cofinal. We turn \(f\) into a cofinal map \(g: \gamma \to \lambda\) by letting \[
    g(\beta) = \text{the } \alpha \text{ such that } |f(\beta)| = \aleph_\alpha
\] (and \(g(\beta) = 0\) if \(f(\beta)\) is finite). Since \(f(\beta) < \aleph_\lambda\), \(g(\beta) < \lambda\). If \(\xi < \lambda\), pick \(\beta\) with \(f(\beta) > \aleph_\xi\). Then \(|f(\beta)| \geq \aleph_\xi\), so \(g(\beta) \geq \xi\). Hence \(g\) is cofinal in \({}\lambda\).




For example, \(\operatorname{cf}(\aleph_{\omega+\omega}) = \operatorname{cf}(\omega+\omega) = \omega\).

Cofinality of the continuum
Cofinality also puts a restriction on the possible values of \(2^\kappa\). To prove this, we need a fundamental inequality between cardinal sums and products. For a family of cardinals \((\kappa_i)_{i\in I}\), let \[
    \sum_{i \in I} \kappa_i = \left|\bigcup_{i \in I} \{i\} \times \kappa_i \right|, \qquad \prod_{i \in I} \kappa_i = \left| \left\{ g \colon g \text{ function}, \; \operatorname{dom}(g) = I, \; \forall i \; g(i) \in \kappa_i \right\}\right|.
\]







Theorem 13.1 (König’s Theorem) 
(\(\mathsf{AC}\)) Let \((\kappa_i)_{i\in I}\) and \((\lambda_i)_{i\in I}\) be families of cardinals such that \(\kappa_i < \lambda_i\) for all \(i \in I\). Then \[
    \sum_{i \in I} \kappa_i < \prod_{i\in I} \lambda_i.
\]










NoteProof






Proof. The map \((i,\xi) \mapsto g_{i,\xi}\), where \(g_{i,\xi}(i) = \xi+1\) and \(g_{i,\xi}(j) = 0\) for \(j \neq i\), is an injection, so \(\sum \kappa_i \leq \prod \lambda_i\).
Suppose \(f: \bigcup_{i} \{i\}\times \kappa_i \to \prod_i \lambda_i\). We show that \(f\) is not onto. For each \(i \in I\), the set \[
    \{ f(i,\xi)(i) \colon \xi < \kappa_i\} \subseteq \lambda_i
\] has cardinality \(\leq \kappa_i < \lambda_i\), so we can let \(y(i)\) be the least element of \(\lambda_i\) not in this set. Then \(y \in \prod_i \lambda_i\), but \(y \neq f(i,\xi)\) for all \(i, \xi\), since \(y\) and \(f(i,\xi)\) differ at coordinate \(i\).
(The Axiom of Choice is needed to ensure that the sets on both sides are well-orderable, so that their cardinalities are defined; for families of arbitrary sets, one uses \(\mathsf{AC}\) to choose the witnesses \(y(i)\).)











Proposition 13.4 
If \(\kappa \geq \aleph_0\), then \(\operatorname{cf}(2^\kappa) > \kappa\).










NoteProof






Proof. Suppose \(f: \delta \to 2^\kappa\) is cofinal with \(\delta \leq \kappa\), so that \[
    2^\kappa = \bigcup_{\gamma < \delta} f(\gamma).
\] Then \(|f(\gamma)| < 2^\kappa\) for all \(\gamma < \delta\), and by König’s Theorem, \[\begin{align*}
    2^\kappa = \left|\bigcup_{\gamma<\delta} f(\gamma)\right| & \leq \sum_{\gamma < \delta} |f(\gamma)| \\
    & < \prod_{\gamma < \delta} 2^\kappa = (2^\kappa)^\delta = 2^{\kappa \cdot \delta} = 2^\kappa,
\end{align*}\] where the last equality uses \(\delta \leq \kappa\). This is a contradiction.











Corollary 13.1 
\(2^{\aleph_0} \neq \aleph_\omega\).










NoteProof






Proof. \(\operatorname{cf}(2^{\aleph_0}) > \aleph_0 = \operatorname{cf}(\aleph_\omega)\).

title: Cofinality and Inaccessible Cardinals
text:
Inaccessible cardinals
We have seen that successor cardinals are regular, and that \(\aleph_\lambda\) for “small” limits \({}\lambda\) are singular. This suggests the question:






TipQuestion



Are there regular limit cardinals, i.e. regular cardinals of the form \(\aleph_\lambda\) with \(\lambda\) limit?


If \(\aleph_\lambda\) is a regular limit cardinal, then by Proposition 13.3 and Proposition 13.1, \[
    \aleph_\lambda = \operatorname{cf}(\aleph_\lambda) = \operatorname{cf}(\lambda) \leq \lambda,
\] and since always \(\lambda \leq \aleph_\lambda\), we must have \(\aleph_\lambda = \lambda\). So a regular limit cardinal must be very large: it is a fixed point of the \(\aleph\)-function.
This is captured by the notion of inaccessibility.







Definition 13.4 (Hausdorff 1908, Tarski, Zermelo 1930) 
An uncountable cardinal \(\kappa > \omega\) is

weakly inaccessible if \[\begin{align*}
  \operatorname{reg}(\kappa) \; &  \wedge \;  \exists \lambda (\operatorname{lim}(\lambda) \;  \wedge\;  \kappa = \aleph_\lambda)\\
                      (& \Leftrightarrow \operatorname{reg}(\kappa) \;  \wedge \;  \forall \alpha < \kappa \; \, \alpha^+ < \kappa)
\end{align*}\]
(strongly) inaccessible if \[\begin{equation*}
  \operatorname{reg}(\kappa) \;  \wedge \;  \forall \alpha < \kappa \;\; 2^{\alpha} < \kappa
\end{equation*}\]





Every strongly inaccessible cardinal is weakly inaccessible, since \(\alpha^+ \leq 2^\alpha\). Under the Generalized Continuum Hypothesis,
  \((\mathsf{GCH}) \quad \forall \alpha \;\;  2^{\aleph_\alpha} = \aleph_{\alpha}^+\)
weakly and strongly inaccessible cardinals coincide.
If \(\kappa\) is (weakly) inaccessible, then \(\kappa = \aleph_\kappa\), as shown above.

Inaccessibles and the von Neumann hierarchy
The cardinality of \(V_\alpha\) grows rather fast relative to \({}\alpha\). For example,
\[
    |V_{\omega+\alpha}| = \beth_\alpha
\]
where the beth function \(\beth_\alpha\) is defined as \[\begin{gather*}
    \beth_0 = \aleph_0 \\
    \beth_{\alpha+1} = 2^{\beth_\alpha} \\
    \beth_{\lambda} = \sup \{ \beth_\alpha \colon \alpha < \lambda\} \quad \text{ $\lambda$ limit}
\end{gather*}\]
The existence of inaccessible cardinals ensures that the von Neumann hierarchy is “long enough” for \({}\alpha\) to eventually “catch up” with the cardinality of \(V_\alpha\).







Proposition 13.5 
If \({}\kappa\) is strongly inaccessible, then \(|V_\kappa| = \kappa\).










NoteProof






Proof. Since \(\kappa \subseteq V_\kappa\), \(|V_\kappa| \geq \kappa\). For the other inequality, it suffices to show that \(|V_\alpha| < \kappa\) for all \(\alpha < \kappa\), since then \(|V_\kappa| = |\bigcup_{\alpha<\kappa} V_\alpha| \leq \kappa \cdot \kappa = \kappa\).
We show \(|V_\alpha| < \kappa\) by induction on \(\alpha < \kappa\): if \(|V_\alpha| < \kappa\), then \(|V_{\alpha+1}| = 2^{|V_\alpha|} < \kappa\) since \({}\kappa\) is strongly inaccessible. If \(\lambda < \kappa\) is a limit, then \(V_\lambda\) is a union of \(|\lambda| < \kappa\) many sets, each of size \(< \kappa\), so by regularity of \({}\kappa\), \(|V_\lambda| < \kappa\).




This in turn implies we can bound the cardinality of elements of \(V_\kappa\).







Proposition 13.6 
Suppose \({}\kappa\) is strongly inaccessible and \(x\subseteq V_\kappa\). Then
\[
    x \in V_\kappa \; \Leftrightarrow \; |x| < \kappa.
\]










NoteProof






Proof. (\(\Rightarrow\)) If \(x \in V_\kappa\), then \(x \in V_\alpha\) for some \(\alpha < \kappa\), and by transitivity \(x \subseteq V_\alpha\). By the proof of Proposition 13.5, \(|x| \leq |V_\alpha| < \kappa\).
(\(\Leftarrow\)) Since \(x \subseteq V_\kappa\), each \(y \in x\) has rank \(< \kappa\). Since \(|x| < \kappa\), by regularity of \({}\kappa\),
\[
    \operatorname{rank}(x) = \sup\{\operatorname{rank}(y)+1 \colon y \in x\} < \kappa
\]
which implies \(x \in V_\kappa\).




We have already seen that for limit \(\alpha > \omega\), \(V_\alpha\) is a model of all \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) axioms except Replacement.







Theorem 13.2 
If \({}\kappa\) is strongly inaccessible, then \(V_\kappa \models \mathsf{ZFC}\).










NoteProof






Proof. We verify that \(V_\kappa\) satisfies the axiom of Replacement. Suppose \(x \in V_\kappa\) and \(f:x \to V_\kappa\) is a function. Then \(f[x] \subseteq V_\kappa\), and by Proposition 13.6, \(|f[x]| \leq |x| < \kappa\). Applying the other direction of Proposition 13.6 to \(f[x]\), we obtain \(f[x] \in V_\kappa\), as desired.




Suppose an inaccessible cardinal exists, and let \({}\kappa\) be the least inaccessible.
It is not hard to verify that
\[
V_\kappa \models \mathsf{ZFC}+ \text{``there does not exist an inaccessible cardinal''}.
\]
(You verify that being an inaccessible cardinal is absolute for \(V_\kappa\).) Therefore, the existence of an inaccessible cardinal is not provable from \(\mathsf{ZFC}\). This fact also follows from Gödel’s second incompleteness theorem.

title: Incompleteness and Consistency Strength
text: Incompleteness and Consistency Strength

title: Incompleteness and Consistency Strength
section: The price of the foundational loop
text:
The price of the foundational loop
We asked of a foundational theory that it be strong enough to formalize its own metatheory. \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) meets this demand: formulas, proofs, and the axioms of \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) itself are finite syntactic objects, and \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) can represent and reason about them, just as it represents “\(2 + 8 = 10\)” by a formal shadow \(\ulcorner 2 \urcorner + \ulcorner 8 \urcorner = \ulcorner 10 \urcorner\).
Gödel’s incompleteness theorems show that this strength comes at a price. A theory that can talk about its own proofs cannot prove its own consistency. Rather than a defect, this turns out to be a measuring device: it lets us compare theories by how much consistency they can certify. Large cardinal axioms will serve as the scale.
Our guiding question:






TipQuestion



Can we prove that \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) + “there is an inaccessible cardinal” is consistent, assuming that \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) is consistent?


We already know that \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) does not prove the existence of an inaccessible cardinal (if \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) is consistent). The answer to the question above will be a much stronger no.

title: Incompleteness and Consistency Strength
text:
Gödel’s incompleteness theorems

Arithmetization
Throughout this section, \({}T\) is a first-order theory satisfying the following conditions.

\({}T\) is recursively axiomatized: there is an algorithm that decides whether a given formula is an axiom of \({}T\).
\({}T\) interprets enough arithmetic: the axioms of Robinson’s arithmetic \(\mathsf{Q}\) (a weak, finitely axiomatized fragment of Peano arithmetic \(\mathsf{PA}\)) are provable in \({}T\), possibly after translating the language of arithmetic into the language of \({}T\).

\(\mathsf{ZFC}\) satisfies both conditions. It has infinitely many axioms because of the Comprehension and Replacement schemes, but it is decidable whether a formula is an instance of one of them. Arithmetic is interpreted via \({}\omega\) with ordinal addition and multiplication.
The first step is to turn syntax into arithmetic. Fix an effective coding of symbols, formulas, and finite sequences of formulas by natural numbers. Write \(\ulcorner \varphi \urcorner\) for the code (Gödel number) of \({}\varphi\), and also for the numeral representing it in the language of arithmetic. Inside \(\mathsf{ZFC}\), one can just as well code syntax by hereditarily finite sets.
Since \({}T\) is recursively axiomatized, the relation
\[
    \operatorname{Prf}_T(p, x) \; :\iff \; p \text{ codes a $T$-proof of the formula coded by } x
\]
is decidable: one only needs to check that every step of the finite sequence coded by \(p\) is an axiom or follows from earlier steps by a rule of inference. Decidable relations can be expressed in arithmetic by formulas with only bounded quantifiers \(\forall y < t\), \(\exists y < t\) (more precisely, by formulas that \({}T\) proves equivalent to such formulas on all numerals). We call such formulas \(\Delta^0_0\). Note the analogy with the set-theoretic \(\Delta_0\) formulas from Models of Set Theory.
A formula is \(\Sigma^0_1\) if it has the form \(\exists y\, \theta\) with \(\theta\) in \(\Delta^0_0\), and \(\Pi^0_1\) if it has the form \(\forall y\, \theta\) with \(\theta\) in \(\Delta^0_0\).







Definition 14.1 
The provability predicate of \({}T\) is the \(\Sigma^0_1\) formula \[
    \operatorname{Prov}_T(x) \;:\equiv\; \exists p \; \operatorname{Prf}_T(p, x),
\] and the consistency statement of \({}T\) is the \(\Pi^0_1\) sentence \[
    \operatorname{Con}(T) \;:\equiv\; \neg\, \operatorname{Prov}_T(\ulcorner 0 = 1 \urcorner).
\]





\(\operatorname{Con}(T)\) is a sentence of arithmetic. It says “no natural number codes a \(T\)-proof of \(0 = 1\).” It is a statement about \(\mathbb{N}\) and nothing more, and it can be checked instance by instance: each single number either codes such a proof or it does not.

Observe the two levels at work. “\({}T\) is consistent” is a statement of the metatheory. \(\operatorname{Con}(T)\) is its formal shadow, a sentence that \({}T\) itself can attempt to prove.
The key bridge between true arithmetic facts and provability is the following.







Lemma 14.1 (\(\Sigma^0_1\)-completeness) 
If \({}\sigma\) is a \(\Sigma^0_1\) sentence that is true in \(\mathbb{N}\), then \(\mathsf{Q}\vdash \sigma\), and hence \(T \vdash \sigma\).




In particular, if \(T \vdash \varphi\), then the statement \(\operatorname{Prov}_T(\ulcorner \varphi \urcorner)\) is a true \(\Sigma^0_1\) sentence (a proof exists), so \(T \vdash \operatorname{Prov}_T(\ulcorner \varphi \urcorner)\).


The diagonal lemma
The second ingredient is a way to construct self-referential sentences.







Lemma 14.2 (Diagonal lemma) 
For every formula \(\psi(x)\) with one free variable, there is a sentence \({}\sigma\) such that \[
    T \vdash \sigma \leftrightarrow \psi(\ulcorner \sigma \urcorner).
\]







The first incompleteness theorem
Apply Lemma 14.2 to \(\psi(x) :\equiv \neg \operatorname{Prov}_T(x)\). We obtain a sentence \({}G\), the Gödel sentence of \({}T\), such that
\[
    T \vdash G \leftrightarrow \neg \operatorname{Prov}_T(\ulcorner G \urcorner).
\]
Informally, \({}G\) says “I am not provable in \({}T\).”







Theorem 14.1 (Gödel’s first incompleteness theorem) 
If \({}T\) is consistent, then \(T \nvdash G\). If \({}T\) is moreover \(\omega\)-consistent, then also \(T \nvdash \neg G\).










NoteProof






Proof. Suppose \(T \vdash G\). By \(\Sigma^0_1\)-completeness, \(T \vdash \operatorname{Prov}_T(\ulcorner G \urcorner)\). But from \(G\) and the defining property of \({}G\), also \(T \vdash \neg \operatorname{Prov}_T(\ulcorner G \urcorner)\). Hence \({}T\) is inconsistent.
Now suppose \(T \vdash \neg G\), so \(T \vdash \operatorname{Prov}_T(\ulcorner G \urcorner)\), that is, \(T \vdash \exists p\, \operatorname{Prf}_T(p, \ulcorner G \urcorner)\). By the first part, \(T \nvdash G\), so no number \(n\) codes a proof of \({}G\), and by \(\Sigma^0_1\)-completeness \(T \vdash \neg \operatorname{Prf}_T(\underline{n}, \ulcorner G \urcorner)\) for every \(n\). This is exactly what \(\omega\)-consistency rules out.




The assumption of \(\omega\)-consistency can be weakened to plain consistency by a cleverer choice of self-referential sentence (Rosser’s trick). We will not need this.







Corollary 14.1 
If \({}T\) is consistent, then \({}G\) is true in \(\mathbb{N}\) but not provable in \({}T\).










NoteProof






Proof. \({}G\) is equivalent to \(\neg \operatorname{Prov}_T(\ulcorner G \urcorner)\), which states exactly what Theorem 14.1 established.







The second incompleteness theorem
The proof of the first part of Theorem 14.1 was finitistic: it used nothing but elementary reasoning about finite syntactic objects. By the thesis that every finitistic argument can be formalized, \({}T\) should be able to carry it out internally. Making this precise is laborious, and the standard route goes through three properties of \(\operatorname{Prov}_T\), the Hilbert–Bernays–Löb derivability conditions. For all sentences \({}\varphi, \psi\):

(D1) If \(T \vdash \varphi\), then \(T \vdash \operatorname{Prov}_T(\ulcorner \varphi \urcorner)\).
(D2) \(T \vdash \operatorname{Prov}_T(\ulcorner \varphi\to \psi \urcorner) \to \big(\operatorname{Prov}_T(\ulcorner \varphi \urcorner) \to \operatorname{Prov}_T(\ulcorner \psi \urcorner)\big)\).
(D3) \(T \vdash \operatorname{Prov}_T(\ulcorner \varphi \urcorner) \to \operatorname{Prov}_T(\ulcorner \operatorname{Prov}_T(\ulcorner \varphi \urcorner) \urcorner)\).

(D1) is Lemma 14.1. (D2) formalizes modus ponens. (D3) is (D1) formalized inside \({}T\): it is a formalized version of \(\Sigma^0_1\)-completeness, and its verification is where the real work lies. We take (D1)–(D3) for granted.







Theorem 14.2 (Gödel’s second incompleteness theorem) 
If \({}T\) is consistent, then \(T \nvdash \operatorname{Con}(T)\).










NoteProof






Proof. We show \(T \vdash \operatorname{Con}(T) \to G\). Then \(T \vdash \operatorname{Con}(T)\) would imply \(T \vdash G\), contradicting Theorem 14.1.
Write \(P(\varphi)\) for \(\operatorname{Prov}_T(\ulcorner \varphi \urcorner)\). Since \(T \vdash G \to \neg P(G)\), (D1) and (D2) give \[
    T \vdash P(G) \to P(\neg P(G)).
\] By (D3), \(T \vdash P(G) \to P(P(G))\). Using (D1) and (D2) once more, applied to the tautology \(P(G) \to (\neg P(G) \to 0 = 1)\), we can combine the two: \[
    T \vdash P(G) \to P(0 = 1).
\] Contraposing, \(T \vdash \neg P(0=1) \to \neg P(G)\), that is, \(T \vdash \operatorname{Con}(T) \to \neg P(G)\). Since \(T \vdash \neg P(G) \to G\), we obtain \(T \vdash \operatorname{Con}(T) \to G\).




This settles Hilbert’s program in the negative: finitistic metamathematics can be formalized in \(\mathsf{ZFC}\), so if it could establish the consistency of \(\mathsf{ZFC}\), then \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) would prove \(\operatorname{Con}(\mathsf{ZFC})\).


Consistency and models
For set theory, the most useful form of \(\operatorname{Con}(\mathsf{ZFC})\) is semantic. In Models of Set Theory we used Gödel’s completeness theorem in the metatheory: if \(\mathsf{ZF}\) is consistent, then it has a model. Both the soundness and completeness theorems are themselves theorems of \(\mathsf{ZFC}\), when the satisfaction relation \(M \models \varphi\) for set-sized structures \(M\) is defined inside \(\mathsf{ZFC}\). This gives:







Proposition 14.1 
\[
    \mathsf{ZFC}\vdash \; \operatorname{Con}(\mathsf{ZFC}) \leftrightarrow \exists M\, (M \models \mathsf{ZFC}).
\]




Combining this with Theorem 14.2:







Corollary 14.2 
If \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) is consistent, then \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) does not prove that there exists a set model of \(\mathsf{ZFC}\). In particular, \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) does not prove the existence of a transitive model of \(\mathsf{ZFC}\), or of an ordinal \({}\alpha\) with \(V_\alpha \models \mathsf{ZFC}\).

title: Incompleteness and Consistency Strength
text:
Inaccessible cardinals and consistency
Let \(\mathsf{IC}\) denote the axiom “there exists a (strongly) inaccessible cardinal.” Recall from Large Cardinals that if \({}\kappa\) is inaccessible, then \(V_\kappa \models \mathsf{ZFC}\). With Proposition 14.1, this yields:







Proposition 14.2 
\[
    \mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{IC} \;\vdash\; \operatorname{Con}(\mathsf{ZFC}).
\]










NoteProof






Proof. Argue in \(\mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{IC}\). Let \({}\kappa\) be inaccessible. Then \(V_\kappa\) is a set and \(V_\kappa \models \mathsf{ZFC}\), so \(\operatorname{Con}(\mathsf{ZFC})\) holds by Proposition 14.1.











Corollary 14.3 
If \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) is consistent, then \(\mathsf{ZFC}\nvdash \mathsf{IC}\).










NoteProof






Proof. If \(\mathsf{ZFC}\vdash \mathsf{IC}\), then \(\mathsf{ZFC}\vdash \operatorname{Con}(\mathsf{ZFC})\) by Proposition 14.2, contradicting Theorem 14.2.




We had seen a second proof of Corollary 14.3 in Large Cardinals: if \({}\kappa\) is the least inaccessible, then \(V_\kappa \models \mathsf{ZFC}+ \neg\mathsf{IC}\), since being inaccessible is absolute for \(V_\kappa\). Formalized, this argument shows
\[
    \mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{IC} \;\vdash\; \operatorname{Con}(\mathsf{ZFC}+ \neg \mathsf{IC}).
\]
So the absoluteness argument tells us that \(\neg\mathsf{IC}\) is consistent relative to \(\mathsf{IC}\). The second incompleteness theorem tells us much more: we cannot even show that \(\mathsf{IC}\) is consistent relative to \(\mathsf{ZFC}\).







Theorem 14.3 
If \(\mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{IC}\) is consistent, then \[
    \mathsf{ZFC}\nvdash \; \operatorname{Con}(\mathsf{ZFC}) \to \operatorname{Con}(\mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{IC}).
\]










NoteProof






Proof. Suppose \(\mathsf{ZFC}\vdash \operatorname{Con}(\mathsf{ZFC}) \to \operatorname{Con}(\mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{IC})\). Then the same implication is provable in the stronger theory \(\mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{IC}\). By Proposition 14.2, \(\mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{IC} \vdash \operatorname{Con}(\mathsf{ZFC})\). Combining the two, \[
    \mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{IC} \;\vdash\; \operatorname{Con}(\mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{IC}),
\] and by Theorem 14.2, \(\mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{IC}\) is inconsistent.




In other words, the existence of an inaccessible cardinal is not merely unprovable in \(\mathsf{ZFC}\). It is a genuinely stronger assumption: accepting it commits us to new arithmetic truths, such as \(\operatorname{Con}(\mathsf{ZFC})\), that \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) cannot reach.

Two kinds of independence
Compare this with the Continuum Hypothesis. By Gödel’s constructible universe \({}L\) and Cohen’s method of forcing (which we will study later),
\[
    \operatorname{Con}(\mathsf{ZFC}) \iff \operatorname{Con}(\mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{CH}) \iff \operatorname{Con}(\mathsf{ZFC}+ \neg\mathsf{CH}),
\]
and these equivalences are provable in a weak base theory. So both \(\mathsf{CH}\) and \(\mathsf{IC}\) are independent of \(\mathsf{ZFC}\), but in different ways.

\(\mathsf{CH}\) is equiconsistent independent: adding \(\mathsf{CH}\) or its negation costs nothing in terms of consistency.
\(\mathsf{IC}\) is strength-increasing independent: adding it proves new \(\Pi^0_1\) sentences.

title: Incompleteness and Consistency Strength
text:
Consistency strength
The phenomenon of the previous section can be organized into an ordering of theories. We fix a weak base theory \({}B\), say \(\mathsf{PA}\), or \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) when we compare extensions of \(\mathsf{ZFC}\), and consider recursively axiomatized theories extending \({}B\).







Definition 14.2 (Consistency strength) 
Let \({}T\) and \({}S\) be theories. Define \[
    T \le_{\operatorname{Con}} S \;:\iff\; B \vdash \operatorname{Con}(S) \to \operatorname{Con}(T).
\] We say \({}T\) and \({}S\) are equiconsistent, \(T \equiv_{\operatorname{Con}} S\), if \(T \le_{\operatorname{Con}} S\) and \(S \le_{\operatorname{Con}} T\). We write \(T <_{\operatorname{Con}} S\) if \(T \le_{\operatorname{Con}} S\) and \(S \vdash \operatorname{Con}(T)\).




The relation \(\le_{\operatorname{Con}}\) is reflexive and transitive. The notation \(<_{\operatorname{Con}}\) is justified by the following generalization of Theorem 14.3.







Proposition 14.3 
Suppose \({}S\) is consistent and \(S \vdash \operatorname{Con}(T)\). Then \(S \not\le_{\operatorname{Con}} T\).










NoteProof






Proof. Suppose \(B \vdash \operatorname{Con}(T) \to \operatorname{Con}(S)\). Since \({}S\) extends \({}B\) and \(S \vdash \operatorname{Con}(T)\), we get \(S \vdash \operatorname{Con}(S)\), contradicting Theorem 14.2.











Example 14.1 
The following relations hold.








Relation
Method





\(\mathsf{ZF}\equiv_{\operatorname{Con}} \mathsf{ZFC}\equiv_{\operatorname{Con}} \mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{GCH}\)
the inner model \({}L\)
Gödel 1938


\(\mathsf{ZFC}\equiv_{\operatorname{Con}} \mathsf{ZFC}+ \neg\mathsf{CH}\)
forcing
Cohen 1963


\(\mathsf{PA} <_{\operatorname{Con}} \mathsf{ZFC}\)
\({}\omega\) is a model of \(\mathsf{PA}\)



\(\mathsf{ZFC}<_{\operatorname{Con}} \mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{IC}\)
\(V_\kappa \models \mathsf{ZFC}\)
Proposition 14.2


\(\mathsf{ZF}+ \mathsf{DC}+ \text{``every set of reals is Lebesgue measurable''} \equiv_{\operatorname{Con}} \mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{IC}\)
forcing / the inner model \({}L\)
Solovay 1970, Shelah 1984







The last line connects to the measure problem: in \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) there are non-measurable sets of reals, but if we drop full Choice and keep only Dependent Choice, “every set of reals is Lebesgue measurable” is consistent, at exactly the cost of an inaccessible cardinal.

Upper and lower bounds
How does one establish such equiconsistencies? There are two directions.

Upper bounds: build a model. To show \(T \le_{\operatorname{Con}} S\), one assumes a model of \({}S\) and builds from it a model of \({}T\). The models \(V_\kappa\) and forcing extensions are of this kind. Solovay’s half of the last example starts with an inaccessible and builds, by forcing, a model of \(\mathsf{ZF}+ \mathsf{DC}\) in which every set of reals is measurable.
Lower bounds: find the large cardinal in an inner model. To show \(S \le_{\operatorname{Con}} T\), one assumes \({}T\) and shows that some inner model, such as \({}L\), satisfies \({}S\). Shelah’s half of the example shows that if all (\(\Sigma^1_3\)) sets of reals are measurable, then \(\omega_1\) is an inaccessible cardinal in \({}L\).

A remarkable empirical fact: all “natural” theories studied so far line up linearly under \(\le_{\operatorname{Con}}\), and large cardinal axioms provide a scale against which they can be measured. There is no known explanation for this phenomenon, and one can construct artificial theories (using self-reference) that are incomparable.

title: Incompleteness and Consistency Strength
text:
Weakly compact cardinals
To see that the consistency hierarchy continues above inaccessibles, we return to the partition properties from Large Cardinals. Recall that \(\kappa \to (\lambda)^2_2\) means that every partition \(F : [\kappa]^2 \to \{0, 1\}\) has a homogeneous set of size \({}\lambda\), and that Ramsey’s theorem gives \(\aleph_0 \to (\aleph_0)^2_2\).







Definition 14.3 
An uncountable cardinal \({}\kappa\) is weakly compact if \(\kappa \to (\kappa)^2_2\).




Write \(\mathsf{WC}\) for the axiom “there exists a weakly compact cardinal.”

Weakly compact cardinals are inaccessible







Proposition 14.4 
Every weakly compact cardinal is regular.





For the strong limit property, we compare well-orders with the lexicographic order on \(2^\lambda\), the set of functions \(f: \lambda \to \{0, 1\}\): \[
    f <_{\mathop{\mathrm{lex}}} g \;:\iff\; f(\xi) < g(\xi), \text{ where $\xi$ is least with } f(\xi) \neq g(\xi).
\] This is a linear order. Its key property is that it contains no long well-ordered sequences.







Lemma 14.3 (Sierpiński) 
For every infinite cardinal \({}\lambda\), \((2^\lambda, <_{\mathop{\mathrm{lex}}})\) has no strictly increasing and no strictly decreasing sequence of length \(\lambda^+\).











Exercise 14.1 Prove Lemma 14.3.
Hint: Suppose \((f_\alpha)_{\alpha < \lambda^+}\) is strictly increasing. First let \(\gamma \leq \lambda\) be least such that the restrictions \(f_\alpha \mid_{\gamma}\) take \(\lambda^+\) many values, and pass to a subsequence to reduce to the case where all restrictions \(f_\alpha \mid_{\xi}\), \(\xi < \gamma\), take at most \({}\lambda\) values in total. Then let \(\xi_\alpha\) be least where \(f_\alpha\) and \(f_{\alpha+1}\) differ and show that \(\alpha \mapsto f_\alpha \mid_{\xi_\alpha}\) is injective.











Proposition 14.5 
Every weakly compact cardinal is inaccessible.









Weakly compact cardinals are strictly stronger
Weakly compact cardinals are much larger than the first inaccessible.









Proposition 14.6 
\[
    \mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{WC} \;\vdash\; \operatorname{Con}(\mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{IC}),
\] and hence, if \(\mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{WC}\) is consistent, \(\mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{IC} <_{\operatorname{Con}} \mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{WC}\).

title: Incompleteness and Consistency Strength
text:
The large cardinal hierarchy
We have climbed two rungs of a much longer ladder.
\[
\begin{align}
    \mathsf{ZFC}\;<_{\operatorname{Con}}\; \text{inaccessible} & \;<_{\operatorname{Con}}\; \text{weakly compact} \\
    & \;<_{\operatorname{Con}}\; \text{Ramsey} \;<_{\operatorname{Con}}\; \text{measurable} \;<_{\operatorname{Con}}\; \cdots
\end{align}
\]


The rungs are genuinely separated. For example, if \({}\kappa\) is measurable, then the set of weakly compact cardinals below \({}\kappa\) belongs to every normal ultrafilter on \({}\kappa\), so \({}\kappa\) is the \(\kappa\)-th weakly compact cardinal.
The ladder continues far beyond measurables, through strong, Woodin, and supercompact cardinals, all the way up to axioms that assert the existence of nontrivial elementary embeddings \(j : V_\lambda \to V_\lambda\).
There is a ceiling. Kunen’s inconsistency theorem shows, in \(\mathsf{ZFC}\), that there is no nontrivial elementary embedding \(j : V \to V\). Large cardinal axioms are therefore not arbitrary: the most naive strengthening is outright inconsistent.


What does it mean to accept a large cardinal?
Theorem 14.3 shows that the consistency of \(\mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{IC}\) can never be established on the basis of \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) alone. So why do set theorists regard large cardinal axioms as legitimate, or even as true? Several kinds of reasons are commonly offered.

Reflection and the iterative conception. The universe \(V\) is built in stages \(V_\alpha\), and it should be “too large” to be fully described from within. An inaccessible \({}\kappa\) is a stage \(V_\kappa\) that already looks like the whole universe as far as \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) can tell. Indescribable cardinals strengthen this: no property of a given complexity can distinguish \(V_\kappa\) from \(V\).
Fruitfulness and convergence. Large cardinals settle questions about sets of reals that \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) leaves open, and very different approaches lead to the same large cardinal hypotheses, as with the measurability example above.
Track record. Decades of intensive study have not produced a contradiction from the axioms below Kunen’s bound.

Whatever one makes of these, the incompleteness theorems give large cardinals a precise arithmetic meaning. Each rung of the ladder proves new \(\Pi^0_1\) theorems, namely the consistency of the rungs below it. In this sense, accepting a stronger large cardinal is a commitment about the natural numbers: that certain searches for contradictions will never succeed.

title: Incompleteness and Consistency Strength
text:
References

K. Kunen, The Foundations of Mathematics and Set Theory (2011): incompleteness, models of set theory, and inaccessible cardinals.
T. Jech, Set Theory (3rd millennium ed.): weakly compact and indescribable cardinals, and Sierpiński’s lemma.
A. Kanamori, The Higher Infinite: the large cardinal hierarchy and its history.
R. M. Solovay, “A model of set theory in which every set of reals is Lebesgue measurable,” Annals of Mathematics 92 (1970).
S. Shelah, “Can you take Solovay’s inaccessible away?” Israel Journal of Mathematics 48 (1984).
