title: Abstract Sets and Mappings
text:
Sets as a category
In \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) the primitive notion is membership: a set is determined by its elements, and everything else (pairs, functions, …) is coded by membership. In Lawvere’s approach the primitive notions are sets and mappings between them, together with composition of mappings. An abstract set has no internal structure beyond the fact that its elements can be told apart; everything we want to say about a set must be expressed through the mappings into and out of it. Even “element” becomes a derived notion: an element of \(A\) is a particular kind of mapping into \(A\).
crumbs: The View from Category Theory - Topoi

title: Abstract Sets and Mappings
text:
Categories







Definition 14.1 (Category (L–R, Definition 1.13)) A category \(\mathcal{C}\) has the following data:

Objects, denoted \(A, B, C, \dots\)
Arrows, denoted \(f, g, h, \dots\) (also called morphisms or maps).
To each arrow \(f\) is assigned an object \(\operatorname{dom}(f)\), its domain, and an object \(\operatorname{cod}(f)\), its codomain. If \(\operatorname{dom}(f) = A\) and \(\operatorname{cod}(f) = B\) we write \(f \colon A \to B\) or \(A \xrightarrow{\;f\;} B\).
Composition: to each pair \(f \colon A \to B\) and \(g \colon B \to C\) is assigned an arrow \(gf \colon A \to C\), called “the composite \(g\) following \(f\)” (also written \(g \circ f\)).
Identities: to each object \(A\) is assigned an arrow \(1_{A} \colon A \to A\), called “the identity on \(A\)”.

These data satisfy the axioms

Associativity: if \(A \xrightarrow{\;f\;} B \xrightarrow{\;g\;} C \xrightarrow{\;h\;} D\), then \(h(gf) = (hg)f\);
Identity: if \(f \colon A \to B\), then \(f = f\,1_{A}\) and \(f = 1_{B}\,f\).





Note that \(gf\) is only defined when the codomain of \(f\) is exactly the domain of \(g\). A diagram of objects and arrows is commutative if any two paths of arrows with the same start and end have equal composites; for example, the triangle formed by \(f \colon A \to B\), \(g \colon B \to C\) and \(m \colon A \to C\) commutes precisely when \(m = gf\).







Definition 14.2 (Isomorphism) Objects \(A\) and \(B\) of a category are isomorphic, written \(A \cong B\), if there are arrows \(f \colon A \to B\) and \(g \colon B \to A\) with \(gf = 1_{A}\) and \(fg = 1_{B}\). Such an \(f\) is an isomorphism.











Definition 14.3 (Terminal and initial objects) An object \(T\) of a category \(\mathcal{C}\) is terminal if for every object \(A\) of \(\mathcal{C}\) there is exactly one arrow \(A \to T\). An object \(I\) is initial if for every object \(A\) there is exactly one arrow \(I \to A\).











Remark 14.1. The book introduces “terminal” and “initial” only for the category of sets (see the axioms below), but the definitions make sense in any category, and that is how they are used in Exercise 14.6.
crumbs: The View from Category Theory - Topoi

title: Abstract Sets and Mappings
text:
The axioms of Chapter 1
We write \(\mathcal{S}\) for the category of abstract sets and (arbitrary) mappings.






NoteAxiom: \(\mathcal{S}\) is a category



Abstract sets and mappings form a category, whose objects are called sets and whose arrows are called mappings.








NoteAxiom: Terminal set



There is a set \(\mathbf{1}\) such that for any set \(A\) there is exactly one mapping \(A \to \mathbf{1}\).


The book gives this unique mapping the same name \(A\) as its domain; to avoid confusion we write it \(!_{A} \colon A \to \mathbf{1}\). In a given discussion \(\mathbf{1}\) denotes a chosen terminal set (by Exercise 14.5 (b) the choice makes no difference).







Definition 14.4 (Element (L–R, Definition 1.3)) An element of a set \(A\) is any mapping whose codomain is \(A\) and whose domain is \(\mathbf{1}\), i.e. any \(a \colon \mathbf{1}\to A\).




Thus element is a special case of mapping, and evaluation is a special case of composition: if \(f \colon A \to B\) and \(a \colon \mathbf{1}\to A\), then \(fa \colon \mathbf{1}\to B\) is an element of \(B\), and we define the value of \(f\) at \(a\) by \(f(a) := fa\). Associativity then gives \((gf)(a) = g(f(a))\).







Definition 14.5 (Generalized element (L–R, §1.6)) A generalized element of \(A\) (or variable element of \(A\) varying over \(T\)) is an arbitrary mapping \(x \colon T \to A\) with codomain \(A\); its domain \(T\) need not be \(\mathbf{1}\).











Definition 14.6 (Separator (L–R, Definition 1.14)) An object \(S\) in a category \(\mathcal{C}\) is a separator if and only if whenever \(f_1, f_2 \colon X \to Y\) are arrows of \(\mathcal{C}\) with the same domain and the same codomain, then \[
\bigl(\forall x\, [\, x \colon S \to X \;\Rightarrow\; f_1 x = f_2 x \,]\bigr)
\;\Longrightarrow\; f_1 = f_2 .
\]










NoteAxiom: The terminal object \(\mathbf{1}\) separates mappings in \(\mathcal{S}\)



A one-element set \(\mathbf{1}\) is a separator in \(\mathcal{S}\); that is, if \(f_1, f_2 \colon X \to Y\), then \[
\bigl(\forall x\, [\, x \colon \mathbf{1}\to X \;\Rightarrow\; f_1 x = f_2 x \,]\bigr)
\;\Longrightarrow\; f_1 = f_2 .
\]


In words: two mappings with the same domain and codomain that have the same value at every element are equal. Contrapositively, if \(f_1 \neq f_2\) there is an element \(x\) of \(X\) with \(f_1(x) \neq f_2(x)\).






NoteAxiom: Initial set



There is a set \(\mathbf{0}\) such that for any set \(A\) there is exactly one mapping \(\mathbf{0}\to A\).








NoteAxiom: Nondegeneracy of \(\mathcal{S}\)



\[
\mathbf{0}\not\cong \mathbf{1}.
\]









Definition 14.7 (Coseparator (L–R, Definition 1.19)) An object \(V\) of a category \(\mathcal{C}\) is a coseparator if for any \(A\) and any parallel pair \(a_0, a_1 \colon T \to A\) (of generalized elements of \(A\)), \[
\bigl(\forall \varphi\, [\, \varphi \colon A \to V \;\Rightarrow\;
\varphi a_0 = \varphi a_1 \,]\bigr)
\;\Longrightarrow\; a_0 = a_1 .
\] Equivalently: if \(a_0 \neq a_1\), then there is some \(\varphi \colon A \to V\) with \(\varphi a_0 \neq \varphi a_1\). We say that \(V\) can discriminate elements if this condition holds for \(T = \mathbf{1}\).




A mapping \(\varphi \colon A \to V\) is thought of as a (\(V\)-valued) property of the elements of \(A\), so a coseparator is an object of values with enough properties to tell elements apart.







Remark 14.2 (The set \(\mathbf{2}\) (L–R, §1.7)). The book provisionally assumes a set \(\mathbf{2}\) with exactly two elements \(0, 1 \colon \mathbf{1}\to \mathbf{2}\) (made precise by the axioms of Chapter 2) and claims (Claim 1.21) that \(\mathbf{2}\) is a coseparator in \(\mathcal{S}\). None of the exercises below depend on this.

title: Abstract Sets and Mappings
text:
Exercises
Two consequences of the axioms Terminal set and Initial set are used again and again below:






TipA recurring observation



The only mapping \(\mathbf{1}\to \mathbf{1}\) is \(1_{\mathbf{1}}\), and the only mapping \(\mathbf{0}\to \mathbf{0}\) is \(1_{\mathbf{0}}\). More generally, any two arrows into a terminal object with the same domain are equal, and any two arrows out of an initial object with the same codomain are equal.



Separators







Exercise 14.1 (L–R 1.15) In the category of abstract sets \(\mathcal{S}\), any set \(A\) with at least one element \(x_0 \colon \mathbf{1}\to A\) is also a separator.










TipSolution





Let \(f_1, f_2 \colon X \to Y\) and suppose that \(f_1 a = f_2 a\) for every \(a \colon A \to X\). We must show \(f_1 = f_2\). Since \(\mathbf{1}\) is a separator (axiom), it suffices to show \(f_1 x = f_2 x\) for every element \(x \colon \mathbf{1}\to X\).
So fix \(x \colon \mathbf{1}\to X\) and consider the generalized element \[
a := x\,!_{A} \colon A \xrightarrow{\;!_{A}\;} \mathbf{1}\xrightarrow{\;x\;} X ,
\] the constant map with value \(x\). By hypothesis \(f_1 a = f_2 a\), i.e. \(f_1 (x\,!_{A}) = f_2 (x\,!_{A})\). Composing on the right with the given element \(x_0 \colon \mathbf{1}\to A\) and using associativity, \[
f_1\, x\, (!_{A}\, x_0) \;=\; f_2\, x\, (!_{A}\, x_0).
\] Now \(!_{A} x_0 \colon \mathbf{1}\to \mathbf{1}\), and the only mapping \(\mathbf{1}\to \mathbf{1}\) is \(1_{\mathbf{1}}\). Hence \(!_{A} x_0 = 1_{\mathbf{1}}\), and by the identity law \(f_1 x = f_2 x\). As \(x\) was arbitrary, \(f_1 = f_2\).









NoteRemarks





The key idea is to turn an element \(x\) of \(X\) into a generalized element \(A \to X\) by making it constant, and then to recover \(x\) by evaluating at the element \(x_0\) of \(A\). Without \(x_0\) we could not cancel \(!_{A}\), and Exercise 14.2 shows that the hypothesis cannot be dropped.










Exercise 14.2 (L–R 1.16) In the category of abstract sets \(\mathcal{S}\) the initial set \(\mathbf{0}\) is not a separator. (Assume that two sets \(A\) and \(B\) exist with at least two maps \(A \to B\).)










TipSolution





By assumption there are \(f_1, f_2 \colon A \to B\) with \(f_1 \neq f_2\). For \(\mathbf{0}\) to be a separator we would need: if \(f_1 x = f_2 x\) for every \(x \colon \mathbf{0}\to A\), then \(f_1 = f_2\). But for any \(x \colon \mathbf{0}\to A\), both \(f_1 x\) and \(f_2 x\) are mappings \(\mathbf{0}\to B\), and by the axiom Initial set there is exactly one such mapping. Hence \(f_1 x = f_2 x\) for all \(x \colon \mathbf{0}\to A\), while \(f_1 \neq f_2\). So \(\mathbf{0}\) is not a separator.









NoteRemarks





Why is the extra assumption needed? The axioms of Chapter 1 alone do not guarantee two distinct parallel mappings. Consider the category with two objects \(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{1}\) and only three arrows: \(1_{\mathbf{0}}\), \(1_{\mathbf{1}}\), and one arrow \(u \colon \mathbf{0}\to \mathbf{1}\) (composition is forced). In it \(\mathbf{1}\) is terminal, \(\mathbf{0}\) is initial, every hom-set has at most one element (so every object, including \(\mathbf{0}\), is a separator, and in particular \(\mathbf{1}\) separates), and \(\mathbf{0}\not\cong \mathbf{1}\) because there is no arrow \(\mathbf{1}\to \mathbf{0}\). So all the axioms of Chapter 1 hold, yet \(\mathbf{0}\) is a separator. This is a first example of a model of a fragment of the categorical axioms, much like the small models of fragments of \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) we studied earlier.
Once the set \(\mathbf{2}\) with elements \(0 \neq 1 \colon \mathbf{1}\to \mathbf{2}\) is available (Chapter 2), one can take \(A = \mathbf{1}\), \(B = \mathbf{2}\).
Compare with Exercise 14.1: \(\mathbf{0}\) fails precisely because it has no elements (Exercise 14.3).





The empty set







Exercise 14.3 (L–R 1.18) How many mappings are there from \(\mathbf{0}\) to \(\mathbf{1}\)? From \(\mathbf{0}\) to \(\mathbf{0}\)? From \(\mathbf{1}\) to \(\mathbf{0}\)? (And so how many elements does \(\mathbf{0}\) have?)
Hint: To answer the third question requires more axioms than do the other two.










TipSolution





From \(\mathbf{0}\) to \(\mathbf{1}\): exactly one. This follows from Initial set (with \(A = \mathbf{1}\)), and equally from Terminal set (with \(A = \mathbf{0}\)). Call it \(u \colon \mathbf{0}\to \mathbf{1}\).
From \(\mathbf{0}\) to \(\mathbf{0}\): exactly one, by Initial set with \(A = \mathbf{0}\). Since \(1_{\mathbf{0}}\) is such a mapping, it is \(1_{\mathbf{0}}\).
From \(\mathbf{1}\) to \(\mathbf{0}\): none. Suppose, for a contradiction, that \(x \colon \mathbf{1}\to \mathbf{0}\). Then

\(u x \colon \mathbf{1}\to \mathbf{1}\), so \(u x = 1_{\mathbf{1}}\) (Terminal set);
\(x u \colon \mathbf{0}\to \mathbf{0}\), so \(x u = 1_{\mathbf{0}}\) (Initial set).

Thus \(x\) and \(u\) are mutually inverse and \(\mathbf{0}\cong \mathbf{1}\), contradicting Nondegeneracy. Hence there is no mapping \(\mathbf{1}\to \mathbf{0}\).
Since elements of \(\mathbf{0}\) are by definition mappings \(\mathbf{1}\to \mathbf{0}\), \(\mathbf{0}\) has no elements: it is an empty set, which justifies the name.









NoteRemarks






The first two answers use one axiom each; the third uses Terminal set, Initial set, and Nondegeneracy.
The argument shows that, given the other axioms, Nondegeneracy is equivalent to the apparently stronger statement “there is no mapping \(\mathbf{1}\to \mathbf{0}\)”. The converse is immediate: an isomorphism \(\mathbf{0}\cong \mathbf{1}\) includes a mapping \(\mathbf{1}\to \mathbf{0}\).
Extension. If there is any mapping \(h \colon A \to \mathbf{0}\), then \(A \cong \mathbf{0}\). With \(e \colon \mathbf{0}\to A\) the unique map, \(he = 1_{\mathbf{0}}\) by initiality. For \(eh = 1_{A}\) one needs one more axiom: \(A\) has no elements (an element \(a\) would give an element \(ha\) of \(\mathbf{0}\)), so \(eh\) and \(1_{A}\) agree at every element vacuously, and they are equal because \(\mathbf{1}\) separates mappings.
Contrast with \(\mathsf{ZFC}\): there, \(\emptyset\) has no elements by definition, and is unique by Extensionality. Here, the emptiness of \(\mathbf{0}\) is a theorem about mappings, derived from a property (initiality) that does not mention elements at all.






Coseparators







Exercise 14.4 (L–R 1.20) Use the fact that \(\mathbf{1}\) is a separator in the category of abstract sets to show that (in that category), if \(V\) can discriminate elements, then it can discriminate generalized elements. Thus, in \(\mathcal{S}\) the general \(T\) in Definition 14.7 could safely be replaced by \(T = \mathbf{1}\).










TipSolution





Assume \(V\) discriminates elements: for every set \(A\) and all \(b_0, b_1 \colon \mathbf{1}\to A\), \[
\bigl(\forall \varphi \colon A \to V,\ \varphi b_0 = \varphi b_1\bigr)
\;\Longrightarrow\; b_0 = b_1 . \tag{*}
\] Let \(a_0, a_1 \colon T \to A\) be generalized elements such that \(\varphi a_0 = \varphi a_1\) for every \(\varphi \colon A \to V\). We show \(a_0 = a_1\). Because \(\mathbf{1}\) separates mappings, it suffices to show \(a_0 t = a_1 t\) for every element \(t \colon \mathbf{1}\to T\).
Fix \(t \colon \mathbf{1}\to T\). Then \(a_0 t\) and \(a_1 t\) are elements of \(A\), and for every \(\varphi \colon A \to V\), by associativity, \[
\varphi (a_0 t) = (\varphi a_0) t = (\varphi a_1) t = \varphi (a_1 t).
\] By \((*)\), \(a_0 t = a_1 t\). Since \(t\) was arbitrary, \(a_0 = a_1\).
The converse (discriminating generalized elements implies discriminating elements) is trivial, since elements are generalized elements with \(T = \mathbf{1}\). So in \(\mathcal{S}\) the two conditions are equivalent.









NoteRemarks






Before starting, write out exactly what must be shown: there are two layers of quantifiers (over \(t\) and over \(\varphi\)). Note that \((*)\) cannot be applied directly to \(a_0, a_1\), which are not elements.
Associativity does all the work: “evaluate first, then apply \(\varphi\)” equals “apply \(\varphi\), then evaluate”.
This is the dual of the role of the separator: \(\mathbf{1}\) lets us reduce statements about generalized elements to statements about ordinary elements. In categories where \(\mathbf{1}\) is not a separator (e.g. groups or vector spaces, see Exercise 14.6) the reduction fails, which is why Definition 14.7 is stated for general \(T\).






Uniqueness properties







Exercise 14.5 (L–R 1.28)  

Show that identity arrows in a category are unique, i.e. if \(1_{A} \colon A \to A\) and \(1_{A}' \colon A \to A\) both satisfy the equations for identity arrows, then \(1_{A} = 1_{A}'\).
Show that the set \(\mathbf{1}\) is unique “up to unique isomorphism”, i.e. if \(\mathbf{1}'\) also satisfies the axiom of the terminal set, then there are unique mappings \(f \colon \mathbf{1}\to \mathbf{1}'\) and \(g \colon \mathbf{1}' \to \mathbf{1}\), and that \(gf = 1_{\mathbf{1}}\) and \(fg = 1_{\mathbf{1}'}\).
Similarly, show that the empty set \(\mathbf{0}\) is unique up to unique isomorphism.











TipSolution





(a) The identity equations say: \(h\,1_{A} = h\) for every \(h \colon A \to B\), and \(1_{A}\,k = k\) for every \(k \colon C \to A\); likewise for \(1_{A}'\). Consider the composite \(1_{A}\,1_{A}'\). Using that \(1_{A}'\) is a right identity, with \(h = 1_{A}\), we get \(1_{A}\,1_{A}' = 1_{A}\). Using that \(1_{A}\) is a left identity, with \(k = 1_{A}'\), we get \(1_{A}\,1_{A}' = 1_{A}'\). Hence \[
1_{A} = 1_{A}\,1_{A}' = 1_{A}' .
\]
(b) Since \(\mathbf{1}'\) satisfies the terminal set axiom, there is exactly one mapping \(f \colon \mathbf{1}\to \mathbf{1}'\); since \(\mathbf{1}\) does, there is exactly one mapping \(g \colon \mathbf{1}' \to \mathbf{1}\). Now \(gf \colon \mathbf{1}\to \mathbf{1}\), and the only mapping \(\mathbf{1}\to \mathbf{1}\) is \(1_{\mathbf{1}}\); so \(gf = 1_{\mathbf{1}}\). Symmetrically, \(fg \colon \mathbf{1}' \to \mathbf{1}'\) and the only such mapping is \(1_{\mathbf{1}'}\), so \(fg = 1_{\mathbf{1}'}\). Thus \(\mathbf{1}\cong \mathbf{1}'\). The isomorphism is unique: any isomorphism \(\mathbf{1}\to \mathbf{1}'\) is in particular a mapping \(\mathbf{1}\to \mathbf{1}'\), hence equals \(f\).
(c) Dually, let \(\mathbf{0}'\) also satisfy the initial set axiom. There is exactly one \(f \colon \mathbf{0}\to \mathbf{0}'\) (initiality of \(\mathbf{0}\)) and exactly one \(g \colon \mathbf{0}' \to \mathbf{0}\) (initiality of \(\mathbf{0}'\)). Then \(gf \colon \mathbf{0}\to \mathbf{0}\) must equal \(1_{\mathbf{0}}\), the only mapping \(\mathbf{0}\to \mathbf{0}\), and \(fg \colon \mathbf{0}' \to \mathbf{0}'\) must equal \(1_{\mathbf{0}'}\). So \(f\) is an isomorphism, and it is the only one, since it is the only mapping \(\mathbf{0}\to \mathbf{0}'\) at all.









NoteRemarks






The proofs use nothing specific to \(\mathcal{S}\): in any category, identities are unique and terminal (initial) objects are unique up to unique isomorphism. This is what justifies speaking of “the” terminal set: any statement about it is insensitive to which terminal set was chosen.
In (a), only “\(1_{A}'\) is a right identity” and “\(1_{A}\) is a left identity” are used, exactly as for identity elements of a monoid.
In (b), both composites must be checked; one-sided inverses do not make an isomorphism.
Compare with \(\mathsf{ZFC}\): \(\emptyset\) is literally unique by Extensionality, while \(\{\emptyset\}\), \(\{\{\emptyset\}\}\), and \(\{7\}\) are all different one-element sets. In the categorical approach these are indistinguishable: the theory only ever pins objects down up to (unique) isomorphism.






Categories of structures







Exercise 14.6 (L–R 1.30)  

Show that (finite-dimensional) vector spaces as objects and linear transformations as arrows form a category with composition of arrows defined by composition of mappings. Show that a one-dimensional space \(S\) is a separator; is it a coseparator? Is the terminal object a separator?
Show that groups as objects and group homomorphisms as arrows form a category with composition of arrows defined by composition of mappings. Show that the additive group of integers is a separator.
Show that partially ordered sets as objects and monotone (= order-preserving) mappings as arrows form a category with composition of arrows defined by composition of mappings. Is the terminal object a separator in this category? Is there a coseparator?
A finite state machine with two inputs \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) is a finite set \(Q\) of “states” and a pair of endomaps \(\alpha, \beta \colon Q \to Q\) that effect the elementary state transitions of which the machine is capable. Given another such machine with state set \(Q'\), a homomorphism is a mapping \(\varphi \colon Q \to Q'\) of state sets preserving the transitions in the sense that \[
\varphi\alpha = \alpha'\varphi \qquad\text{and}\qquad
\varphi\beta = \beta'\varphi ,
\] where \(\alpha', \beta' \colon Q' \to Q'\) denote the corresponding state transitions of the second machine. Define composition of homomorphisms and show that a category results.





In parts (a)–(c), “separator”, “coseparator” and “terminal object” are meant in the sense of Definition 14.6, Definition 14.7 and Definition 14.3, applied to the category at hand. In particular, the “elements” \(x \colon S \to X\) that a separator \(S\) uses to test arrows are arrows of that category (linear maps, homomorphisms, monotone maps), not arbitrary functions.






TipSolution: a remark common to (a)–(d)





In each case the arrows are certain mappings between underlying sets, composition is composition of mappings, and the identity arrow on an object is the identity mapping of its underlying set. Therefore, once we know that

the identity mapping is an arrow, and
the composite of two arrows is again an arrow,

the associativity and identity laws hold automatically, because they hold for mappings in \(\mathcal{S}\). So in each part the only real work in “show that a category results” is checking (i) and (ii). Strictly speaking an arrow should be recorded as the triple (domain, codomain, underlying mapping), since the same function can be an arrow between different structures on the same underlying sets; nothing below depends on this.









TipSolution to (a): vector spaces





Fix a field \(k\) and consider finite-dimensional vector spaces over \(k\) with linear maps.
Category. The identity map is linear. If \(f \colon U \to V\) and \(g \colon V \to W\) are linear then \(gf(\lambda u + \mu u') = g(\lambda f u + \mu f u') = \lambda\, gf u + \mu\, gf u'\), so \(gf\) is linear.
A one-dimensional space \(S\) is a separator. Fix a nonzero \(s \in S\), so \(S = \{\lambda s : \lambda \in k\}\). For every vector \(v\) in a space \(X\) the map \(x_v \colon S \to X\), \(x_v(\lambda s) = \lambda v\), is linear, and \(x_v(s) = v\). Now suppose \(f_1, f_2 \colon X \to Y\) satisfy \(f_1 x = f_2 x\) for all linear \(x \colon S \to X\). Then for every \(v \in X\), \[
f_1(v) = f_1 x_v (s) = f_2 x_v (s) = f_2(v),
\] so \(f_1 = f_2\). (In fact linear maps \(S \to X\) correspond bijectively to vectors of \(X\) via \(x \mapsto x(s)\); this is the sense in which \(S\) plays the role of \(\mathbf{1}\).)
\(S\) is also a coseparator. Let \(a_0, a_1 \colon T \to A\) be linear with \(a_0 \neq a_1\). Then there is \(t \in T\) with \(w := a_0(t) - a_1(t) \neq 0\). Extend \(\{w\}\) to a basis \(\{w, e_2, \dots, e_n\}\) of \(A\) and let \(\varphi \colon A \to S\) be the linear map with \(\varphi(w) = s\) and \(\varphi(e_i) = 0\). Then \[
\varphi a_0 (t) - \varphi a_1 (t) = \varphi(w) = s \neq 0,
\] so \(\varphi a_0 \neq \varphi a_1\). (We had to use generalized elements \(T \to A\) here, because maps out of the terminal object carry no information in this category; see the next point.)
The terminal object is not a separator. The zero space \(\{0\}\) is terminal: from any \(X\) there is exactly one linear map to it, the zero map. It is also initial: the only linear map \(\{0\} \to X\) sends \(0 \mapsto 0\). So for any \(f_1, f_2 \colon X \to Y\) and any \(x \colon \{0\} \to X\), both \(f_1 x\) and \(f_2 x\) are the unique map \(\{0\} \to Y\), hence equal. Taking \(f_1 = 1_{S}\) and \(f_2 = 0\) (distinct, since \(s \neq 0\)) shows that \(\{0\}\) does not separate.









TipSolution to (b): groups





Category. The identity map is a homomorphism. If \(f \colon G \to H\) and \(g \colon H \to K\) are homomorphisms then \(gf(xy) = g(f(x)f(y)) = gf(x)\, gf(y)\).
\((\mathbb{Z}, +)\) is a separator. For each element \(x\) of a group \(X\) the map \(h_x \colon \mathbb{Z}\to X\), \(h_x(n) = x^n\), is a homomorphism (since \(x^{m+n} = x^m x^n\)) with \(h_x(1) = x\). If \(f_1, f_2 \colon X \to Y\) satisfy \(f_1 h = f_2 h\) for every homomorphism \(h \colon \mathbb{Z}\to X\), then for every \(x \in X\), \[
f_1(x) = f_1 h_x(1) = f_2 h_x(1) = f_2(x),
\] so \(f_1 = f_2\). (As in (a), homomorphisms \(\mathbb{Z}\to X\) correspond bijectively to elements of \(X\), because \(\mathbb{Z}\) is the free group on one generator.)









TipSolution to (c): partially ordered sets





Category. The identity is monotone. If \(f, g\) are monotone and \(x \le y\) then \(f(x) \le f(y)\), hence \(g f(x) \le g f(y)\).
The terminal object is a separator. The one-element poset \(\mathbf{1}= \{\ast\}\) is terminal (the constant map \(X \to \mathbf{1}\) is monotone and is the only map). Every function \(\mathbf{1}\to X\) is monotone, so monotone maps \(\mathbf{1}\to X\) correspond exactly to points of \(X\). If \(f_1 x = f_2 x\) for all \(x \colon \mathbf{1}\to X\), then \(f_1\) and \(f_2\) agree at every point, so they are equal as functions, hence as arrows. So, unlike (a) and (b), \(\mathbf{1}\) is a separator here.
There is a coseparator: the two-element chain \(\mathbf{2}= \{0 < 1\}\). Let \(a_0, a_1 \colon T \to A\) be monotone with \(a_0 \neq a_1\); pick \(t\) with \(p := a_0(t) \neq q := a_1(t)\). By antisymmetry, \(p \not\le q\) or \(q \not\le p\); say \(p \not\le q\) (otherwise swap the roles of \(p\) and \(q\)). Define \(\varphi \colon A \to \mathbf{2}\) by \[
\varphi(z) =
\begin{cases}
  1 & \text{if } p \le z,\\
  0 & \text{otherwise,}
\end{cases}
\] the indicator of the up-set \({\uparrow}p\). It is monotone: if \(z \le z'\) and \(\varphi(z) = 1\) then \(p \le z \le z'\), so \(\varphi(z') = 1\). And \(\varphi(p) = 1 \neq 0 = \varphi(q)\) since \(p \not\le q\). Hence \(\varphi a_0 (t) \neq \varphi a_1 (t)\), so \(\varphi a_0 \neq \varphi a_1\).









TipSolution to (d): finite state machines





Objects are triples \((Q, \alpha, \beta)\) with \(\alpha, \beta \colon Q \to Q\); an arrow \((Q, \alpha, \beta) \to (Q', \alpha', \beta')\) is a mapping \(\varphi \colon Q \to Q'\) with \(\varphi\alpha = \alpha'\varphi\) and \(\varphi\beta = \beta'\varphi\).
Composition is composition of the underlying mappings: given \(\varphi \colon (Q, \alpha, \beta) \to (Q', \alpha', \beta')\) and \(\psi \colon (Q', \alpha', \beta') \to (Q'', \alpha'', \beta'')\), set \(\psi \circ \varphi := \psi\varphi\). It is a homomorphism, by associativity in \(\mathcal{S}\): \[
(\psi\varphi)\alpha = \psi(\varphi\alpha) = \psi(\alpha'\varphi)
= (\psi\alpha')\varphi = (\alpha''\psi)\varphi = \alpha''(\psi\varphi),
\] and the same computation with \(\beta\) in place of \(\alpha\).
Identities: \(1_{Q}\) is a homomorphism \((Q, \alpha, \beta) \to (Q, \alpha, \beta)\), since \(1_{Q}\alpha = \alpha = \alpha\,1_{Q}\), and likewise for \(\beta\).
By the common remark above, associativity and the identity laws are inherited from \(\mathcal{S}\), so machines and their homomorphisms form a category.









NoteRemarks






Terminal = initial. In vector spaces (and in groups) the zero space (trivial group) is both terminal and initial. So in these categories \(\mathbf{0}\cong \mathbf{1}\): the Nondegeneracy axiom fails. This is a good way to see why Nondegeneracy is a genuine axiom and not a triviality.
Separators replace \(\mathbf{1}\). In (a) and (b) the terminal object sees nothing, and a different object (\(k\), respectively \(\mathbb{Z}\)) does the job of “detecting elements”. In each case that object is the free structure on one generator, so maps out of it are the same as elements of the underlying set.
Groups have no coseparator. If \(C\) were one, take a simple group \(G\) of cardinality larger than \(C\) (alternating groups \(A_n\), \(n \ge 5\), give arbitrarily large finite examples). The kernel of any homomorphism \(\varphi \colon G \to C\) is normal, hence trivial or all of \(G\); it cannot be trivial for cardinality reasons, so \(\varphi\) is trivial. Then no \(\varphi\) distinguishes two different elements of \(G\) (viewed as homomorphisms \(\mathbb{Z}\to G\)).
The order on the value object matters. The discrete two-element poset (no order relations between its two points) is not a coseparator in posets: monotone maps into it are constant on connected components, so for instance the two elements of the chain \(\mathbf{2}\) cannot be told apart by maps into it.
Finite dimension is only used in (a) for the easy extension of \(\{w\}\) to a basis; with the Axiom of Choice the same argument works for all vector spaces.
Machines preview a later theme of the book (Chapter 10): many categories of structures are categories of “sets with endomaps”. The terminal machine has one state with \(\alpha = \beta = \mathrm{id}\), so elements \(\mathbf{1}\to (Q, \alpha, \beta)\) are exactly the states fixed by both \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\). Hence \(\mathbf{1}\) is not a separator: for \(Q = \{0, 1\}\) with \(\alpha = \beta\) both equal to the swap there are no maps from \(\mathbf{1}\) at all, but \(1_{Q}\) and the swap are two distinct homomorphisms \(Q \to Q\).

TipQuestion



Posets satisfy every axiom of Chapter 1. What distinguishes them from abstract sets?


In posets a monotone bijection need not be an isomorphism: the identity function from the discrete two-element poset to the chain \(\mathbf{2}\) is monotone and bijective, but its inverse is not monotone. Such behaviour is ruled out by the further axioms of the book, which make the category of abstract sets a topos.

title: Parts, Characteristic Functions, and Inverse Images
text:
Where we are
Throughout, \(\mathcal{S}\) denotes the category of abstract sets and mappings of L–R. So far we have the following axioms: \(\mathcal{S}\) is a category (L–R §1.4); it has a terminal object \(1\) (§1.2) and an initial object \(0\) (§1.5); it has binary sums (§2.1); \(1\) separates mappings (§1.5); and the axiom of §2.4, recalled below.
crumbs: The View from Category Theory - Topoi
15  Parts, Characteristic Functions, and Inverse Images

title: Parts, Characteristic Functions, and Inverse Images
text:
Elements and parts







Definition 15.1 An element of \(X\) is a map \(x\colon 1\to X\).










NoteAxiom: \(1\) separates mappings (L–R §1.5)



If \(f,g\colon X\to Y\) satisfy \(fx=gx\) for every element \(x\) of \(X\), then \(f=g\).









Definition 15.2 (L–R §§2.2–2.3, Def. 2.24) 
Let \(X\) be a set.

A part of \(X\) is a monomorphism \(i\colon A\rightarrowtail X\).
For parts \(i\colon A\rightarrowtail X\) and \(j\colon B\rightarrowtail X\), we say \(i\) is included in \(j\), written \(i\subseteq_X j\), if there is a map \(k\colon A\to B\) with \(jk=i\). (Such a \(k\) is unique, since \(j\) is monic.)
Parts \(i\) and \(j\) are equivalent, written \(i\equiv_X j\), if \(i\subseteq_X j\) and \(j\subseteq_X i\).
An element \(x\) of \(X\) is a member of the part \(i\colon A\rightarrowtail X\), written \(x\in_X i\), if \(x=ia\) for some element \(a\) of \(A\). (Such an \(a\) is unique.)

We often drop the subscript \(X\).




Equivalent parts have the same members: if \(i=jk\) and \(x=ia\), then \(x=j(ka)\).







Lemma 15.1 
Every element \(x\colon 1\to X\) is a part of \(X\).










NoteProof






Proof. If \(xa=xb\) for \(a,b\colon T\to 1\), then \(a=b\) because \(1\) is terminal. So \(x\) is monic.










ImportantConvention: elements, not generalized elements



L–R define membership for generalized elements \(x\colon T\to X\) with arbitrary domain \(T\), and their Definition 2.20 of characteristic function quantifies over all of these. For abstract sets it makes no difference whether we use all generalized elements or only elements \(1\to X\), by Proposition 15.1. In these notes we work with elements only.









Proposition 15.1 (Elements suffice; L–R pp. 36–37) 
Let \(i\) and \(j\) be parts of \(X\). If every element of \(X\) that is a member of \(i\) is also a member of \(j\), then \(i\subseteq_X j\). Consequently, two parts with the same members are equivalent.




L–R justify this informally by the “arbitrariness of mappings” and promise a more explicit argument. One such argument uses the axiom of §2.4 together with the separator axiom; see Exercise 15.2.


Characteristic functions
Fix the set \(2\) with its element \(\mathrm{true}\colon 1\to 2\).







Definition 15.3 (L–R Def. 2.20) 
A map \(\varphi\colon X\to 2\) is a characteristic function of a part \(i\) of \(X\) if for every element \(x\) of \(X\), \[
x\in i \iff \varphi x=\mathrm{true}.
\]










NoteAxiom: Membership representation via truth values (L–R §2.4)




Every map \(\varphi\colon X\to 2\) is the characteristic function of some part of \(X\).
Every part \(i\) of \(X\) has exactly one characteristic function, denoted \(\chi_i\).



Exercise 15.3 shows that our definition of characteristic function agrees with L–R’s version for generalized elements.







Proposition 15.2 (L–R Prop. 2.22) 
Parts \(i\) and \(j\) of \(X\) are equivalent if and only if \(\chi_i=\chi_j\).










NoteProof






Proof. If \(i\equiv j\), then \(i\) and \(j\) have the same members, so \(\chi_i\) is also a characteristic function of \(j\). By uniqueness, \(\chi_i=\chi_j\). Conversely, if \(\chi_i=\chi_j\), then for every element \(x\), \(x\in i \iff \chi_i x=\mathrm{true}\iff \chi_j x=\mathrm{true}\iff x\in j\). By Proposition 15.1, \(i\equiv j\).











Example 15.1 (L–R Ex. 2.21) 
By Lemma 15.1, \(\mathrm{true}\colon 1\rightarrowtail 2\) is a part of \(2\). Its characteristic function is \(1_2\). Indeed, since the only map \(1\to 1\) is \(1_1\), an element \(y\) of \(2\) is a member of \(\mathrm{true}\) exactly when \(y=\mathrm{true}\), that is, when \(1_2\,y=\mathrm{true}\).











Remark 15.1. L–R point out right after the axiom that it is special to \(\mathcal{S}\) and to the so-called Boolean toposes. In a general topos there is still an object of truth values, usually written \(\Omega\) with an element \(\mathrm{true}\colon 1\to\Omega\), satisfying (1) and (2); but \(\Omega\) need not have just two elements. L–R §6.2 gives an example with three truth values.

15  Parts, Characteristic Functions, and Inverse Images

title: Parts, Characteristic Functions, and Inverse Images
text:
Inverse image of a part
In naive set theory, the preimage of \(B\subseteq Y\) under \(f\colon X\to Y\) is \(\{x\in X : f(x)\in B\}\). The categorical version is defined by the same membership condition. This operation goes under many names: inverse image, preimage, substitution, pullback.







Definition 15.4 (L–R §2.5) 
Let \(f\colon X\to Y\) and let \(j\) be a part of \(Y\). A part \(i\) of \(X\) is an inverse image of \(j\) along \(f\) if for every element \(x\) of \(X\), \[
x\in i \iff fx\in j .
\]











Proposition 15.3 
Any two inverse images of \(j\) along \(f\) are equivalent.










NoteProof






Proof. They have the same members, so this follows from Proposition 15.1.




We may therefore speak of the inverse image and write it \(f^{-1}(j)\), as L–R do (Ex. 2.39), keeping in mind that it is determined only up to equivalence.
L–R simply assert at the start of §2.5 that inverse images exist. In fact, existence is a consequence of the axiom of §2.4, and the proof yields L–R’s Theorem 2.33 at the same time.







Theorem 15.1 (Existence of inverse images; L–R Thm. 2.33) 
Let \(f\colon X\to Y\) and let \(j\) be a part of \(Y\). The part of \(X\) whose characteristic function is \(\chi_j\circ f\) is an inverse image of \(j\) along \(f\). In particular, inverse images always exist, and \[
\chi_{f^{-1}(j)}=\chi_j\circ f .
\]










NoteProof






Proof. By part (1) of the axiom, \(\chi_j\circ f\colon X\to 2\) is the characteristic function of some part \(i\) of \(X\). For every element \(x\) of \(X\), \[
x\in i \iff \chi_j(fx)=\mathrm{true}\iff fx\in j ,
\] using the definition of characteristic function first for \(i\), then for \(j\). So \(i\) is an inverse image of \(j\) along \(f\), and its characteristic function is \(\chi_j\circ f\).











Remark 15.2 (Comparison with ZFC). Part (1) of the axiom is a comprehension principle: for every “predicate” \(\varphi\colon X\to 2\) there is a part of \(X\) consisting of the elements where \(\varphi\) is true, \(\{x\in X: \varphi x=\mathrm{true}\}\). Compare the Comprehension (Separation) axiom of \(\mathsf{ZFC}\). There is an important difference: \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) separates by arbitrary formulas, while here we may separate only by predicates that are already given as maps \(X\to 2\). Richer forms of comprehension become available later, once we have exponentials and quantifiers.











Proposition 15.4 (L–R Prop. 2.31) 
For any \(\psi\colon Y\to 2\), the map \(\psi\) is a characteristic function of \(\psi^{-1}(\mathrm{true})\). Consequently, \(\psi=\chi_j\) if and only if \(j\equiv\psi^{-1}(\mathrm{true})\).










NoteProof






Proof. By Example 15.1, \(y\in\mathrm{true}\) iff \(y=\mathrm{true}\). Hence \(x\in\psi^{-1}(\mathrm{true})\) iff \(\psi x\in\mathrm{true}\) iff \(\psi x=\mathrm{true}\), which proves the first claim. If \(j\equiv\psi^{-1}(\mathrm{true})\), then \(j\) has the same members as \(\psi^{-1}(\mathrm{true})\), so \(\psi\) is a characteristic function of \(j\). Conversely, if \(\psi=\chi_j\), then \(j\) and \(\psi^{-1}(\mathrm{true})\) have the same characteristic function, so they are equivalent by Proposition 15.2.











Proposition 15.5 (Functoriality of inverse image; L–R Ex. 2.30) 
Let \(f\colon X\to Y\) and \(g\colon Y\to Z\), and let \(j,j'\) be parts of \(Y\) and \(k\) a part of \(Z\).

\(1_Y^{-1}(j)\equiv j\).
\((g\circ f)^{-1}(k)\equiv f^{-1}(g^{-1}(k))\).
If \(j\subseteq j'\), then \(f^{-1}(j)\subseteq f^{-1}(j')\). In particular, if \(j\equiv j'\), then \(f^{-1}(j)\equiv f^{-1}(j')\).











NoteProof






Proof. Each statement is proved by comparing members and applying Proposition 15.1. (a) \(x\in1_Y^{-1}(j)\) iff \(x\in j\). (b) For an element \(x\) of \(X\), \[
x\in(gf)^{-1}(k) \iff g(fx)\in k \iff fx\in g^{-1}(k) \iff x\in f^{-1}(g^{-1}(k)) .
\] (c) If \(j=j'k'\) and \(x\in f^{-1}(j)\), then \(fx\in j\), so \(fx\in j'\), so \(x\in f^{-1}(j')\).




Note the reversal of order in (b): pulling back along \(g\circ f\) is pulling back along \(g\) first, then along \(f\). L–R call this the contravariant functoriality of inverse image. The section on functors explains the terminology.







Remark 15.3. L–R prove Theorem 15.1 differently: by Proposition 15.4 and Proposition 15.5, \[
(\chi_j f)^{-1}(\mathrm{true})\equiv f^{-1}(\chi_j^{-1}(\mathrm{true}))\equiv f^{-1}(j),
\] so \(\chi_j f\) is the characteristic function of \(f^{-1}(j)\). This argument only works once we know that \(f^{-1}(j)\) exists, which is why we proved existence first. The section on representability explains what lies behind L–R’s argument.




The next proposition anticipates the notion of pullback, which we study in L–R §3.5.







Proposition 15.6 (L–R Ex. 2.29) 
Let \(j\colon B\rightarrowtail Y\) be a part of \(Y\), let \(f\colon X\to Y\), and let \(i\colon A\rightarrowtail X\) be \(f^{-1}(j)\).

There is a unique \(f'\colon A\to B\) with \(jf'=fi\); that is, \(f\) restricted to \(i\) lands in \(j\).
If \(m\) is any part of \(X\) such that \(fm=jg\) for some \(g\), then \(m\subseteq i\).

Thus \(f^{-1}(j)\) is the largest part of \(X\) on which \(f\) lands in \(j\).




Part (b) follows from Proposition 15.1: if \(x=mc\) is a member of \(m\), then \(fx=j(gc)\in j\), so \(x\in i\). Part (a) is Exercise 15.4.







Definition 15.5 (L–R Def. 2.36) 
A part \(m\) of \(Y\) is an intersection of parts \(i\) and \(j\) of \(Y\), written \(m=i\cap j\), if for every element \(y\) of \(Y\), \(y\in m\) iff (\(y\in i\) and \(y\in j\)).











Proposition 15.7 (L–R Ex. 2.35, Rem. 2.37) 
Let \(i\colon A\rightarrowtail Y\) and \(j\) be parts of \(Y\), and let \(k=i^{-1}(j)\). Then \(i\circ k\) is an intersection \(i\cap j\).










NoteProof






Proof. A composite of monos is monic, so \(ik\) is a part. If \(y=i(ka)\), then \(y\in i\), and \(y\in j\) because \(ka\in i^{-1}(j)\). Conversely, if \(y\in i\) and \(y\in j\), write \(y=ia\); then \(ia\in j\), so \(a\in i^{-1}(j)\), say \(a=kb\), and \(y=ikb\in ik\).

15  Parts, Characteristic Functions, and Inverse Images

title: Parts, Characteristic Functions, and Inverse Images
section: Hom-sets and the category of sets
text:
Hom-sets and the category of sets

Two kinds of sets
From now on we must keep two levels apart.

\(\mathcal{S}\) is the category of abstract sets that we are axiomatizing. Its objects are the things we study.
\(\mathsf{Set}\) is the category of sets of our metatheory (for instance, sets in the sense of \(\mathsf{ZFC}\)), with functions between them. These are the sets we use to talk about \(\mathcal{S}\).

In this section the collections we attach to an object of \(\mathcal{S}\) (its elements, its parts, its characteristic functions) are objects of \(\mathsf{Set}\), not of \(\mathcal{S}\).







Definition 15.6 (Hom-sets) 
For objects \(X\), \(Y\) of a category \(\mathsf{C}\), write \(\mathsf{C}(X,Y)\) for the set of morphisms \(X\to Y\). (A common alternative notation is \(\operatorname{Hom}_\mathsf{C}(X,Y)\).)











Remark 15.4. Chapter 5 of L–R constructs, for sets \(X\) and \(Y\), an object \(Y^X\) of \(\mathcal{S}\) whose elements correspond to maps \(X\to Y\): an internal version of the external hom-set \(\mathcal{S}(X,Y)\). Do not confuse the two. In particular, we do not write \(Y^X\) for the hom-set.






Restating what we know







Definition 15.7 
For a set \(X\), let \(\operatorname{Sub}(X)\) be the set of equivalence classes of parts of \(X\), partially ordered by inclusion.1 L–R say “part”; the standard term is subobject, hence the notation. We usually write \(j\) for the equivalence class of \(j\).




In this notation:

The elements of \(X\) form the hom-set \(\mathcal{S}(1,X)\).
The separator axiom says: if \(f,g\in\mathcal{S}(X,Y)\) agree on every \(x\in\mathcal{S}(1,X)\), then \(f=g\).
Proposition 15.1 says: the function \(\operatorname{Sub}(X)\to\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{S}(1,X))\) sending a part to its set of members is injective.
The axiom of §2.4 says the following.








Proposition 15.8 
For every set \(X\), the assignment \(j\mapsto\chi_j\) is a well-defined bijection \[
\chi_X\colon \operatorname{Sub}(X)\longrightarrow\mathcal{S}(X,2).
\]










NoteProof






Proof. Part (2) of the axiom gives the assignment on parts, and Proposition 15.2 (\(\Rightarrow\)) shows it is well defined on equivalence classes. It is injective by Proposition 15.2 (\(\Leftarrow\)) and surjective by part (1) of the axiom.

15  Parts, Characteristic Functions, and Inverse Images

title: Parts, Characteristic Functions, and Inverse Images
text:
Functors

Moving things along a map
Given \(f\colon X\to Y\) in \(\mathcal{S}\), how do the collections attached to \(X\) relate to those attached to \(Y\)?








Collection
How \(f\) moves it
Direction




Elements
\(x\mapsto f\circ x\), \(\;\mathcal{S}(1,X)\to\mathcal{S}(1,Y)\)
forward


Characteristic functions
\(\varphi\mapsto\varphi\circ f\), \(\;\mathcal{S}(Y,2)\to\mathcal{S}(X,2)\)
backward


Parts
\(j\mapsto f^{-1}(j)\), \(\;\operatorname{Sub}(Y)\to\operatorname{Sub}(X)\)
backward



Maps out of a fixed object (elements) are pushed forward by composing after \(f\). Maps into a fixed object (characteristic functions) are pulled back by composing before \(f\).
In each case two laws hold. The identity map moves nothing: \[
1_X\circ x=x,\qquad \varphi\circ 1_X=\varphi,\qquad 1_X^{-1}(j)\equiv j.
\] Moving along a composite is moving in two steps, with the order preserved or reversed: \[
(g\circ f)\circ x=g\circ(f\circ x),\qquad
\varphi\circ(g\circ f)=(\varphi\circ g)\circ f,\qquad
(g\circ f)^{-1}(k)\equiv f^{-1}(g^{-1}(k)) .
\] For elements and characteristic functions these are just the identity and associativity laws of a category; for parts, it is Proposition 15.5. A rule for moving things along maps that obeys these two laws is called a functor.


Functors and variance







Definition 15.8 (Riehl §1.3) 
Let \(\mathsf{C}\) and \(\mathsf{D}\) be categories. A functor \(F\colon\mathsf{C}\to\mathsf{D}\) consists of

an object \(Fc\) of \(\mathsf{D}\) for each object \(c\) of \(\mathsf{C}\), and
a morphism \(Ff\colon Fc\to Fc'\) of \(\mathsf{D}\) for each morphism \(f\colon c\to c'\) of \(\mathsf{C}\),

such that \[
F(1_c)=1_{Fc}\qquad\text{and}\qquad F(g\circ f)=Fg\circ Ff
\] for every object \(c\) and every composable pair \(f\), \(g\).











Example 15.2 \(\mathsf{Set}\) is a category, as is \(\mathsf{Pos}\), the category of partially ordered sets and order-preserving maps. Every category has an identity functor.




Some of the rules in the table reverse the direction of maps. These are handled by reversing the arrows of the domain category.







Definition 15.9 (Riehl §1.2) 
The opposite category \(\mathsf{C}^\mathrm{op}\) has the same objects as \(\mathsf{C}\), and a morphism \(f^\mathrm{op}\colon c'\to c\) in \(\mathsf{C}^\mathrm{op}\) for each morphism \(f\colon c\to c'\) in \(\mathsf{C}\). Composition is defined by \(f^\mathrm{op}\circ g^\mathrm{op}=(g\circ f)^\mathrm{op}\), and identities are \(1_c^\mathrm{op}\).




Exercise 15.1 asks you to check that \(\mathsf{C}^\mathrm{op}\) is a category.







Definition 15.10 (Variance) 
A contravariant functor from \(\mathsf{C}\) to \(\mathsf{D}\) is a functor \(F\colon\mathsf{C}^\mathrm{op}\to\mathsf{D}\). Unwinding the definitions, it sends each \(f\colon c\to c'\) to a morphism \(Ff\colon Fc'\to Fc\) in the opposite direction, with \[
F(1_c)=1_{Fc}\qquad\text{and}\qquad F(g\circ f)=Ff\circ Fg .
\] A functor \(\mathsf{C}\to\mathsf{D}\) is called covariant when we want to stress the contrast. The variance of a functor says whether it preserves or reverses the direction of morphisms.











Proposition 15.9 (Hom-functors) 
Let \(c\) be an object of a category \(\mathsf{C}\) whose hom-sets are sets.

There is a functor \(\mathsf{C}(c,-)\colon\mathsf{C}\to\mathsf{Set}\) sending \(x\) to \(\mathsf{C}(c,x)\) and \(f\colon x\to y\) to \[
f_*\colon\mathsf{C}(c,x)\to\mathsf{C}(c,y),\qquad h\mapsto f\circ h .
\]
There is a functor \(\mathsf{C}(-,c)\colon\mathsf{C}^\mathrm{op}\to\mathsf{Set}\) sending \(x\) to \(\mathsf{C}(x,c)\) and \(f\colon x\to y\) to \[
f^*\colon\mathsf{C}(y,c)\to\mathsf{C}(x,c),\qquad h\mapsto h\circ f .
\]











NoteProof






Proof. 

\((1_x)_*h=1_x\circ h=h\) and \((g\circ f)_*h=(g\circ f)\circ h=g\circ(f\circ h)=g_*f_*h\).
\((1_x)^*h=h\) and \((g\circ f)^*h=h\circ(g\circ f)=(h\circ g)\circ f=f^*g^*h\).





So the functor laws for hom-functors are the identity and associativity axioms of a category. Two special cases are the first two rows of the table:

\(\mathcal{S}(1,-)\colon\mathcal{S}\to\mathsf{Set}\), the elements functor (covariant);
\(\mathcal{S}(-,2)\colon\mathcal{S}^\mathrm{op}\to\mathsf{Set}\), the characteristic functions functor (contravariant).

The third row is also a functor.







Theorem 15.2 
There is a functor \(\operatorname{Sub}\colon\mathcal{S}^\mathrm{op}\to\mathsf{Set}\) sending \(X\) to \(\operatorname{Sub}(X)\) and \(f\colon X\to Y\) to \[
f^{-1}(-)\colon\operatorname{Sub}(Y)\to\operatorname{Sub}(X),\qquad j\mapsto f^{-1}(j).
\]










NoteProof






Proof. The function \(f^{-1}(-)\) is well defined on equivalence classes by Proposition 15.5 (c). The functor laws are Proposition 15.5 (a) and (b).











Remark 15.5 (Why equivalence classes?). At the level of individual monos, inverse image is not a function: its defining membership condition determines \(f^{-1}(j)\) only up to equivalence. The functor laws also hold only up to equivalence: \((g\circ f)^{-1}(k)\) and \(f^{-1}(g^{-1}(k))\) are equivalent parts, not literally the same mono. Passing to equivalence classes makes \(f^{-1}(-)\) a genuine function and turns these equivalences into the equalities the definition of a functor requires.











Remark 15.6. By Proposition 15.5 (c), each \(f^{-1}(-)\) preserves inclusion, so \(\operatorname{Sub}\) is in fact a functor \(\mathcal{S}^\mathrm{op}\to\mathsf{Pos}\).











Remark 15.7 (Notation). Riehl writes \(f^*\) for precomposition with \(f\). Many authors also write \(f^*\) for inverse image along \(f\). Theorem 15.3 below shows that the two operations correspond under \(\chi\), so the clash is harmless. In these notes, inverse image is written \(f^{-1}(-)\).






Faithfulness and the separator axiom







Definition 15.11 
A functor \(F\colon\mathsf{C}\to\mathsf{D}\) is faithful if for all objects \(c,c'\), the function \(\mathsf{C}(c,c')\to\mathsf{D}(Fc,Fc')\), \(f\mapsto Ff\), is injective.











Proposition 15.10 
The axiom that \(1\) separates mappings holds if and only if the elements functor \(\mathcal{S}(1,-)\colon\mathcal{S}\to\mathsf{Set}\) is faithful.










NoteProof






Proof. For \(f,g\colon X\to Y\) we have \(f_*=g_*\) as functions \(\mathcal{S}(1,X)\to\mathcal{S}(1,Y)\) exactly when \(fx=gx\) for every element \(x\). Faithfulness says that this forces \(f=g\), which is the separator axiom.




A category whose terminal object separates mappings is called well-pointed. In the categories of variable sets we will meet later (L–R §6.2), \(\mathcal{S}(1,-)\) is still a functor but is no longer faithful: distinct maps can agree on all elements. This is why L–R use generalized elements \(T\to X\) in their definitions.







Remark 15.8 (Mixed variance). Letting both arguments vary gives a functor of two variables, \(\mathsf{C}(-,-)\colon\mathsf{C}^\mathrm{op}\times\mathsf{C}\to\mathsf{Set}\), contravariant in the first argument and covariant in the second. The exponential \(Y^X\) of L–R Chapter 5 behaves the same way.

15  Parts, Characteristic Functions, and Inverse Images

title: Parts, Characteristic Functions, and Inverse Images
text:
Natural transformations
We now have two contravariant functors \(\operatorname{Sub}\) and \(\mathcal{S}(-,2)\), and for each \(X\) a bijection \(\chi_X\colon\operatorname{Sub}(X)\to\mathcal{S}(X,2)\) between their values. The question is whether this comparison respects the way both functors move along maps. Is “transport, then compare” the same as “compare, then transport”?







Definition 15.12 (Riehl §1.4) 
Let \(F,G\colon\mathsf{C}\to\mathsf{D}\) be functors. A natural transformation \(\alpha\colon F\Rightarrow G\) consists of a morphism \(\alpha_c\colon Fc\to Gc\) in \(\mathsf{D}\) for each object \(c\) of \(\mathsf{C}\) (the components of \(\alpha\)), such that for every morphism \(f\colon c\to c'\) of \(\mathsf{C}\) the following square commutes: \[
\begin{CD}
Fc @>{\alpha_c}>> Gc \\
@V{Ff}VV @VV{Gf}V \\
Fc' @>>{\alpha_{c'}}> Gc'
\end{CD}
\qquad\text{that is,}\qquad Gf\circ\alpha_c=\alpha_{c'}\circ Ff .
\] A natural isomorphism is a natural transformation all of whose components are isomorphisms. We write \(F\cong G\).




For contravariant functors \(F,G\colon\mathsf{C}^\mathrm{op}\to\mathsf{Set}\) and a morphism \(f\colon x\to y\) of \(\mathsf{C}\), the naturality square reads \[
\begin{CD}
Fy @>{\alpha_y}>> Gy \\
@V{Ff}VV @VV{Gf}V \\
Fx @>>{\alpha_x}> Gx
\end{CD}
\] Naturality only makes sense for two functors of the same variance; otherwise there is no square to check.







Example 15.3 
Let \(u\colon Z\to Z'\) be a morphism of \(\mathsf{C}\). Postcomposition with \(u\) gives, for each \(x\), a function \(u_*\colon\mathsf{C}(x,Z)\to\mathsf{C}(x,Z')\). These form a natural transformation \(u_*\colon\mathsf{C}(-,Z)\Rightarrow\mathsf{C}(-,Z')\): for \(f\colon x\to y\) the square \[
\begin{CD}
\mathsf{C}(y,Z) @>{u_*}>> \mathsf{C}(y,Z') \\
@V{f^*}VV @VV{f^*}V \\
\mathsf{C}(x,Z) @>>{u_*}> \mathsf{C}(x,Z')
\end{CD}
\] commutes because \(u\circ(h\circ f)=(u\circ h)\circ f\). Once again, naturality is associativity.




Now the main case.







Theorem 15.3 
The bijections \(\chi_X\) form a natural isomorphism \[
\chi\colon\operatorname{Sub}\Longrightarrow\mathcal{S}(-,2).
\]










NoteProof






Proof. Each component is a bijection by Proposition 15.8. Naturality means that for every \(f\colon X\to Y\) the square \[
\begin{CD}
\operatorname{Sub}(Y) @>{\chi_Y}>> \mathcal{S}(Y,2) \\
@V{f^{-1}(-)}VV @VV{f^*}V \\
\operatorname{Sub}(X) @>>{\chi_X}> \mathcal{S}(X,2)
\end{CD}
\] commutes, that is, \(\chi_{f^{-1}(j)}=\chi_j\circ f\) for every part \(j\) of \(Y\). This is Theorem 15.1.




In words: parts of \(X\) are the same thing as maps \(X\to 2\), compatibly with every map \(f\). The axiom of §2.4 supplies the bijections, and L–R’s Theorem 2.33 says that they are compatible with inverse images.







Remark 15.9 (What “natural” means). Informally, a natural comparison is one that is defined uniformly in \(X\), without choosing anything specific to \(X\). Bijections that depend on choices, such as a chosen listing of the elements of \(X\), are typically not natural.

15  Parts, Characteristic Functions, and Inverse Images

title: Parts, Characteristic Functions, and Inverse Images
text:
Representability and the universal element
Theorem 15.3 says that the functor \(\operatorname{Sub}\) is isomorphic to a hom-functor. This situation has a name.







Definition 15.13 (Riehl §2.1) 
A functor \(F\colon\mathsf{C}^\mathrm{op}\to\mathsf{Set}\) is representable if there is an object \(c\) of \(\mathsf{C}\) and a natural isomorphism \(\mathsf{C}(-,c)\cong F\). We then say that \(c\) represents \(F\).




So \(\operatorname{Sub}\) is represented by \(2\). The next lemma shows that a natural transformation out of a hom-functor can be built from a single element.







Lemma 15.2 
Let \(F\colon\mathsf{C}^\mathrm{op}\to\mathsf{Set}\) be a functor, \(c\) an object of \(\mathsf{C}\), and \(u\in Fc\). Then the functions \[
\theta_x\colon\mathsf{C}(x,c)\to Fx,\qquad \varphi\mapsto(F\varphi)(u),
\] form a natural transformation \(\theta\colon\mathsf{C}(-,c)\Rightarrow F\).










NoteProof






Proof. For \(f\colon x'\to x\) and \(\varphi\colon x\to c\), functoriality of \(F\) gives \[
\theta_{x'}(f^*\varphi)=F(\varphi\circ f)(u)=(Ff\circ F\varphi)(u)=Ff\big(\theta_x(\varphi)\big),
\] which is the naturality condition.











Definition 15.14 
An element \(u\in Fc\) is a universal element of \(F\) if the natural transformation \(\theta\) of Lemma 15.2 is a natural isomorphism. Equivalently: for every object \(x\) and every \(a\in Fx\) there is exactly one \(\varphi\colon x\to c\) with \((F\varphi)(u)=a\).











Theorem 15.4 
The part \(\mathrm{true}\colon 1\rightarrowtail 2\) is a universal element of \(\operatorname{Sub}\). Explicitly, for every set \(X\) and every part \(j\) of \(X\), there is exactly one \(\varphi\colon X\to 2\) with \(j\equiv\varphi^{-1}(\mathrm{true})\), and the resulting isomorphism \(\theta\) is the inverse of \(\chi\).










NoteProof






Proof. Here \(\theta_X(\varphi)=\varphi^{-1}(\mathrm{true})\). By Proposition 15.4, this is the part whose characteristic function is \(\varphi\), so \(\chi_X(\theta_X(\varphi))=\varphi\). Also by Proposition 15.4, \(\theta_X(\chi_X(j))=\chi_j^{-1}(\mathrm{true})\equiv j\). So \(\theta_X=\chi_X^{-1}\) is a bijection for every \(X\).




Note that the naturality of \(\theta\) came for free, from functoriality of \(\operatorname{Sub}\) alone (Lemma 15.2). The content of the axiom of §2.4 is that this particular \(\theta\), built from \(\mathrm{true}\), has bijective components. This is the idea behind L–R’s proof of Theorem 2.33.







Remark 15.10 (Preview: the Yoneda lemma). In the situation of Lemma 15.2, the identity \(1_c\in\mathsf{C}(c,c)\) is sent to \(\theta_c(1_c)=(F1_c)(u)=u\). The Yoneda lemma (Riehl §2.2) says that this is the general pattern: every natural transformation \(\alpha\colon\mathsf{C}(-,c)\Rightarrow F\) equals the \(\theta\) built from the element \(u=\alpha_c(1_c)\). In our case, \(\chi^{-1}\) is determined by \(\chi_2^{-1}(1_2)=\mathrm{true}\) (Example 15.1). So the entire correspondence between parts and characteristic functions is encoded in one piece of data: the part \(\mathrm{true}\) of \(2\).











Corollary 15.1 
The truth-value object is unique up to unique isomorphism: if \(v\colon 1\rightarrowtail V\) is also a universal element of \(\operatorname{Sub}\), there is exactly one isomorphism \(\psi\colon 2\to V\) with \(\psi\circ\mathrm{true}=v\).




The proof is Exercise 15.8. It is a special case of a general fact: an object representing a functor is unique up to unique isomorphism.







Remark 15.11. In topos theory, the axiom “there is an object \(\Omega\) with a universal element \(\mathrm{true}\colon 1\rightarrowtail\Omega\) of \(\operatorname{Sub}\)” is called the existence of a subobject classifier. Its usual formulation uses pullbacks, which we introduce in L–R §3.5; Proposition 15.6 is a preview.

text:
Exercises







Exercise 15.1 
Verify that \(\mathsf{C}^\mathrm{op}\) satisfies the axioms of a category.











Exercise 15.2 
Prove Proposition 15.1, using L–R’s Definition 2.20, which quantifies over generalized elements \(T\to X\), and the axiom that \(1\) separates mappings.










TipHint





Let \(i\colon A\rightarrowtail X\). Compare \(\chi_j\circ i\) with \(\mathrm{true}_A=\mathrm{true}\circ !_A\) on elements of \(A\), then apply Definition 2.20 to the generalized element \(i\).










Exercise 15.3 
Using Proposition 15.1, show that \(\varphi\colon X\to 2\) is a characteristic function of a part \(i\) in our sense (testing elements only) if and only if it is one in the sense of L–R’s Definition 2.20 (testing all generalized elements).











Exercise 15.4 
Prove Proposition 15.6 (a).










TipHint





Use the separator axiom to show \(\chi_j\circ f\circ i=\mathrm{true}_A\), then use Exercise 15.3.










Exercise 15.5 
For \(f\colon X\to Y\), show that \(f^{-1}(1_Y)\equiv 1_X\) and that \(f^{-1}(j_1\cap j_2)\equiv f^{-1}(j_1)\cap f^{-1}(j_2)\) (L–R Ex. 2.39).











Exercise 15.6 
Show that the inverses of the components of a natural isomorphism form a natural transformation.











Exercise 15.7 
Show that every functor sends isomorphisms to isomorphisms. Conclude that if \(X\cong Y\) in \(\mathcal{S}\), then \(\operatorname{Sub}(X)\cong\operatorname{Sub}(Y)\) in \(\mathsf{Set}\).











Exercise 15.8 
Prove Corollary 15.1.










TipHint





Let \(\varphi\colon V\to 2\) satisfy \(v\equiv\varphi^{-1}(\mathrm{true})\), and \(\psi\colon 2\to V\) satisfy \(\mathrm{true}\equiv\psi^{-1}(v)\). Use Proposition 15.5 and the uniqueness in Theorem 15.4 to show \(\varphi\psi=1_2\), and similarly \(\psi\varphi=1_V\).










Exercise 15.9 
By Lemma 15.1, \(x\mapsto x\) sends \(\mathcal{S}(1,X)\) to parts of \(X\). Explain why it makes no sense to ask whether this is a natural transformation \(\mathcal{S}(1,-)\Rightarrow\operatorname{Sub}\).











Exercise 15.10 
Granting that \(2\) has exactly two elements, \(\mathrm{true}\) and \(\mathrm{false}\), there are exactly four maps \(u\colon 2\to 2\). By Example 15.3, each gives a natural transformation \(u_*\colon\mathcal{S}(-,2)\Rightarrow\mathcal{S}(-,2)\). Using \(\chi\), describe what each one does to parts. (The Yoneda lemma will show that these are all the natural transformations \(\mathcal{S}(-,2)\Rightarrow\mathcal{S}(-,2)\).)











Exercise 15.11 
Show that the elements functor preserves products in the following sense: if \(X\xleftarrow{p}P\xrightarrow{q}Y\) is a product diagram in \(\mathcal{S}\) (L–R §3.3), then \(x\mapsto(px,qx)\) is a bijection \(\mathcal{S}(1,P)\to\mathcal{S}(1,X)\times\mathcal{S}(1,Y)\).

15  Parts, Characteristic Functions, and Inverse Images

title: Finite Limits and Colimits
text:
Where we are going
Here is the definition we are aiming for.






NoteElementary topos (preview)



A category \(\mathcal{E}\) is an elementary topos if

\(\mathcal{E}\) has all finite limits;
\(\mathcal{E}\) has all finite colimits;
\(\mathcal{E}\) has exponentials \(B^A\) (it is cartesian closed);
\(\mathcal{E}\) has a subobject classifier \(1 \xrightarrow{\top} \Omega\).



Today is about (1) and (2). Next time we do (3) and (4). The category \(\mathcal{S}\) of abstract sets will then be a topos with some extra properties: \(1\) separates maps, there is a natural numbers object, and choice holds.
We have already met several pieces of (1) and (2) in Chapters 1–2: the terminal set \(1\), the initial set \(0\), binary sums \(A_0 + A_1\), and inverse images of parts. The point of today is that these are all instances of two general constructions, limits and colimits, and that a handful of special cases suffice to build all the others.
A remark on method. In \(\mathcal{S}\) we may test equations between maps on elements \(1 \to X\), since \(1\) separates. In a general topos this fails. So we will phrase everything with generalized elements \(x : T \to X\) for arbitrary \(T\). Every argument below then works in any category with the relevant structure.



Splittings and isomorphisms







Definition 18.1 (Retraction, section) For maps \(X \xrightarrow{i} Y \xrightarrow{r} X\) with \(ri = 1_X\), we call \(r\) a retraction (left inverse) of \(i\), and \(i\) a section (right inverse) of \(r\).











Proposition 18.1 If \(i\) has a retraction, then \(i\) is a monomorphism. Dually, if \(r\) has a section, then \(r\) is an epimorphism.










NoteProof






Proof. If \(ix_1 = ix_2\), then \(x_1 = (ri)x_1 = r(ix_1) = r(ix_2) = (ri)x_2 = x_2\). This is “dividing by \(i\) on the left”. The dual statement has the dual proof.




A mono with a retraction is called split. The converse of Proposition 18.1 is special to sets:

In \(\mathcal{S}\), every mono \(X \rightarrowtail Y\) with \(X \neq 0\) splits. Pick \(x_0 : 1 \to X\) and let \(X'\) be the complement of \(X\) in \(Y\), so \(Y = X + X'\). Define \(r\) by cases: \(r\) is \(1_X\) on \(X\) and constantly \(x_0\) on \(X'\).
In continuous settings this fails. The inclusion of the circle \(S^1 \hookrightarrow \mathbb{R}^2\) has no continuous retraction. It does have one into \(\mathbb{R}^2\setminus\{0\}\), namely \(y \mapsto y/|y|\).

The proof for \(\mathcal{S}\) used complements. In a general topos, parts need not have complements. Toposes in which they always do are called Boolean. This is our first glimpse of how intuitionistic logic enters.







Definition 18.2 \(f : X \to Y\) is an isomorphism if there is \(g : Y \to X\) with \(gf = 1_X\) and \(fg = 1_Y\).











Proposition 18.2 If \(rf = 1_X\) and \(fs = 1_Y\), then \(r = s\). In particular, two-sided inverses are unique; we write \(f^{-1}\).










NoteProof






Proof. \(r = r1_Y = r(fs) = (rf)s = 1_Xs = s\).




In \(\mathcal{S}\), isomorphisms are exactly the bijections. Given bijective \(f\), define $g(y) = $ the unique \(x\) with \(fx = y\). Then \(gf\) and \(fg\) agree with the identities on elements, and \(1\) separates. No choice is needed, because \(g\) is uniquely determined.



Products







Definition 19.1 (Product) A product of objects \(A, B\) in a category \(\mathcal{C}\) is an object \(P\) with maps \(A \xleftarrow{\pi_A} P \xrightarrow{\pi_B} B\) such that for every \(X\) and every pair \(f : X \to A\), \(g : X \to B\) there is a unique \(h : X \to P\) with \(\pi_A h = f\) and \(\pi_B h = g\).
\[
\begin{array}{ccc}
& & A \\
& \overset{f}{\nearrow} & \big\uparrow{\scriptstyle \pi_A} \\
X & \xrightarrow{\;\;h\;=\;\langle f,g \rangle\;\;} & A \times B \\
& \underset{g}{\searrow} & \big\downarrow{\scriptstyle \pi_B} \\
& & B
\end{array}
\]




We write \(P = A\times B\) and \(h = \langle f,g \rangle\). Equivalently, composition with \(\pi_A, \pi_B\) is a bijection \[
\mathcal{C}(X, A\times B) \;\cong\; \mathcal{C}(X,A) \times \mathcal{C}(X,B).
\] So a map into a product is the same thing as a pair of maps. That is the operational content of a product, and it is what we use in practice.






NoteAxiom: Binary products



Any two sets \(A, B\) have a product \(A \times B\).


Computing with generalized elements. For \(x : T \to X\), \[
\langle f,g \rangle\,x = \langle fx,\, gx \rangle.
\] Both sides are maps \(T \to A\times B\) with projections \(fx\) and \(gx\). By the uniqueness clause they are equal. This is how “ordered pairs” are recovered without ever defining them.
Examples.

In \(\mathcal{S}\): the cartesian product with the usual projections.
In a poset viewed as a category: \(a \times b\) is the greatest lower bound \(a \wedge b\).
In \(\mathbf{Grp}\), \(\mathbf{Top}\), \(\mathbf{Vect}\): the direct product with the product structure.
In \(\mathcal{S}\) with \(2 = \{0,1\}\): a pair \(\varphi, \psi : X \to 2\) of characteristic maps is a single map \(\langle \varphi,\psi \rangle : X \to 2\times 2\). Composing with the truth table \(\& : 2 \times 2 \to 2\) gives the characteristic map of the intersection of the two parts. Logical operations are maps out of products of truth-value objects. This returns with \(\Omega \times \Omega \to \Omega\) in a general topos.

Graphs and diagonals. The graph of \(f : A \to B\) is \(\gamma_f = \langle 1_A, f \rangle : A \to A \times B\). Since \(\pi_A \gamma_f = 1_A\), the graph is a split mono, hence a part of \(A \times B\). A generalized element \(\langle x,y \rangle\) is a member of it iff \(y = fx\). The special case \(\delta_A = \langle 1_A, 1_A \rangle : A \to A\times A\) is the diagonal.

Uniqueness up to unique isomorphism







Proposition 19.1 If \((P, \pi_A, \pi_B)\) and \((P', \pi'_A, \pi'_B)\) are both products of \(A\) and \(B\), there is a unique isomorphism \(h : P \to P'\) with \(\pi'_A h = \pi_A\) and \(\pi'_B h = \pi_B\).










NoteProof






Proof. The universal property of \(P'\) gives \(h : P \to P'\) commuting with the projections. That of \(P\) gives \(k : P' \to P\). Now \(kh : P \to P\) satisfies \(\pi_A (kh) = \pi_A\) and \(\pi_B(kh) = \pi_B\). But \(1_P\) satisfies the same equations, so uniqueness forces \(kh = 1_P\). Symmetrically, \(hk = 1_{P'}\).




This argument uses nothing but “existence + uniqueness of induced maps”. It therefore applies verbatim to every universal construction below: equalizers, pullbacks, limits, and dually sums, coequalizers, pushouts. We will not repeat it. It is why we may say “the product” and why “equations” like \(1 \times A = A\) or \(A \times B = B \times A\) mean specified isomorphisms.
This is a point worth pausing on. In \(\mathsf{ZFC}\), \(A \times B\) is one particular set of Kuratowski pairs. Here, any object with the universal property is a product, and nothing we can say distinguishes between them.




Equalizers







Definition 20.1 (Equalizer) Given \(A \underset{g}{\overset{f}{\rightrightarrows}} B\), an equalizer of \(f\) and \(g\) is a map \(e : E \to A\) such that

\(fe = ge\);
for every \(x : T \to A\) with \(fx = gx\) there is a unique \(\bar x : T \to E\) with \(e\bar x = x\).

\[
E \xrightarrow{\;e\;} A \underset{g}{\overset{f}{\rightrightarrows}} B
\]











Proposition 20.1 Every equalizer is a monomorphism. Hence it is a part of \(A\), and for any \(x : T \to A\), \[
x \in e \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad fx = gx.
\]










NoteProof






Proof. Suppose \(e y_1 = e y_2 =: x\). Then \(fx = gx\), and both \(y_1\) and \(y_2\) are factorizations of \(x\) through \(e\). By uniqueness, \(y_1 = y_2\). The membership statement is a restatement of clause 2.




So the equalizer is the categorical form of comprehension by an equation: \(\{a \in A : f(a) = g(a)\}\).
Examples.

The unit circle is the equalizer of \(\mathbb{R}^2 \rightrightarrows \mathbb{R}\) given by \((x,y) \mapsto x^2+y^2\) and the constant map \(1\). This is Descartes’ idea: figures are cut out by equations.
In \(\mathbf{Grp}\), the kernel of \(\varphi: G \to H\) is the equalizer of \(\varphi\) and the trivial homomorphism.
The equalizer of the two projections \(\pi_0, \pi_1 : B \times B \rightrightarrows B\) is the diagonal \(\delta_B\).

The last example lets us build all equalizers from products and inverse images: the equalizer of \(f, g\) is the inverse image of the diagonal \(\delta_B\) along \(\langle f,g \rangle : A \to B\times B\) (L-R Exercise 3.32). Elementwise, \(\langle fx, gx \rangle \in \delta_B\) iff \(fx = gx\).



Pullbacks







Definition 21.1 (Pullback) Given \(A_0 \xrightarrow{f_0} B \xleftarrow{f_1} A_1\), a pullback (or fibered product) is an object \(P\) with maps \(\pi_0, \pi_1\) making the square commute, \[
\begin{CD}
P @>{\pi_1}>> A_1\\
@V{\pi_0}VV @VV{f_1}V\\
A_0 @>{f_0}>> B
\end{CD}
\] such that for all \(a_0 : T \to A_0\), \(a_1 : T\to A_1\) with \(f_0 a_0 = f_1 a_1\) there is a unique \(a : T \to P\) with \(\pi_0 a = a_0\) and \(\pi_1 a = a_1\). We write \(P = A_0 \times_B A_1\).




In \(\mathcal{S}\): \(A_0 \times_B A_1 = \{(a_0,a_1) \in A_0\times A_1 : f_0 a_0 = f_1 a_1\}\). This description already suggests how to construct pullbacks.







Proposition 21.1 If a category has binary products and equalizers, it has pullbacks.










NoteProof






Proof. Form \(A_0 \times A_1\) with projections \(p_0, p_1\), and let \(e : P \rightarrowtail A_0 \times A_1\) be the equalizer of \(f_0 p_0\) and \(f_1 p_1\). Set \(\pi_k = p_k e\). A pair \(a_0, a_1\) with \(f_0 a_0 = f_1 a_1\) is a map \(\langle a_0,a_1 \rangle : T \to A_0\times A_1\) equalizing \(f_0p_0\) and \(f_1p_1\). So it factors uniquely through \(e\).




Pullbacks are remarkably versatile. Many earlier constructions are special cases:







Data \(A_0 \xrightarrow{f_0} B \xleftarrow{f_1} A_1\)
Pullback




\(B = 1\) (so \(f_0, f_1\) are forced)
the product \(A_0 \times A_1\)


\(f_1 = j\) a mono (a part of \(B\))
the inverse image \(f_0^{-1}(j)\), a part of \(A_0\)


\(f_0, f_1\) both monos
the intersection of the two parts


\(f_1 = b : 1 \to B\) an element
the fiber of \(f_0\) over \(b\)


\(f_0 = f_1 = f : A \to B\)
the kernel pair of \(f\), i.e. \(\{(a,a') : fa = fa'\}\)



The second row needs one small fact. It will be used constantly once we have the subobject classifier.







Lemma 21.1 Monos are stable under pullback: in the square of Definition 21.1, if \(f_1\) is mono, then so is \(\pi_0\).










NoteProof






Proof. Let \(\pi_0 y = \pi_0 y'\). Then \(f_1 \pi_1 y = f_0 \pi_0 y = f_0 \pi_0 y' = f_1 \pi_1 y'\), so \(\pi_1 y = \pi_1 y'\) since \(f_1\) is mono. Now \(y\) and \(y'\) have the same two projections. By uniqueness in the pullback property, \(y = y'\).




Combining the first row with the construction of equalizers from products and inverse images gives the converse of Proposition 21.1:







Proposition 21.2 If a category has a terminal object and pullbacks, it has binary products and equalizers.







Finite limits in general
All of the above are instances of one notion. The input is a diagram: a family of objects with some maps between them. Following L-R, a diagram shape is a directed graph \(J \underset{c}{\overset{d}{\rightrightarrows}} I\) (vertices \(I\), edges \(J\), domain map \(d\), codomain map \(c\)). A diagram of that shape in \(\mathcal{C}\) consists of objects \(A_i\) (\(i \in I\)) and maps \(f_j : A_{d(j)} \to A_{c(j)}\) (\(j \in J\)). The shape is finite if \(I\) and \(J\) are finite.







Definition 22.1 (Limit) A cone over the diagram with vertex \(L\) is a family \(\pi_i : L \to A_i\) with \(f_j \pi_{d(j)} = \pi_{c(j)}\) for all \(j\). A limit is a cone that is universal: every cone \((a_i : T \to A_i)_i\) factors as \(a_i = \pi_i a\) through a unique \(a : T \to L\).




In words: a map \(T \to L\) is the same thing as a compatible family of maps \(T \to A_i\). In \(\mathcal{S}\), \(L\) is the set of compatible families of elements \((a_i)_{i\in I}\) with \(f_j(a_{d(j)}) = a_{c(j)}\).



Shape
Limit




empty graph
terminal object \(1\)


two vertices, no edges
binary product


\(\bullet \rightrightarrows \bullet\)
equalizer


\(\bullet \to \bullet \leftarrow \bullet\)
pullback









NoteAxiom: Finite limits



\(\mathcal{S}\) has limits of all finite diagrams.


It is enough to check a few cases.







Theorem 22.1 If a category has finite products (including the empty product, i.e. a terminal object) and equalizers, then it has all finite limits.










NoteProof






Proof. (Sketch; this is Proposition 21.1 writ large.) Form the two products \(\prod_{i\in I} A_i\) and \(\prod_{j\in J} A_{c(j)}\) and two maps between them, specified by their components. Writing \(p_i\) for the projections of the first product and \(q_j\) for those of the second, define \[
\textstyle\prod_{i} A_i \underset{v}{\overset{u}{\rightrightarrows}} \prod_{j} A_{c(j)},
\qquad
q_j\, u = p_{c(j)}, \qquad q_j\, v = f_j\, p_{d(j)} .
\] A family \((a_i)_i\), i.e. a map \(\langle a_i \rangle_i : T \to \prod_i A_i\), is equalized by \(u\) and \(v\) iff \(a_{c(j)} = f_j a_{d(j)}\) for every edge \(j\), i.e. iff it is a cone. So if \(e : L \rightarrowtail \prod_i A_i\) is the equalizer of \(u\) and \(v\), then \(\pi_i = p_i e\) is the limit cone.











Corollary 22.1 A category with a terminal object and pullbacks has all finite limits.




So for the topos axioms we can take “finite limits” to mean “\(1\) and pullbacks”, or “\(1\), binary products, and equalizers”. These are the forms we will actually check in examples.
Foundational aside. Compare this with \(\mathsf{ZFC}\). There, \(\{a \in A : f(a) = g(a)\}\) comes from Separation, and \(A \times B\) is built from Pairing, Union, Power Set, and Separation. Here, these constructions are axiomatized directly by what they do, and no internal membership structure of the objects is ever invoked.



Colimits by duality
Every category \(\mathcal{C}\) has an opposite \(\mathcal{C}^\mathrm{op}\): same objects, all arrows reversed. A colimit in \(\mathcal{C}\) is a limit in \(\mathcal{C}^\mathrm{op}\). So every definition and theorem above dualizes for free: reverse the arrows, swap “mono” and “epi”.








Shape
Limit
Colimit

terminal \(1\)
initial \(0\)

\(\bullet \rightrightarrows \bullet\)
equalizer

\(\bullet\to\bullet\leftarrow\bullet\) / \(\bullet\leftarrow\bullet\to\bullet\)

Definition 23.1 (Coequalizer) Given \(A \underset{g}{\overset{f}{\rightrightarrows}} B\), a coequalizer is \(q : B \to Q\) with \(qf = qg\) such that every \(h : B \to Z\) with \(hf = hg\) factors as \(h = \bar h q\) for a unique \(\bar h : Q \to Z\). \[
A \underset{g}{\overset{f}{\rightrightarrows}} B \xrightarrow{\;q\;} Q
\]




Dually to Proposition 20.1, every coequalizer is an epimorphism.
In \(\mathcal{S}\). \(Q = B/{\sim}\), where \(\sim\) is the equivalence relation generated by \(f(a) \sim g(a)\) for \(a \in A\), and \(q\) is the quotient map. A map out of \(Q\) is a map out of \(B\) that respects the identifications. Equalizers are comprehension (cutting out by an equation); coequalizers are quotients (gluing by identifications).
Pushouts are the dual of pullbacks. In \(\mathcal{S}\), the pushout of \(B_0 \xleftarrow{f_0} A \xrightarrow{f_1} B_1\) is \((B_0 + B_1)/{\sim}\) with \(f_0(a) \sim f_1(a)\), i.e. \(B_0\) and \(B_1\) glued along \(A\). In \(\mathbf{Top}\), gluing two closed disks along their boundary circle gives the sphere \(S^2\).
By duality, from Theorem 22.1 and Corollary 22.1:







Theorem 23.1 A category has all finite colimits iff it has an initial object, binary sums, and coequalizers, iff it has an initial object and pushouts.










NoteAxiom: Finite colimits



\(\mathcal{S}\) has colimits of all finite diagrams.









Remark 23.1 (Finite colimits come for free in a topos). In Lawvere and Tierney’s original axiomatization, finite colimits were an explicit axiom. It was later shown that they follow from finite limits together with power objects (i.e. exponentials plus a subobject classifier). This is due to Mikkelsen, with a slick proof by Paré (1974) via the monadicity of the power-object functor. So axiom (2) in our preview is redundant. We keep it on the list because it is convenient, and because Lawvere–Rosebrugh assume the initial set and binary sums as axioms for \(\mathcal{S}\) long before power objects are available.




The duality between limits and colimits is a feature of the definitions, not a symmetry of \(\mathcal{S}\). For instance, \(0\) is a strict initial object: any map \(X \to 0\) is an isomorphism. The dual statement (every map \(1 \to X\) is an isomorphism) is plainly false. So \(\mathcal{S}^\mathrm{op}\) is a perfectly good category with finite limits and colimits, but it is not “like \(\mathcal{S}\)”. Strictness of \(0\), together with disjointness of sums, holds in every topos. Other asymmetries, such as “every epi splits” (the Axiom of Choice), are special to \(\mathcal{S}\) and will be among the extra axioms that single it out.



Summary

Finite limits = terminal object + pullbacks (equivalently: finite products + equalizers). They give us products, graphs, diagonals, equalizers (comprehension by equations), inverse images, intersections, fibers, and kernel pairs.
Finite colimits = initial object + pushouts (equivalently: finite sums + coequalizers). They give us sums and quotients. In a topos they follow from the other axioms.
Method. Every construction is specified by a universal property (existence + uniqueness of an induced map). This determines it up to unique isomorphism and is tested on generalized elements \(T \to X\).
Next time: exponentials \(B^A\) (maps as an object) and the subobject classifier \(\Omega\) (parts as maps). Together with today’s axioms, these give the full definition of an elementary topos.



Exercises







Exercise 25.1 Show from the universal property that \(B \times A \cong A \times B\) and \(1 \times A \cong A\). Which equation needs the uniqueness clause? (L-R 3.21, 3.22)











Exercise 25.2 Show that the equalizer of \(f, g : A \rightrightarrows B\) is the inverse image of the diagonal \(\delta_B\) along \(\langle f,g \rangle\). (L-R 3.32)











Exercise 25.3 (Pasting lemma) In a commutative diagram \[
\begin{CD}
X @>>> Y @>>> Z\\
@VVV @VVV @VVV\\
U @>>> V @>>> W
\end{CD}
\] suppose the right square is a pullback. Show that the left square is a pullback iff the outer rectangle is.











Exercise 25.4 Show that the kernel pair \(K \rightrightarrows A\) of \(f : A \to B\) (the pullback of \(f\) along itself) is, in \(\mathcal{S}\), the equivalence relation \(\{(a,a') : fa = fa'\}\). Then show that the coequalizer of the kernel pair is \(A \to f(A)\), the image of \(f\). (L-R 3.44)











Exercise 25.5 Let \(X\) be a set. Show that the slice category \(\mathcal{S}/X\) (objects: maps \(E \to X\); arrows: commuting triangles) has all finite limits. What is the terminal object? What is the product of \(E \to X\) and \(F \to X\)? (L-R 3.48)











Exercise 25.6 Show that \(\mathbf{Grp}\) has all finite limits. Does it have finite colimits? What is the sum of \(\mathbb{Z}\) and \(\mathbb{Z}\)? (L-R 3.47)

Where we are
The axioms on \(\mathcal{S}\) so far (L–R, Ch. 1–3):
Every one of these axioms has the same shape: an object is introduced together with a bijection between two kinds of maps. For products, maps into \(Y_0 \times Y_1\) correspond to pairs of maps; for sums, maps out of \(A + B\) correspond to pairs of maps; for \(2\), maps into \(2\) correspond to parts. Chapter 5 makes this shape explicit and then uses it for one more construction.

\(\mathcal{S}\) is a category

Associative composition, identities.

Terminal set \(1\); initial set \(0\); \(1\) separates mappings

Elements of \(A\) are maps \(1 \to A\), and maps are determined by their values on elements.

Binary sums

\(A + B\) with injections, universal among pairs \(A \to Y\), \(B \to Y\).

Finite inverse limits

Products and equalizers (hence pullbacks and all finite limits).

Membership via truth values

Every part of \(A\) has a unique characteristic map \(A \to 2\), and every \(A \to 2\) is one.
