title: Mapping Sets and Exponentials
section: The two-level pattern, illustrated by products
text:
The two-level pattern, illustrated by products
L–R write the defining property of the product as a “fraction” \[
\frac{\;X \longrightarrow Y_0 \times Y_1\;}{\;X \longrightarrow Y_0, \quad X \longrightarrow Y_1\;}
\] meaning: there is a natural process turning a map of the upper kind into one of the lower kind, a natural process in the other direction, and the two are mutually inverse.
Level 1 (crude): “there is such an invertible process, for all \(X, Y_0, Y_1\).”
Level 2 (refined): the process is carried out by a functorial construction plus composition with one specific map. And the specific map is obtained by bootstrapping: feed the crude process an identity map.

Downward. Take \(X = Y_0 \times Y_1\) and put \(1_{Y_0\times Y_1}\) above the bar. Below the bar we get two specific maps — the projections \(p_0, p_1\). The general downward process is then composition with them: \(f \mapsto (p_0 f, \, p_1 f)\).
Upward. Take \(Y_0 = Y_1 = X\) and put \((1_X, 1_X)\) below the bar. Above the bar we get a specific map, the diagonal \(\delta_X = \langle 1_X, 1_X\rangle : X \to X \times X\). Using the functoriality of \(\times\) on maps, \[
(f_0 \times f_1)\langle x_0, x_1\rangle = \langle f_0 x_0, f_1 x_1 \rangle,
\qquad (g_0 \times g_1)(f_0 \times f_1) = (g_0 f_0) \times (g_1 f_1),
\] the general upward process is \[
\langle f_0, f_1 \rangle = (f_0 \times f_1)\,\delta_X .
\] (Check it by composing both sides with \(p_0\) and \(p_1\).)


The pattern. Universal property \(=\) natural bijection of hom-sets. Applying the bijection to an identity produces a universal map (here \(p_0, p_1\) and \(\delta_X\)), and the general bijection is “apply the functor, then compose with the universal map.”

We now run exactly this program for a new construction.

title: Mapping Sets and Exponentials
text:
Exponentiation

The crude idea
For sets \(B\), \(Y\) we want a set \(Y^B\) with \[
\frac{\;X \longrightarrow Y^B\;}{\;X \times B \longrightarrow Y\;}
\] natural in \(X\) (and \(Y\)). Bootstrap immediately with \(X = 1\): since \(1 \times B \cong B\), \[
\frac{\;1 \longrightarrow Y^B\;}{\;B \longrightarrow Y\;}
\] so the elements of \(Y^B\) must correspond exactly to the maps \(B \to Y\). This determines what \(Y^B\) “is,” just as the case \(X = 1\) of the product property told us that the elements of \(Y_0 \times Y_1\) are pairs of elements.


Families of maps, and naming schemes
A map \(f : X \times B \to Y\) (a “function of two variables”) is the same as a family of maps \(B \to Y\) parametrized by \(X\): for each element \(x : 1 \to X\) put \[
f_x : B \xrightarrow{\ \langle x \circ !_B,\, 1_B\rangle\ } X \times B \xrightarrow{\ f\ } Y,
\qquad f_x(b) = f(x, b).
\] Think of \(X\) as a set of names and of \(f\) as a naming scheme: \(x\) names \(f_x\). A naming scheme may or may not have the two properties

every map \(B \to Y\) has at least one name (\(x \mapsto f_x\) is onto), and
every nameable map has only one name (\(x \mapsto f_x\) is one-to-one).

A scheme with both properties is a universal naming scheme. We then write \(Y^B\) for the set of names, \(\mathrm{eval}: Y^B \times B \to Y\) for the scheme (“evaluation”), and \(\ulcorner f \urcorner\) for the unique name of \(f : B \to Y\): \[
\mathrm{eval}(\ulcorner f \urcorner, b) = f(b).
\]


The axiom
A universal scheme compares uniquely to every scheme, and that is what we take as the axiom.






NoteAxiom: Exponentiation



For any sets \(B, Y\) there is a set \(Y^B\) and a map \(\mathrm{eval}: Y^B \times B \to Y\) such that for every \(X\) and every \(f : X \times B \to Y\) there is a unique \(\ulcorner f \urcorner : X \to Y^B\) with \[
\mathrm{eval}\circ (\ulcorner f \urcorner \times 1_B) = f .
\] \[
\begin{array}{ccc}
Y^B \times B & \xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{eval}\ } & Y \\[2pt]
{\scriptstyle \ulcorner f \urcorner \times 1_B}\Big\uparrow & \nearrow_{\scriptstyle f} & \\[2pt]
X \times B & &
\end{array}
\]


We call \(\ulcorner f \urcorner\) the transpose (or name, or curried form) of \(f\). Explicitly, \(\ulcorner f \urcorner(x) = \ulcorner f_x \urcorner\): the parametrized name of \(f\) assigns to \(x\) the name of \(f_x\).
Note the bootstrap again: \(\mathrm{eval}\) is the map corresponding to \(1_{Y^B}\), i.e. the unique \(f\) with \(\ulcorner f \urcorner = 1_{Y^B}\). It plays the role the projections played for products.






TipComparison with \(\mathsf{ZFC}\)





In \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) the set of functions \({}^B Y\) is constructed: it is carved out of \(\mathcal{P}(B \times Y)\) by Separation, so its existence is a consequence of Power Set. Here the direction is reversed: \(Y^B\) is primitive, characterized only by how maps into it behave, and the power set will appear below as the special case \(2^B\). Note also that the hom-set \(\mathcal{S}(B, Y)\) is a collection in the metatheory; the axiom says that it is internalized by an object of \(\mathcal{S}\), whose elements \(1 \to Y^B\) correspond to it.





Example: three descriptions of a motion
Let \(B\) be the particles of a cloud, \(E\) the points of space, \(T\) the instants of a time interval. A motion of the cloud can be given in three equivalent ways: \[
T \longrightarrow E^B, \qquad T \times B \longrightarrow E, \qquad B \longrightarrow E^T .
\] The first assigns to each instant a placement of the cloud; the middle one assigns to each instant and particle a position; the last assigns to each particle its path. The passage between the outer two uses the axiom twice and the twist \(B \times T \cong T \times B\) once.
Maps into a mapping set can always be “transformed down,” but maps out of a mapping set (operators, functionals) cannot. That is why the choice of description matters:

center of mass is a functional \(E^B \to E\), so to get the trajectory of the center of mass we need the motion in the form \(T \to E^B\) and compose: \(T \to E^B \to E\);
velocity is an operator \(E^T \to V^T\), so to get the velocity field we need \(B \to E^T\), compose to get \(B \to V^T\), and transpose twice to get \(T \to V^B\) (the velocity field at each instant).

title: Mapping Sets and Exponentials
text:
Functoriality and naturality

Exponentials are functorial in both variables







Proposition 17.1 (Covariance in the base (L–R 5.2)) 
Given \(\varphi : Y_1 \to Y_2\), there is a unique \(\varphi^B : Y_1^B \to Y_2^B\) with \[
\varphi^B \ulcorner g \urcorner = \ulcorner \varphi g \urcorner \quad \text{for all } g : B \to Y_1 .
\]










NoteProof






Proof. To make a map into \(Y_2^B\), it suffices to make a map \(Y_1^B \times B \to Y_2\); take \(\varphi \circ \mathrm{eval}_1\) and set \(\varphi^B := \ulcorner \varphi\, \mathrm{eval}_1 \urcorner\), so \(\mathrm{eval}_2(\varphi^B \times 1_B) = \varphi\,\mathrm{eval}_1\). Then \[
\mathrm{eval}_2(\varphi^B\ulcorner g \urcorner \times 1_B)
= \mathrm{eval}_2(\varphi^B \times 1_B)(\ulcorner g \urcorner \times 1_B)
= \varphi\, \mathrm{eval}_1(\ulcorner g \urcorner \times 1_B) = \varphi g
= \mathrm{eval}_2(\ulcorner \varphi g \urcorner \times 1_B),
\] and the uniqueness clause of the axiom gives \(\varphi^B\ulcorner g \urcorner = \ulcorner \varphi g \urcorner\). The argument works verbatim for generalized elements \(g : X \times B \to Y_1\).











Proposition 17.2 (Contravariance in the exponent (L–R 5.4, 5.5)) 
Given \(\beta : B_2 \to B_1\), there is a unique \(Y^\beta : Y^{B_1} \to Y^{B_2}\) with \[
Y^\beta \ulcorner g \urcorner = \ulcorner g \beta \urcorner, \qquad\text{namely}\qquad Y^\beta = \ulcorner \mathrm{eval}_1 \circ (1 \times \beta) \urcorner .
\] Moreover \(Y^{\beta\alpha} = Y^\alpha Y^\beta\) and \(Y^{1_B} = 1\).










NoteProof






Proof. The construction of \(Y^\beta\) is as in Proposition 17.1. For the composition law, evaluate both sides on a name: \(Y^\alpha Y^\beta \ulcorner g \urcorner = Y^\alpha\ulcorner g\beta \urcorner = \ulcorner (g\beta)\alpha \urcorner\) and \(Y^{\beta\alpha}\ulcorner g \urcorner = \ulcorner g(\beta\alpha) \urcorner\). These agree by associativity of composition — the proposition is “a higher expression of associativity.”




When \(\beta\) is a monomorphism, \(Y^\beta\) is restriction of maps to a part of the domain.
In the language of last time (cf. L–R Ex. 5.17):

\((-)^B : \mathcal{S}\to \mathcal{S}\), \(Y \mapsto Y^B\), \(\varphi \mapsto \varphi^B\) is a (covariant) functor,
\(Y^{(-)} : \mathcal{S}^{op} \to \mathcal{S}\), \(B \mapsto Y^B\), \(\beta \mapsto Y^\beta\) is a contravariant functor,
\(- \times B : \mathcal{S}\to \mathcal{S}\), \(X \mapsto X \times B\), \(\xi \mapsto \xi \times 1_B\) is a functor.



The transpose is a natural bijection
Fix \(B\). For each \(X\) and \(Y\) the axiom gives a bijection \[
\theta_{X,Y} : \mathcal{S}(X \times B,Y) \;\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }\; \mathcal{S}(X,Y^B), \qquad f \mapsto \ulcorner f \urcorner.
\]







Proposition 17.3 (Naturality of transposition) 
For \(\xi : X' \to X\) and \(\varphi : Y \to Y'\), \[
\ulcorner f \circ (\xi \times 1_B) \urcorner = \ulcorner f \urcorner \circ \xi,
\qquad
\ulcorner \varphi \circ f \urcorner = \varphi^B \circ \ulcorner f \urcorner.
\] That is, \(\theta\) is a natural isomorphism between the functors \(\mathcal{S}(-\times B,-)\) and \(\mathcal{S}(-,(-)^B)\) from \(\mathcal{S}^{op}\times\mathcal{S}\) to sets.










NoteProof






Proof. The second identity is Proposition 17.1 for generalized elements. For the first, \(\mathrm{eval}(\ulcorner f \urcorner\xi \times 1_B) = \mathrm{eval}(\ulcorner f \urcorner \times 1_B)(\xi \times 1_B) = f(\xi \times 1_B)\), so \(\ulcorner f \urcorner\xi\) satisfies the defining equation of \(\ulcorner f(\xi\times 1_B) \urcorner\); apply uniqueness.




So the crude “bar” notation of L–R means precisely: a natural isomorphism of hom-functors. Two consequences are worth stating now.
1. Representability. For fixed \(B, Y\), the contravariant functor \(X \mapsto \mathcal{S}(X \times B,Y)\) is isomorphic to \(\mathcal{S}(-,Y^B)\); one says \(Y^B\) represents it. The axiom can be read as: “this functor is representable.” (We will see in a few weeks that this pins \(Y^B\) down up to unique isomorphism — the Yoneda lemma.)
2. Adjunction. Naturality in both variables says that \(-\times B\) is left adjoint to \((-)^B\), written \(- \times B \dashv (-)^B\). This is the formal definition we will meet next week; for now, compare the two universal maps with the product case:









product \(\;Y_0 \times Y_1\)
exponential \(\;Y^B\)




bijection
\(\dfrac{X \to Y_0 \times Y_1}{X \to Y_0,\; X \to Y_1}\)
\(\dfrac{X \to Y^B}{X \times B \to Y}\)


universal map from \(1\) above the bar
projections \(p_0, p_1\)
\(\mathrm{eval}: Y^B \times B \to Y\)


universal map from \(1\) below the bar
diagonal \(\delta_X\)
\(\eta_X = \ulcorner 1_{X\times B} \urcorner : X \to (X\times B)^B\)


downward process
\(f \mapsto (p_0 f, p_1 f)\)
\(g \mapsto \mathrm{eval}\circ (g \times 1_B)\)


upward process
\(\langle f_0, f_1\rangle = (f_0\times f_1)\,\delta_X\)
\(\ulcorner f \urcorner = f^B \circ \eta_X\)



The last entry is the second naturality identity applied to \(\varphi = f\) and the identity: \(\ulcorner f \urcorner = \ulcorner f \circ 1_{X\times B} \urcorner = f^B\ulcorner 1_{X \times B} \urcorner\). In elements, \(\eta_X(x) = \ulcorner b \mapsto \langle x, b\rangle \urcorner\). (\(\eta\) and \(\mathrm{eval}\) are the unit and counit of the adjunction.)






TipOptional: composition is itself a map (L–R 5.6)





Transposing \(Y_2^{Y_1} \times Y_1^B \times B \xrightarrow{1 \times \mathrm{eval}} Y_2^{Y_1} \times Y_1 \xrightarrow{\mathrm{eval}} Y_2\) gives \[
c : Y_2^{Y_1} \times Y_1^B \to Y_2^B, \qquad c(\ulcorner \varphi \urcorner, \ulcorner g \urcorner) = \ulcorner \varphi g \urcorner.
\] Transposing once more gives \(Y_2^{Y_1} \to (Y_2^B)^{(Y_1^B)}\), \(\ulcorner \varphi \urcorner\mapsto \ulcorner \varphi^B \urcorner\): the functor \((-)^B\) is itself represented by an internal map. The operation that defines a category is internalized.
crumbs: The View from Category Theory - Topoi

title: Mapping Sets and Exponentials
text:
Power objects
Combine the truth-value axiom with the exponential axiom: \[
\frac{\;1 \longrightarrow 2^B\;}{\;B \longrightarrow 2\;}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\frac{\;B \longrightarrow 2\;}{\;\text{part of } B\;}.
\] So the elements of \(2^B\) are names of parts of \(B\) — \(2^B\) is the power set, now as a special case of mapping sets. The evaluation map is membership: if \(\varphi\) is the characteristic map of the part \(i\), then \[
[\, b \in i \,] := \mathrm{eval}(\ulcorner \varphi \urcorner, b) = \varphi(b) \in 2 .
\] Contravariant functoriality has a familiar meaning:







Exercise 17.1 (L–R 5.7) For \(\beta : B_2 \to B_1\), the map \(2^\beta : 2^{B_1} \to 2^{B_2}\) represents taking inverse images along \(\beta\) of parts of \(B_1\). (Use: the inverse image of a part is a pullback, and the characteristic map of a pullback is a composite.)










TipTeaser: Cantor’s theorem without elements





Compare Cantor’s theorem in the cardinals notes. Lawvere’s fixed point theorem, which we will see later, shows: if \(g : B \times B \to Y\) is such that every map \(B \to Y\) is of the form \(g(b_0, -)\), then every \(\tau: Y \to Y\) has a fixed point. Since \(\neg : 2 \to 2\) has no fixed point, no \(B \to 2^B\) can be onto names. The diagonal argument is the bootstrap with \(\delta_B\).
crumbs: The View from Category Theory - Topoi

title: Mapping Sets and Exponentials
text:
The exponential laws
To justify the notation \(Y^B\) we want \(|Y^B| = |Y|^{|B|}\) for finite sets, and more generally the rules of exponent arithmetic as isomorphisms. L–R check each one by constructing explicit inverse maps and testing on elements. With naturality we can do all of them with one lemma.







Lemma 17.1 (Representability lemma) 
If there are bijections \(\theta_T : \mathcal{S}(T,A) \cong \mathcal{S}(T,A')\) natural in \(T\), then \(a := \theta_A(1_A) : A \to A'\) is an isomorphism (and \(\theta_T = a \circ -\)). The same holds with \(\mathcal{S}(A,T) \cong \mathcal{S}(A',T)\) natural in \(T\).










NoteProof






Proof. For \(h : T \to A\), naturality applied to \(h\) gives \(\theta_T(h) = \theta_T(1_A \circ h) = \theta_A(1_A) \circ h = a h\). Let \(a' := \theta_{A'}^{-1}(1_{A'}) : A' \to A\). Then \(a a' = \theta_{A'}(a') = 1_{A'}\), and \(\theta_A(a' a) = a a' a = a = \theta_A(1_A)\), so \(a'a = 1_A\) since \(\theta_A\) is injective. This is the bootstrap once more: everything is determined by where the identity goes.




So to prove \(A \cong A'\) it suffices to give a natural bijection between maps from an arbitrary \(T\) into \(A\) and into \(A'\) — i.e., to compare generalized elements.







Proposition 17.4 (Exponential laws (L–R 5.8–5.10)) 
\[
\begin{aligned}
Y^1 &\cong Y, & 1^B &\cong 1, & (Y_0 \times Y_1)^B &\cong Y_0^B \times Y_1^B,\\
Y^{X \times B} &\cong (Y^B)^X, & Y^0 &\cong 1, & Y^{A+B} &\cong Y^A \times Y^B .
\end{aligned}
\]










NoteProof






Proof. Each is a chain of natural bijections, followed by Lemma 17.1. For example: \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{S}(T,(Y^B)^X) &\cong \mathcal{S}(T \times X,Y^B) \cong \mathcal{S}((T \times X) \times B,Y) \\
&\cong \mathcal{S}(T \times (X \times B),Y) \cong \mathcal{S}(T,Y^{X\times B}),
\end{aligned}
\] using the associativity isomorphism of products (natural in \(T\)) in the middle. Similarly \[
\mathcal{S}(T,(Y_0\times Y_1)^B) \cong \mathcal{S}(T\times B,Y_0 \times Y_1)
\cong \mathcal{S}(T \times B,Y_0) \times \mathcal{S}(T\times B,Y_1)
\cong \mathcal{S}(T,Y_0^B \times Y_1^B).
\] \(Y^1 \cong Y\) and \(1^B \cong 1\) are the same kind of one-line computation.
The laws involving \(0\) and \(+\) need one more ingredient, which is interesting in its own right.











Theorem 17.1 (Exponentials force distributivity) 
In any category with finite products, finite sums, and exponentials, \[
T \times 0 \cong 0, \qquad (A + B) \times T \cong A \times T + B \times T .
\]










NoteProof






Proof. Now we use the contravariant version of the lemma, natural in the codomain \(Y\): \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{S}((A+B) \times T,Y) &\cong \mathcal{S}(A+B,Y^T) \cong \mathcal{S}(A,Y^T) \times \mathcal{S}(B,Y^T) \\
&\cong \mathcal{S}(A \times T,Y) \times \mathcal{S}(B\times T,Y) \cong \mathcal{S}(A \times T + B \times T,Y).
\end{aligned}
\] Likewise \(\mathcal{S}(0 \times T,Y) \cong \mathcal{S}(0,Y^T)\) is a singleton for every \(Y\), so \(0 \times T\) is initial.




Distributivity does not mention exponentials, yet it follows from them (L–R return to this in §7.2): a left adjoint preserves sums, and \(-\times T\) is a left adjoint. With it, \[
\mathcal{S}(T,Y^{A+B}) \cong \mathcal{S}(T\times(A+B),Y) \cong \mathcal{S}(T\times A,Y) \times \mathcal{S}(T\times B,Y)
\cong \mathcal{S}(T,Y^A \times Y^B),
\] and \(\mathcal{S}(T,Y^0) \cong \mathcal{S}(T \times 0,Y) \cong \mathcal{S}(0,Y) \cong \mathcal{S}(T,1)\). This finishes Proposition 17.4.
Counting. Writing a finite \(B\) as \(1 + 1 + \cdots + 1\) (\(n\) summands), the laws give \(Y^B \cong Y \times \cdots \times Y\), so \(|Y^B| = |Y|^n\). In particular \(|2^B| = 2^{|B|}\).






ImportantMethodological point



L–R verify these isomorphisms by checking on elements \(1 \to Y^B\). That is legitimate in \(\mathcal{S}\) because \(1\) separates mappings — but this axiom fails in most toposes. The argument with generalized elements \(T \to Y^B\) uses only the exponential axiom and therefore works in every cartesian closed category.

title: Mapping Sets and Exponentials
text:
Elementary toposes
We can now collect the axioms into a definition that no longer mentions \(\mathcal{S}\).






NoteDefinition: elementary topos



A category \(\mathcal{E}\) is an elementary topos if

\(\mathcal{E}\) has finite limits (a terminal object and pullbacks suffice);
\(\mathcal{E}\) has exponentials: for all \(B, Y\) an object \(Y^B\) with \(\mathrm{eval}: Y^B \times B \to Y\) as in the axiom (a category with 1 and 2 is called cartesian closed);
\(\mathcal{E}\) has a subobject classifier: an object \(\Omega\) and a map \(\mathrm{true} : 1 \to \Omega\) such that for every mono \(m : A' \rightarrowtail A\) there is a unique \(\chi_m : A \to \Omega\) making \[
\begin{array}{ccc}
A' & \longrightarrow & 1\\
{\scriptstyle m}\big\downarrow & & \big\downarrow{\scriptstyle \mathrm{true}}\\
A & \xrightarrow[\ \chi_m\ ]{} & \Omega
\end{array}
\] a pullback.



In \(\mathcal{S}\), \(\Omega = 2\) and condition 3 is L–R’s axiom of membership via truth values, formulated with pullbacks. Conditions 2 and 3 together give power objects \(\Omega^B\), whose elements name parts of \(B\).
Remarkably, what we did not list follows: every elementary topos also has finite colimits (initial object, sums, coequalizers). This is a nontrivial theorem (due to Paré); the distributivity argument above gives a small taste of how much the exponentials carry.

What is special about \(\mathcal{S}\)
\(\mathcal{S}\) is a topos that satisfies further axioms:

\(1\) separates mappings (and \(0 \not\cong 1\)): \(\mathcal{S}\) is well-pointed;
\(\Omega = 2 = 1 + 1\): the topos is Boolean (internal logic is classical);
a natural numbers object (the categorical axiom of infinity);
the axiom of choice: every epimorphism has a section.

These, added to the topos axioms, make up Lawvere’s Elementary Theory of the Category of Sets (ETCS), which L–R summarize in Chapter 6. Comparing with \(\mathsf{ZFC}\): Power Set and Separation are replaced by \(\Omega^B\) and the subobject classifier, Infinity by the natural numbers object, Choice by split epis — and there is no counterpart of Replacement. We take up this comparison in Week 14.


Examples and non-examples

\(\mathcal{S}/X\) (L–R Ex. 5.12): an object is an \(X\)-indexed family \((A_x)_{x\in X}\); exponentials are computed fiberwise, \((Y^B)_x = Y_x^{B_x}\). A topos — “sets varying over a discrete parameter.”
\(G\)-sets for a group \(G\) (Ex. 5.13): \(Y^X\) is the set of all maps \(X \to Y\) with \((g\cdot f)(x) = g\, f(g^{-1}x)\); the inverse is essential. A topos, with \(\Omega = 2\) (trivial action).
\(M\)-sets for a monoid \(M\): the exponential is subtler, and \(\Omega\) is the set of left ideals of \(M\) — e.g. for \(M = (\mathbb{N}, +)\), “sets evolving in discrete time,” \(\Omega\) is infinite. A topos that is not Boolean: here condition 3 holds but \(\Omega \neq 1+1\).
Posets (Ex. 5.14): cartesian closed (\(Y^X\) = monotone maps, ordered pointwise), but not a topos: the identity map from a two-element discrete poset to a two-element chain is mono and epi but not iso, which cannot happen in a topos.
Finite-dimensional vector spaces with \(\times = \oplus\) (Ex. 5.11): not cartesian closed. If \(L(B,Y)\) were an exponential, then \(\dim \mathrm{Hom}(X \oplus B, Y) = (x + b)y\) would equal \(\dim \mathrm{Hom}(X, L(B,Y)) = xby\) for all dimensions. (The correct partner of \(L(B, Y)\) is \(\otimes\), not \(\oplus\).)

title: Mapping Sets and Exponentials
text:
Exercises







Exercise 17.2 L–R 5.3 and 5.16: functoriality of \((-)^B\), and the inverse maps for \(Y^{X\times B} \cong (Y^B)^X\), checked directly.











Exercise 17.3 L–R 5.17 (a)–(d): verify that \(\Delta\), \(-\times B\), \((-)^B\), and \(- \times -\) are functors. Then show that the diagonals \(\delta_X\) form a natural transformation from the identity functor to \((-\times-)\circ\Delta\), and that the \(\eta_X\) form one from the identity to \((-\times B)^B\).











Exercise 17.4 L–R 5.12 (\(\mathcal{S}/X\)) and 5.14 (posets): verify the universal property of the proposed exponentials.











Exercise 17.5 L–R 5.13 for a group \(G\). Bonus: for a monoid \(M\), show that \(Y^X := \{\)equivariant \(f : M \times X \to Y\}\) with \((m\cdot f)(n, x) = f(nm, x)\) is an exponential in \(M\)-sets.











Exercise 17.6 Using only arguments in the style of Lemma 17.1, show that in any cartesian closed category \(A \times (B + C) \cong A \times B + A \times C\) whenever the sums exist, and that any object admitting a map to \(0\) is itself initial.

title: A Gallery of Topoi
text:
What is special about \(\mathcal{S}\)
Recall the properties of \(\mathcal{S}\) that go beyond the topos axioms. For a topos \(\mathcal{E}\):
“Two-valued” was not on our earlier list. It is weaker than Boolean, and the examples below show that the two notions really differ.
In any topos, the parts of an object \(X\) form a lattice \(\operatorname{Sub}(X)\) (intersections are pullbacks, unions are images of sums). Each part \(A\) has a pseudo-complement \(\neg A\), the largest part disjoint from \(A\), and \(\operatorname{Sub}(X)\) is a Heyting algebra. Booleanness says \(A \vee \neg A = X\) for all parts \(A\), i.e. the internal logic satisfies excluded middle.
Two classical theorems connect the properties. We state them without proof (see Goldblatt, Topoi, or Mac Lane–Moerdijk).
Part 2 is the categorical form of a fact you may know from set theory: over a constructive base theory, \(\mathsf{AC}\) implies the law of excluded middle.
crumbs: The View from Category Theory - Topoi

title: A Gallery of Topoi
text:
Well-pointed

\(0 \not\cong 1\), and \(1\) separates maps: if \(f \neq g : A \to B\), there is \(a : 1 \to A\) with \(fa \neq ga\).

Boolean

Every part has a complement; equivalently \([\mathrm{true}, \mathrm{false}] : 1 + 1 \to \Omega\) is an isomorphism.

Two-valued

\(\Omega\) has exactly two elements \(1 \to \Omega\) (equivalently, \(1\) has exactly two parts, \(0\) and \(1\)).

Natural numbers object

An object \(\mathbb{N}\) with \(0 : 1 \to \mathbb{N}\), \(s : \mathbb{N}\to \mathbb{N}\) such that for every \(x_0 : 1 \to X\), \(f : X \to X\) there is a unique \(h : \mathbb{N}\to X\) with \(h0 = x_0\) and \(hs = fh\).

Choice

Every epimorphism has a section.













Theorem 18.1 (Two roads to classical logic) 
Let \(\mathcal{E}\) be a topos.

If \(\mathcal{E}\) is well-pointed, then \(\mathcal{E}\) is Boolean (and two-valued).
(Diaconescu) If every epimorphism in \(\mathcal{E}\) splits, then \(\mathcal{E}\) is Boolean.






Booleanness is the hinge. A topos that fails excluded middle fails both well-pointedness and choice. In \(\mathcal{S}\), the classicality of logic is not a separate assumption; it is forced by choice alone, and also by well-pointedness alone.
crumbs: The View from Category Theory - Topoi

title: A Gallery of Topoi
text:
The easy ones

Finite sets
\(\mathbf{FinSet}\), the full subcategory of finite sets, is a topos: finite limits of finite sets are finite, \(Y^B\) is finite, and \(\Omega = 2\). It is well-pointed, Boolean, and satisfies choice (without any appeal to \(\mathsf{AC}\): a surjection between finite sets has a section by induction).
But it has no natural numbers object (Exercise 18.1). The axiom of infinity is not part of being a topos.


The trivial topos
The category \(\mathbf{1}\) with one object and one arrow is a topos: its single object is terminal, initial, \(\Omega\), and every exponential. Here \(0 \cong 1\). Every statement is “true” — which is why nondegeneracy \(0 \not\cong 1\) appears in the definition of well-pointedness.


Slices: sets over \(X\)
We met \(\mathcal{S}/X\) in the notes on exponentials: an object is a map \(\alpha : A \to X\), i.e. an \(X\)-indexed family of sets \(A_x = \alpha^{-1}(x)\), and everything is computed fiberwise: \[
(A \times_X B)_x = A_x \times B_x, \qquad (Y^B)_x = Y_x^{B_x}, \qquad \Omega = (X \times 2 \to X), \quad \Omega_x = 2 .
\]

Terminal object: \(1_X : X \to X\), one point in every fiber.
Elements \(1 \to A\) are sections of \(\alpha\): a choice of one point in every fiber.
Not well-pointed (for \(|X| \ge 2\)): if one fiber of \(A\) is empty, \(A\) has no elements at all, yet if another fiber has two points, \(A\) has a non-identity automorphism (swap them).
Not two-valued: truth values \(1 \to \Omega\) are maps \(X \to 2\); there are \(2^{|X|}\) of them.
Boolean, with choice, and with a natural numbers object \(X \times \mathbb{N}\to X\): all fiberwise.

So: Boolean, but not well-pointed. “True” is now true at some indices and false at others.







Theorem 18.2 (Fundamental theorem of topos theory) 
If \(\mathcal{E}\) is a topos and \(X\) an object of \(\mathcal{E}\), then \(\mathcal{E}/X\) is a topos.










TipLooking ahead: dependent types





An object of \(\mathcal{E}/X\) is a “type depending on \(x : X\).” Pulling back along \(f : X' \to X\) is substitution, and it has a left adjoint \(\Sigma_f\) and a right adjoint \(\Pi_f\), which are exactly the dependent sum and dependent product of Martin-Löf type theory. This is the interpretation of type theory in locally cartesian closed categories that we return to in Week 14.
crumbs: The View from Category Theory - Topoi

title: A Gallery of Topoi
text:
\(G\)-sets: Boolean without choice
Let \(G\) be a group. An object of \(\mathcal{S}^G\) is a set with a \(G\)-action, a map is an equivariant map. Limits are computed on underlying sets with the induced action; the exponential \(Y^X\) is the set of all maps with \((g\cdot f)(x) = g\, f(g^{-1}x)\) (see the notes on exponentials).

Subobject classifier. A part is a \(G\)-invariant subset. Since \(G\) is a group, the complement of an invariant subset is invariant. So \(\Omega = 2\) with the trivial action, and \(\mathcal{S}^G\) is Boolean and two-valued.
Not well-pointed. Elements \(1 \to X\) are fixed points. If \(G \neq 1\), the action of \(G\) on itself by translation has no fixed points but many automorphisms.
Choice fails. The unique map \(G \to 1\) is surjective, hence an epimorphism. A section \(1 \to G\) would be a fixed point. There is none.

So Diaconescu’s theorem has no converse: Boolean does not imply choice.






TipConnection to Week 5



The first independence proofs for \(\mathsf{AC}\) (Fraenkel, Mostowski) used permutation models: a universe of sets built over atoms, keeping only the sets that are fixed by “enough” permutations of the atoms. These models can be presented as topoi of \(G\)-sets for a group \(G\) of permutations of the atoms (with a topology on \(G\), and only actions with open stabilizers). What we just saw — no fixed point, hence no section — is the simplest instance of why choice fails there.
crumbs: The View from Category Theory - Topoi

title: A Gallery of Topoi
text:
Presheaf topoi
\(\mathcal{S}/X\) and \(\mathcal{S}^G\) are both special cases of one construction.






NoteDefinition: presheaves



Let \(C\) be a small category. A presheaf on \(C\) is a functor \(P : C^{op} \to \mathcal{S}\); for \(x \in P(c)\) and \(f : d \to c\) we write \(x \cdot f := P(f)(x) \in P(d)\) (“restriction of \(x\) along \(f\)”). Maps of presheaves are natural transformations. The category of presheaves is written \(\mathcal{S}^{C^{op}}\).
For each object \(c\), the representable presheaf is \(\mathbf{y}c := C(-, c)\).


Limits of presheaves are computed pointwise: \((P \times Q)(c) = P(c) \times Q(c)\), and so on. A map of presheaves is mono iff each component is injective, and epi iff each component is surjective. So a part of \(P\) is a family of subsets \(A(c) \subseteq P(c)\) closed under restriction.

Guessing \(\Omega\): let the axioms tell you
How could we find \(\Omega\)? Suppose it exists. We need one fact about representables.







Lemma 18.1 (Maps out of a representable) 
For every presheaf \(P\) and object \(c\), the map \(\operatorname{Nat}(\mathbf{y}c, P) \to P(c)\), \(\alpha \mapsto \alpha_c(1_c)\), is a bijection.










NoteProof






Proof. Given \(\alpha\) and \(f : d \to c\), naturality of \(\alpha\) applied to \(f\) and the element \(1_c \in \mathbf{y}c(c)\) gives \[
\alpha_d(f) = \alpha_d(1_c \circ f) = \alpha_c(1_c)\cdot f .
\] So \(\alpha\) is determined by \(x := \alpha_c(1_c)\). Conversely, for any \(x \in P(c)\), the formula \(\alpha_d(f) := x \cdot f\) defines a natural transformation (check naturality using that \(P\) is a functor). This is the bootstrap trick from the notes on exponentials — everything is determined by where the identity goes — and it is a special case of the Yoneda lemma, which we will meet properly soon.




Now combine the lemma with the subobject classifier axiom: \[
\Omega(c) \;\cong\; \operatorname{Nat}(\mathbf{y}c, \Omega) \;\cong\; \operatorname{Sub}(\mathbf{y}c).
\] So \(\Omega(c)\) must be the set of parts of \(\mathbf{y}c\). A part of \(\mathbf{y}c\) is a set \(S\) of arrows with codomain \(c\) that is closed under precomposition: if \(f \in S\) then \(f \circ g \in S\). Such a set is called a sieve on \(c\). Exactly the same reasoning determines the exponential: \((Y^X)(c) \cong \operatorname{Nat}(\mathbf{y}c, Y^X) \cong \operatorname{Nat}(\mathbf{y}c \times X, Y)\).







Theorem 18.3 (Presheaf topoi) 
For every small category \(C\), \(\mathcal{S}^{C^{op}}\) is a topos, with

\(\Omega(c) = \{ S : S \text{ a sieve on } c\}\), and for \(f : d \to c\), \(S \cdot f = \{ g : f \circ g \in S\}\);
$_c = $ the maximal sieve (all arrows into \(c\));
for a part \(A \subseteq X\), the characteristic map \[
\chi_c(x) = \{\, f : d \to c \;:\; x \cdot f \in A(d) \,\};
\]
\((Y^X)(c) = \operatorname{Nat}(\mathbf{y}c \times X, Y)\);
natural numbers object: the constant presheaf with value \(\mathbb{N}\).





The characteristic map has a nice reading: \(\chi(x)\) records all the ways in which \(x\) eventually ends up in \(A\). In \(\mathcal{S}\) there is only one “way” (\(1_c\)), so \(\chi(x)\) is just yes or no.






NoteFact: when is a presheaf topos Boolean?



\(\mathcal{S}^{C^{op}}\) is Boolean if and only if \(C\) is a groupoid (every arrow invertible).




The recipe in action








index category \(C\)
presheaves \(\mathcal{S}^{C^{op}}\)
\(\Omega\)




one object, only the identity
\(\mathcal{S}\)
\(2\)


a set \(X\), only identities
families \((A_x)_{x\in X}\), i.e. \(\mathcal{S}/X\)
\(2\) in each fiber


a group \(G\), one object
\(G\)-sets
\(2\), trivial action


a monoid \(M\), one object
(right) \(M\)-sets
right ideals of \(M\)


the monoid \((\mathbb{N},+)\)
sets with an endomap
\(\mathbb{N}\cup\{\infty\}\), \(n \mapsto n-1\), \(0 \mapsto 0\)


\(V \rightrightarrows E\) (arrows \(s, t\))
directed graphs
2 vertices, 5 edges


the simplex category \(\Delta\)
simplicial sets
(the Week 14 model of HoTT)



A few checks:

For a monoid \(M\) (one object, arrows \(= M\), composition \(=\) multiplication), a sieve is a subset \(S \subseteq M\) with \(S \cdot M \subseteq S\): a right ideal. (For left actions, as in the notes on exponentials, one gets left ideals.) For a group, the only right ideals are \(\varnothing\) and \(G\), recovering \(\Omega = 2\).
For \((\mathbb{N}, +)\) the ideals are \(\varnothing\) and \(k + \mathbb{N}\) for \(k \in \mathbb{N}\). Write \(\infty\) for \(\varnothing\) and \(k\) for \(k + \mathbb{N}\). Acting by \(1\) sends \(k + \mathbb{N}\) to \(\{n : 1 + n \in k + \mathbb{N}\} = (k-1)+\mathbb{N}\) (or \(\mathbb{N}\) if \(k = 0\)). This is the \(\Omega\) for sets with an endomap: \(\chi(x)\) is the time it takes \(x\) to enter \(A\).
For graphs, a presheaf \(X\) has a set of vertices \(X(V)\), a set of edges \(X(E)\), and source and target maps \(X(E) \to X(V)\). Arrows into \(V\): only \(1_V\), so there are two sieves on \(V\). Arrows into \(E\): \(1_E, s, t\), giving five sieves: \(\{1_E, s, t\}, \{s,t\}, \{s\}, \{t\}, \varnothing\). Read: the edge is in the subgraph; it is not, but both endpoints are; only the source is; only the target is; neither endpoint is.



The Sierpiński topos, by hand
The smallest non-Boolean example deserves a complete computation. Let \(C\) be the category with two objects \(0, 1\) and a single non-identity arrow \(u : 1 \to 0\). A presheaf on \(C\) is just a map \[
X_0 \xrightarrow{\ \xi\ } X_1 ,
\] and a morphism is a commuting square. Think of \(X_0\) as “what exists now,” \(X_1\) as “what exists later,” and \(\xi\) as “how things develop.” A part of \(X\) is a pair \(A_0 \subseteq X_0\), \(A_1 \subseteq X_1\) with \(\xi(A_0) \subseteq A_1\): once in \(A\), always in \(A\).
Truth values. Arrows into \(1\): only \(1_1\), so \(\Omega_1 = \{\top, \bot\}\). Arrows into \(0\): \(1_0\) and \(u\), and the sieves are \(\{1_0, u\}\), \(\{u\}\), \(\varnothing\). So \[
\Omega_0 = \{\top, \tfrac12, \bot\} \xrightarrow{\quad} \Omega_1 = \{\top, \bot\}, \qquad \top \mapsto \top,\ \ \tfrac12 \mapsto \top,\ \ \bot \mapsto \bot .
\] For a part \(A \subseteq X\) and \(a \in X_0\), \[
\chi_0(a) =
\begin{cases}
\top & a \in A_0 \quad (\text{true now}),\\
\tfrac12 & a \notin A_0 \text{ but } \xi(a) \in A_1 \quad (\text{not yet, but later}),\\
\bot & \xi(a) \notin A_1 \quad (\text{never}).
\end{cases}
\] You can verify directly that this classifies parts (Exercise 18.2).
Excluded middle fails. Take \(X = 1 = (1 \to 1)\) and the part \(A = (\varnothing, 1)\): the proposition “it is not true now, but it will be.” The pseudo-complement \(\neg A\) must be disjoint from \(A\), so \((\neg A)_1 = \varnothing\), hence \((\neg A)_0 = \varnothing\) as well. Therefore \[
\neg A = 0, \qquad A \vee \neg A = A \neq 1, \qquad \neg\neg A = 1 \neq A .
\] \(A\) is not false (it is not refuted), and yet not true. Its characteristic map is the truth value \((\tfrac12, \top) : 1 \to \Omega\).
The rest of the profile:

Three global truth values \((\top,\top), (\tfrac12, \top), (\bot, \bot)\): not two-valued.
Not well-pointed. An element \(1 \to X\) is just an \(a \in X_0\). The object \(\varnothing \to 2\) has no elements, but two different automorphisms.
Choice fails, by Diaconescu — or directly (Exercise 18.2).







TipKripke models





This is exactly the semantics of intuitionistic logic by Kripke models with two worlds. Functors \(P \to \mathcal{S}\) on a poset \(P\) (i.e. presheaves on \(P^{op}\)) are Kripke models over \(P\): a statement is “true at stage \(p\)” if it holds at \(p\) and at all later stages, and \(\neg\varphi\) is true at \(p\) if \(\varphi\) fails at every later stage. Presheaves on \((\mathbb{N},\le)^{op}\) are “sets through discrete time.”

title: A Gallery of Topoi
text:
Sheaves on a space
Let \(X\) be a topological space and \(\mathcal{O}(X)\) its poset of open sets, viewed as a category (\(V \to U\) iff \(V \subseteq U\)). A presheaf on \(\mathcal{O}(X)\) assigns to each open \(U\) a set \(F(U)\) (“sections over \(U\)”) with restriction maps \(s \mapsto s|_V\) for \(V \subseteq U\). Example: \(F(U) = C(U, \mathbb{R})\).






NoteDefinition: sheaf



A presheaf \(F\) on \(\mathcal{O}(X)\) is a sheaf if whenever \(U = \bigcup_i U_i\) and \(s_i \in F(U_i)\) agree on overlaps (\(s_i|_{U_i\cap U_j} = s_j|_{U_i \cap U_j}\)), there is a unique \(s \in F(U)\) with \(s|_{U_i} = s_i\) for all \(i\).


Continuous functions form a sheaf (“continuity is local”); bounded functions do not. The category \(\mathrm{Sh}(X)\) of sheaves is a topos, with \[
\Omega(U) = \{ V : V \subseteq U \text{ open}\}, \qquad V|_W = V \cap W, \qquad \mathrm{true}_U = U,
\] and for a subsheaf \(A \subseteq F\) and \(s \in F(U)\), \[
\chi_U(s) = \bigcup\{ W \subseteq U \text{ open} : s|_W \in A(W) \} :
\] the truth value of “\(s \in A\)” is the largest open set on which it holds.
Global truth values are the open sets of \(X\), and the logic of truth values is the Heyting algebra \(\mathcal{O}(X)\): \[
U \wedge V = U \cap V, \qquad U \vee V = U \cup V, \qquad \neg U = \operatorname{int}(X \setminus U).
\] In \(\mathbb{R}\), with \(U = (0, \infty)\): \(\neg U = (-\infty, 0)\), so \(U \vee \neg U = \mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\} \neq \mathbb{R}\).

The real numbers in \(\mathrm{Sh}(\mathbb{R})\)
\(\mathrm{Sh}(X)\) has a real numbers object (constructed by Dedekind cuts internally), and it turns out to be the sheaf of continuous real-valued functions, \(U \mapsto C(U, \mathbb{R})\). So an “internal real number” over \(\mathbb{R}\) is a continuous function, e.g. the identity \(x : \mathbb{R}\to \mathbb{R}\). Compute truth values: \[
[\![x < 0]\!] = (-\infty, 0), \qquad [\![x = 0]\!] = \operatorname{int}\{0\} = \varnothing, \qquad [\![x > 0]\!] = (0, \infty).
\] Hence \[
[\![\,x < 0 \;\vee\; x = 0 \;\vee\; x > 0\,]\!] = \mathbb{R}\setminus \{0\} \neq \mathbb{R}.
\] Trichotomy fails for the internal reals. This is not a pathology but a feature: it is the internal reflection of the fact that a continuous function cannot be split, continuously, into “negative,” “zero,” and “positive” cases. Constructive analysis is the mathematics that is valid in all such topoi.

Grothendieck topoi. Replacing \(\mathcal{O}(X)\) by a category with a suitable notion of “covering” (a site) gives the Grothendieck topoi, the setting of modern algebraic geometry. \(\mathcal{S}\), \(\mathcal{S}/X\), \(G\)-sets, all presheaf topoi and all \(\mathrm{Sh}(X)\) are Grothendieck topoi. In fact the Sierpiński topos is \(\mathrm{Sh}\) of the Sierpiński space (Exercise 18.3), and \(\mathcal{S}/X\) is \(\mathrm{Sh}\) of the discrete space \(X\).

title: A Gallery of Topoi
text:
Topoi from logic
The last two examples are only surveyed: each of their constructions would take a set of notes of its own.

Forcing as sheaves
Cohen’s proof that \(\mathsf{CH}\) is independent of \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) (Week 5) can be redone in topos theory (Tierney; Mac Lane–Moerdijk, Ch. VI). Take the poset \(P\) of Cohen’s forcing conditions and form the topos \(\mathrm{Sh}_{\neg\neg}(P)\) of sheaves for the “dense” covering relation. This Cohen topos is Boolean, has a natural numbers object, and internally there is an object strictly between \(\mathbb{N}\) and \(\Omega^{\mathbb{N}}\) in size: \(\mathsf{CH}\) fails. Similarly, Boolean-valued models \(V^{\mathbb{B}}\) correspond to sheaves on a complete Boolean algebra \(\mathbb{B}\). Forcing is “sets varying over conditions.”


Realizability: the effective topos
Hyland’s effective topos \(\mathbf{Eff}\) is built from Kleene’s realizability: a statement is true when some program (an index of a computable function) “realizes” it. In \(\mathbf{Eff}\):

the natural numbers object is the ordinary \(\mathbb{N}\), but every function \(\mathbb{N}\to \mathbb{N}\) is computable (internally, “Church’s thesis” holds);
it is two-valued but not Boolean: excluded middle would require deciding the halting problem;
it is not a Grothendieck topos: it does not arise from sheaves on any site.

Realizability is the ancestor of the “proofs as programs” reading of logic we meet in Week 10: a proof of \(\forall n\, \exists m\, \varphi(n,m)\) in \(\mathbf{Eff}\) comes with an algorithm computing \(m\) from \(n\).

title: A Gallery of Topoi
text:
Non-examples
Topos theory gives quick tests for showing a category is not a topos. In a topos, every map that is both mono and epi is an isomorphism, the initial object is strict, and \(- \times B\) preserves colimits (it is a left adjoint).

\(\mathbf{Pos}\): cartesian closed, but the identity map from the 2-element discrete poset to the 2-element chain is mono and epi without being an iso.
\(\mathbf{Top}\): not even cartesian closed. Not every \(- \times B\) preserves quotients (e.g. \(B = \mathbb{Q}\)).
\(\mathbf{Grp}\): no subobject classifier. If \(\mathrm{true}: 1 \to \Omega\) existed, every subgroup would be the pullback of \(\mathrm{true}\) along a homomorphism, i.e. a kernel, hence normal. But \(S_3\) has non-normal subgroups.
\(\mathcal{S}^{op}\): has finite limits and colimits, but its initial object (the set \(1\)) is not strict.

Homework







Exercise 18.1 Show that \(\mathbf{FinSet}\) has no natural numbers object. (Hint: if \((N, 0, s)\) were one with \(|N| = n\), use the cyclic set \(\mathbb{Z}/(n+1)\) with \(f(k) = k+1\) and the pigeonhole principle on \(0, s0, \dots, s^n 0\).)











Exercise 18.2 The Sierpiński topos.

Verify directly that \(\Omega = (\Omega_0 \to \Omega_1)\) with \(\mathrm{true}= (\top, \top)\) classifies parts: the formula for \(\chi_0\) gives a morphism of presheaves, the pullback of \(\mathrm{true}\) along it is \(A\), and it is the only such morphism.
Let \(E = (2 \xrightarrow{\,1\,} 2)\) and \(B = (2 \to 1)\). Show that \((1_2, !) : E \to B\) is an epimorphism with no section.
Compute \(\neg\neg A\) for every part \(A\) of the object \((2 \to 1)\), where both points of \(X_0\) map to the single point of \(X_1\). Which parts satisfy \(\neg\neg A = A\)?












Exercise 18.3 The Sierpiński space has points \(\{a, b\}\) and open sets \(\varnothing, \{b\}, \{a, b\}\). Show that a sheaf on it amounts to a map \(F(\{a,b\}) \to F(\{b\})\), so that its sheaf topos is the Sierpiński topos. Compare with the two-point discrete space: which properties in the summary table change?











Exercise 18.4 Directed graphs. Using Theorem 18.3, draw \(\Omega\) for graphs: its two vertices, its five edges, and their sources and targets. How many elements \(1 \to \Omega\) are there (the terminal graph is one vertex with one loop)? Find a subgraph without a complement.











Exercise 18.5 In \(\mathrm{Sh}(\mathbb{R})\), compute \(\neg\neg U\) for an open set \(U \subseteq \mathbb{R}\). Find \(U\) with \(\neg\neg U \neq U\).











Exercise 18.6 (Optional.) Let \(M\) be a monoid. Show that the topos of right \(M\)-sets is Boolean iff \(M\) is a group. (Hint: if \(m\) has no right inverse, consider the part \(mM\) of the representable \(M\), and show that \(1\) lies neither in \(mM\) nor in \(\neg(mM)\).)

Step 1: the poset of open sets as a category
Fix a topological space \(X\) and let \(\mathcal{O}(X)\) be the set of its open subsets. Make \(\mathcal{O}(X)\) into a category:
Identities exist because \(U \subseteq U\), and composites exist because \(\subseteq\) is transitive. Associativity and the identity laws hold automatically, since there is at most one arrow between any two objects. (Every poset is a category in this way.)

title: Presheaves and Sheaves: A First Look
section: Step 2: presheaves — data that can be restricted
text:
Step 2: presheaves — data that can be restricted

The model example
For each open set \(U \subseteq X\) let \[
F(U) = C(U, \mathbb{R}),
\] the set of continuous real-valued functions on \(U\). If \(V \subseteq U\), any \(f\) on \(U\) can be restricted to \(f|_V\) on \(V\). So we get maps \[
F(U) \to F(V), \qquad f \mapsto f|_V \qquad (V \subseteq U),
\] and restriction behaves as expected: \[
f|_U = f, \qquad (f|_V)|_W = f|_W \quad \text{for } W \subseteq V \subseteq U.
\] That is the whole definition, abstracted.






NoteDefinition: presheaf



A presheaf \(F\) on \(X\) assigns

to each open set \(U\) a set \(F(U)\), whose elements are called sections over \(U\), and
to each pair \(V \subseteq U\) a restriction map \(F(U) \to F(V)\), \(s \mapsto s|_V\),

such that \(s|_U = s\) and \((s|_V)|_W = s|_W\) whenever \(W \subseteq V \subseteq U\). The elements of \(F(X)\) are called global sections.


In categorical language: a presheaf is a functor \(F : \mathcal{O}(X)^{op} \to \mathcal{S}\). The two rules are exactly preservation of identities and of composition.






TipWhy “op”?



The arrow \(V \to U\) goes from small to big, but restriction goes from big to small. Intuitively, a bigger open set imposes more constraints, so there are fewer sections over it; you can always pass from a section over a big set to one over a small set, but not back.




More examples
In each case the restriction maps are the obvious ones.

Other function spaces: all functions \(U \to \mathbb{R}\); the \(C^1\) functions; the bounded continuous functions.
The constant presheaf: \(F(U) = S\) for a fixed set \(S\), with every restriction map the identity.
Open sets: \(\Omega(U) = \{ W : W \subseteq U \text{ open} \}\), with restriction \(W|_V = W \cap V\).
Sections of a map: for a continuous \(p : E \to X\), let \(F(U) = \{ s : U \to E \text{ continuous} \mid p \circ s = \mathrm{id}_U \}\).
Square roots (a special case of 4): take \(X = \mathbb{C}\setminus \{0\}\), and let \(F(U)\) be the set of continuous \(g : U \to \mathbb{C}\) with \(g(z)^2 = z\) for all \(z \in U\).



Morphisms of presheaves






NoteDefinition: morphism of presheaves



A morphism \(\varphi : F \to G\) is a family of functions \(\varphi_U : F(U) \to G(U)\), one for each open \(U\), that commutes with restriction: \[
\varphi_U(s)|_V = \varphi_V(s|_V) \qquad (s \in F(U),\ V \subseteq U).
\]


This is exactly a natural transformation between the functors \(F\) and \(G\).
Example. Differentiation \(C^1(U) \to C^0(U)\), \(f \mapsto f'\), is a morphism of presheaves: differentiating and then restricting is the same as restricting and then differentiating.

19  Presheaves and Sheaves: A First Look

title: Presheaves and Sheaves: A First Look
section: Step 3: the gluing question — from presheaves to sheaves
text:
Step 3: the gluing question — from presheaves to sheaves
Suppose an open set is covered by smaller ones, \(U = \bigcup_i U_i\), and we are given sections \(s_i \in F(U_i)\) that agree on overlaps: \[
s_i|_{U_i \cap U_j} = s_j|_{U_i \cap U_j} \qquad \text{for all } i, j.
\] Such a family is called compatible. Is there exactly one \(s \in F(U)\) with \(s|_{U_i} = s_i\) for all \(i\)?






NoteDefinition: sheaf



A presheaf \(F\) is a sheaf if for every open cover \(U = \bigcup_i U_i\) and every compatible family \(s_i \in F(U_i)\) there is a unique \(s \in F(U)\) with \(s|_{U_i} = s_i\) for all \(i\).

Existence of \(s\) is the gluing condition.
Uniqueness of \(s\) is the locality condition: a section is determined by its local pieces.



A small but useful consequence: the empty set is covered by the empty family, which is vacuously compatible. So a sheaf always has exactly one section over \(\varnothing\).

Testing the examples
The best way to absorb the definition is to test it.

Continuous functions form a sheaf. Functions that agree on overlaps define a unique function on the union, and continuity is a local property, so the glued function is continuous. The same argument works for all functions, for \(C^1\) functions, and for open sets (\(\Omega\)).
Bounded functions do not. Cover \(\mathbb{R}\) by \(U_n = (n-1, n+1)\), \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\), and let \(s_n\) be the identity function on \(U_n\). Each \(s_n\) is bounded and they agree on overlaps, but the glued function \(x \mapsto x\) is unbounded. Boundedness is a global property, so gluing fails.
The constant presheaf does not. Take \(U = (0,1) \cup (2,3)\) and choose \(a \neq b\) in \(S\) on the two pieces. They agree on the (empty) overlap, but no single element of \(F(U) = S\) restricts to both. It also has the wrong value \(F(\varnothing) = S\). The repaired version is the sheaf of locally constant functions \(U \to S\).
Square roots form a sheaf — with no global section. Gluing holds, as for continuous functions. On any slit plane, e.g. \(\mathbb{C}\setminus (-\infty, 0]\), there are exactly two continuous square roots. But on all of \(X = \mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}\) there is none: \(F(X) = \varnothing\).



Why there is no global square root
Follow a continuous square root once around the origin. As \(z = e^{i\theta}\) runs through \(\theta \in [0, 2\pi]\), a continuous choice of square root must be \(g = e^{i\theta/2}\), which travels only half way around: it starts at \(1\) and ends at \(-1\).


  
    
      
    
  
  
  
    
    
  
  
  
  
  1
  z-plane
  z = eiθ, θ from 0 to 2π
  
  
  g
  
  
    
    
  
  
  
  
  1
  −1
  w-plane
  w = eiθ/2 ends at −1

A continuous square root, followed once around the origin, comes back with the opposite sign.

In sheaf terms: cover \(X\) by the two slit planes \[
U_1 = \mathbb{C}\setminus (-\infty, 0], \qquad U_2 = \mathbb{C}\setminus [0, \infty).
\] Their intersection is the upper half plane together with the lower half plane. If two square roots \(g_1\) on \(U_1\) and \(g_2\) on \(U_2\) agree on the upper half plane, then \(g_2 = -g_1\) on the lower half plane (this is the picture above). So no choice of local square roots is compatible, and there is nothing to glue. The sheaf axiom is not violated; there simply is no compatible family.

Connection to toposes. A map \(1 \to F\) from the terminal sheaf \(1(U) = \{*\}\) is the same as a global section (Exercise 19.1). So the square-root sheaf is an object that is locally nonempty everywhere but has no elements at all. This is the same phenomenon that made \(\mathcal{S}/X\) fail to be well-pointed — now with a topological reason behind it.

title: Presheaves and Sheaves: A First Look
section: Step 4: discrete spaces and the slice \(\mathcal{S}/X\)
text:
Step 4: discrete spaces and the slice \(\mathcal{S}/X\)
If \(X\) is discrete, every subset is open, and every \(U\) is covered by its singletons, which are pairwise disjoint. A compatible family on this cover is any choice of sections \(s_x \in F(\{x\})\), since all overlaps are empty. So the sheaf condition says \[
F(U) \;\cong\; \prod_{x \in U} F(\{x\}),
\] and a sheaf is nothing but the family of sets \(\big(F(\{x\})\big)_{x \in X}\). That is precisely an object of \(\mathcal{S}/X\), with fibers \(A_x = F(\{x\})\): \[
\mathrm{Sh}(X_{\text{discrete}}) \;\simeq\; \mathcal{S}/X .
\] For a general space, a sheaf is still a family of sets indexed by the points (its stalks), but now the family varies continuously. In fact every sheaf is the sheaf of sections of a suitable map \(p : E \to X\) (a local homeomorphism), just as in the square-root example. Sheaves are slices with topology.
crumbs: The View from Category Theory - Topoi
19  Presheaves and Sheaves: A First Look

title: Presheaves and Sheaves: A First Look
text:
Step 5: parts and truth values






NoteDefinition: subsheaf



A subsheaf \(A \subseteq F\) is a choice of subsets \(A(U) \subseteq F(U)\) that is closed under restriction (\(s \in A(U) \Rightarrow s|_V \in A(V)\)) and is itself a sheaf.


Example. Inside \(F = C(-, \mathbb{R})\) take \(A(U) = \{ f \in C(U, \mathbb{R}) : f > 0 \text{ on } U \}\).
Now take a section \(s \in F(U)\) and ask: is \(s\) in \(A\)? In \(\mathcal{S}\) the answer is yes or no. Here the honest answer is “on part of \(U\).” Among the open sets \(W \subseteq U\), some satisfy \(s|_W \in A(W)\). By gluing, \(s\) restricted to their union is in \(A\) as well, so there is a largest such open set. That open set is the truth value: \[
[\![\, s \in A \,]\!] \;=\; \bigcup \{ W \subseteq U \text{ open} : s|_W \in A(W) \}.
\] For \(s = x\) on \(\mathbb{R}\) and \(A\) the positive functions, \([\![\, x \in A \,]\!] = (0, \infty)\).
So the truth-value object of the topos \(\mathrm{Sh}(X)\) is exactly example 3 from Step 2: \[
\Omega(U) = \{ W \subseteq U \text{ open} \}, \qquad \mathrm{true}_U = U,
\] and the characteristic map of \(A \subseteq F\) sends \(s \in F(U)\) to \([\![\, s \in A \,]\!]\).

Where excluded middle goes
Truth values are combined like open sets: \[
[\![\varphi \wedge \psi]\!] = [\![\varphi]\!] \cap [\![\psi]\!], \qquad
[\![\varphi \vee \psi]\!] = [\![\varphi]\!] \cup [\![\psi]\!], \qquad
[\![\neg \varphi]\!] = \operatorname{int}\big(X \setminus [\![\varphi]\!]\big).
\] Negation must give an open set, the largest one disjoint from \([\![\varphi]\!]\), hence the interior. Therefore \[
[\![\, x > 0 \;\vee\; \neg(x > 0) \,]\!] = (0, \infty) \cup \operatorname{int}\big((-\infty, 0]\big)
= \mathbb{R}\setminus \{0\} \;\neq\; \mathbb{R}.
\] Excluded middle fails exactly at the boundary point \(0\), where neither “\(x > 0\)” nor its negation holds on any neighborhood.






TipPresheaves versus sheaves: sieves





For mere presheaves on \(\mathcal{O}(X)\), the natural truth value of “\(s \in A\)” is the whole collection \[
\{ W \subseteq U \text{ open} : s|_W \in A(W) \}.
\] This collection is closed under shrinking — a sieve on \(U\) — and it need not be determined by its union. For example, the sieve generated by \((-\infty, 0)\) and \((0, \infty)\) (all opens contained in one of them) differs from the sieve of all open subsets of \(\mathbb{R}\setminus \{0\}\), although both have union \(\mathbb{R}\setminus \{0\}\). The sheaf condition is exactly what collapses a sieve to its union, which is why sheaves have the simpler \(\Omega\).

19  Presheaves and Sheaves: A First Look

title: Presheaves and Sheaves: A First Look
text:
Step 6: the general picture
Nothing in the definition of a presheaf used that \(\mathcal{O}(X)\) comes from a space. Replace it by any small category \(C\) and you get presheaves \(C^{op} \to \mathcal{S}\): data indexed by the objects of \(C\), restrictable along the arrows of \(C\). The examples from lecture are all of this kind:



index category \(C\)
presheaves on \(C\)




\(\mathcal{O}(X)\)
presheaves on the space \(X\)


a monoid \(M\) (one object)
\(M\)-sets


a group \(G\) (one object)
\(G\)-sets


\(V \rightrightarrows E\)
directed graphs


one arrow \(1 \to 0\)
the Sierpiński topos



The sheaf condition needs extra structure: a specification of which families of arrows “cover” an object. A category with such a specification is a site, and the categories of sheaves on sites are the Grothendieck toposes.

19  Presheaves and Sheaves: A First Look

title: Presheaves and Sheaves: A First Look
text:
Exercises







Exercise 19.1 Let \(1\) be the presheaf with \(1(U) = \{*\}\) for all \(U\). Show that morphisms \(1 \to F\) correspond bijectively to global sections \(F(X)\). (Hint: \(X\) is the largest element of \(\mathcal{O}(X)\).)











Exercise 19.2 Show that \(\Omega(U) = \{ W \subseteq U \text{ open}\}\), with \(W|_V = W \cap V\), is a sheaf. Then show that the subsheaves of \(1\) correspond exactly to the open sets of \(X\).











Exercise 19.3 Let \(F = C(-, \mathbb{R})\) and \(A(U) = \{ f : f \geq 0 \text{ on } U\}\). Show that \(A\) is a subsheaf, and compute \([\![\, x \in A \,]\!]\) for \(x\) the identity function on \(\mathbb{R}\). Why is the answer not \([0, \infty)\)?











Exercise 19.4 Show that the presheaf of locally constant functions \(U \to S\) is a sheaf. Describe its sections over \(U = (0,1) \cup (2,3)\), and over a connected open set.











Exercise 19.5 The Sierpiński space has points \(\{a, b\}\) and open sets \(\varnothing\), \(\{b\}\), \(\{a, b\}\). Show that a sheaf on it amounts to a single map \(F(\{a, b\}) \to F(\{b\})\), and that \(\Omega\) is the map \(\{\varnothing, \{b\}, \{a,b\}\} \to \{\varnothing, \{b\}\}\), \(W \mapsto W \cap \{b\}\). Compare with the Sierpiński topos from lecture.

title: Toposes and Intuitionistic Logic
text:
From truth tables to \(\Omega\)
Recall from L–R, Chapter 3: a part \(A \subseteq X\) has a characteristic map \(\chi_A : X \to 2\), and a truth table such as \(\& : 2 \times 2 \to 2\) acts on parts by composition: \[
X \xrightarrow{\ \langle \chi_A, \chi_B \rangle\ } 2 \times 2 \xrightarrow{\ \&\ } 2
\qquad \text{classifies} \qquad A \cap B .
\] In a topos \(\mathcal{E}\), the same picture holds with \(\Omega\) in place of \(2\): \[
\operatorname{Sub}(X) \;\cong\; \mathcal{E}(X, \Omega),
\] and operations on parts that are natural in \(X\) are induced by maps \(\Omega \times \Omega \to \Omega\). We have already seen, in the Sierpiński topos and in \(\mathrm{Sh}(\mathbb{R})\), that these operations do not satisfy excluded middle. The question is: what laws do they satisfy?
crumbs: The View from Category Theory - Topoi

title: Toposes and Intuitionistic Logic
text:
Intuitionistic logic and Heyting algebras

Intuitionistic logic
Intuitionistic propositional logic has the usual connectives \(\wedge, \vee, \to, \bot\), with \(\neg \varphi\) defined as \(\varphi \to \bot\), and the usual natural deduction rules — except that the law of excluded middle \(\varphi \vee \neg\varphi\) (equivalently, double negation elimination \(\neg\neg\varphi \to \varphi\)) is not a rule.
The informal reading behind it is the BHK interpretation (Brouwer–Heyting–Kolmogorov), which we develop in Week 10:

a proof of \(\varphi \wedge \psi\) is a proof of \(\varphi\) together with a proof of \(\psi\);
a proof of \(\varphi \vee \psi\) is a proof of one of them, together with the information which one;
a proof of \(\varphi \to \psi\) is a method transforming proofs of \(\varphi\) into proofs of \(\psi\);
a proof of \(\exists x\, \varphi(x)\) provides a witness \(a\) and a proof of \(\varphi(a)\).

On this reading, \(\varphi \vee \neg\varphi\) would require a uniform method deciding every proposition, so there is no reason to expect it.







valid intuitionistically
valid only classically




\(\varphi \to \neg\neg\varphi\)
\(\neg\neg\varphi \to \varphi\)


\(\neg\neg\neg\varphi \leftrightarrow \neg\varphi\)
\(\varphi \vee \neg\varphi\)


\((\varphi \to \psi) \to (\neg\psi \to \neg\varphi)\)
\((\neg\psi \to \neg\varphi) \to (\varphi \to \psi)\)


\(\neg(\varphi \vee \psi) \leftrightarrow \neg\varphi \wedge \neg\psi\)
\(\neg(\varphi \wedge \psi) \to \neg\varphi \vee \neg\psi\)


\(\neg\neg(\varphi \vee \neg\varphi)\)
\(((\varphi \to \psi) \to \varphi) \to \varphi\) (Peirce)



The last entry on the left is worth pausing on: excluded middle is not provable, but it is not refutable either.


Heyting algebras






NoteDefinition: Heyting algebra



A Heyting algebra is a lattice \(H\) with least element \(0\) and greatest element \(1\), together with an operation \(\Rightarrow\) such that for all \(a, b, c \in H\) \[
c \le (a \Rightarrow b) \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad c \wedge a \le b .
\] We put \(\neg a := a \Rightarrow 0\), the largest element disjoint from \(a\).


The defining condition should look familiar. It is the exponential law \[
\frac{X \longrightarrow Y^B}{X \times B \longrightarrow Y}
\] for a poset regarded as a category, where \(\times\) is \(\wedge\) and \(Y^B\) is \(B \Rightarrow Y\). So:

A Heyting algebra is exactly a cartesian closed poset with finite joins.

Many facts then come for free from the exponentials lecture. For instance, \(a \wedge -\) is a left adjoint, so it preserves joins: every Heyting algebra is distributive, just as exponentials forced distributivity of \(\times\) over \(+\).
A Boolean algebra is a Heyting algebra in which \(a \vee \neg a = 1\) for all \(a\) (equivalently, \(\neg\neg a = a\)).
Examples.

Every Boolean algebra, with \(a \Rightarrow b = \neg a \vee b\); in particular \(2\).
The open sets \(\mathcal{O}(X)\) of a topological space, with \(U \Rightarrow V = \operatorname{int}\big((X \setminus U) \cup V\big)\) and \(\neg U = \operatorname{int}(X \setminus U)\).
Any finite chain \(0 < a_1 < \dots < 1\), with \(a \Rightarrow b = 1\) if \(a \le b\) and \(a \Rightarrow b = b\) otherwise. The three-element chain \(\{\bot, \tfrac12, \top\}\) is the stage-\(0\) truth values of the Sierpiński topos: \(\neg \tfrac12 = \bot\), \(\neg\neg\tfrac12 = \top\), and \(\tfrac12 \vee \neg\tfrac12 = \tfrac12\).








Theorem 20.1 (Soundness and completeness) 
A propositional formula is provable in intuitionistic logic if and only if it evaluates to \(1\) under every assignment in every Heyting algebra. In fact, the single Heyting algebra \(\mathcal{O}(\mathbb{R})\) suffices (Tarski).




Compare: classical propositional logic is complete for Boolean algebras, and already for the two-element algebra \(2\) — the truth tables.

title: Toposes and Intuitionistic Logic
section: The logic of parts in a topos
text:
The logic of parts in a topos
Throughout, \(\operatorname{Sub}(X)\) is ordered by inclusion of parts: for parts \(i : A \rightarrowtail X\) and \(j : B \rightarrowtail X\), \[
i \subseteq_X j \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad i = j k \text{ for some (necessarily unique) } k : A \to B .
\] On monos this is only a preorder; two monos that factor through each other are isomorphic over \(X\), and \(\operatorname{Sub}(X)\) consists of these equivalence classes, on which \(\subseteq_X\) is a partial order. In terms of characteristic maps, \(A \subseteq_X B\) iff \(\chi_A \wedge \chi_B = \chi_A\).






WarningInclusion is tested at all stages



In \(\mathcal{S}\), \(A \subseteq_X B\) can be checked with elements \(1 \to X\). In a general topos one needs generalized elements \(T \to X\). In the Sierpiński topos, the parts \((\varnothing, 1)\) and \(0\) of \(1\) contain the same global elements (none), yet they are different.









Theorem 20.2 (Parts form Heyting algebras) 
Let \(\mathcal{E}\) be a topos.

For every object \(X\), \(\operatorname{Sub}(X)\) is a Heyting algebra.
For every \(f : Y \to X\), pullback \(f^* : \operatorname{Sub}(X) \to \operatorname{Sub}(Y)\) preserves all the Heyting operations, and it has both adjoints: \[
\exists_f \;\dashv\; f^* \;\dashv\; \forall_f .
\]





Concretely, the top and bottom of \(\operatorname{Sub}(X)\) are \(1_X\) and \(0 \rightarrowtail X\); the meet \(A \cap B\) is the pullback; the join \(A \cup B\) is the image of \(A + B \to X\); and the implication \(A \Rightarrow B\), the largest part \(C\) with \(C \cap A \subseteq_X B\), is \(\forall_i(i^* B)\) for \(i : A \rightarrowtail X\).
In \(\mathcal{S}\), for \(B \subseteq Y\) and \(f : Y \to X\): \[
\exists_f(B) = \{ x : \exists y\,( f(y) = x \wedge y \in B)\}, \qquad
\forall_f(B) = \{ x : \forall y\,( f(y) = x \to y \in B)\}.
\] For a projection \(\pi : X \times Y \to X\) these are literally the quantifiers \(\exists y\) and \(\forall y\). This is Lawvere’s slogan “quantifiers are adjoints”: the rules \[
\frac{\exists y\, \varphi(x,y) \;\vdash\; \psi(x)}{\varphi(x,y) \;\vdash\; \psi(x)}
\qquad\qquad
\frac{\psi(x) \;\vdash\; \forall y\, \varphi(x,y)}{\psi(x) \;\vdash\; \varphi(x,y)}
\] (with \(y\) not free in \(\psi\)) are exactly the two adjunctions.
The operations are maps on \(\Omega\). Because \(\operatorname{Sub}(X) \cong \mathcal{E}(X,\Omega)\) naturally in \(X\), the Heyting operations are induced by maps \[
\wedge,\ \vee,\ \Rightarrow\ : \ \Omega \times \Omega \to \Omega, \qquad \bot : 1 \to \Omega,
\] making \(\Omega\) an internal Heyting algebra — the topos version of the truth tables. For instance, \(\wedge\) classifies the part \(\langle \mathrm{true}, \mathrm{true}\rangle : 1 \rightarrowtail \Omega \times \Omega\), and \(\Rightarrow\) classifies the order relation \(\{(p, q) : p \wedge q = p\} \subseteq \Omega \times \Omega\).
In the examples.

In \(\mathrm{Sh}(X)\): \(\Omega(U) = \mathcal{O}(U)\) with the Heyting operations of open sets, computed on each \(U\).
In presheaves on \(C\): on sieves, \(\wedge\) and \(\vee\) are intersection and union, and \[
(S \Rightarrow T) = \{ f : d \to c \;:\; \text{for all } g,\ \ f g \in S \Rightarrow f g \in T \}.
\]
In \(\mathcal{S}/X\), \(\mathcal{S}^G\): Boolean, computed fiberwise or on underlying sets.

title: Toposes and Intuitionistic Logic
text:
The internal language
The correspondence between parts and formulas can be pushed all the way: every topos comes with an internal language (the Mitchell–Bénabou language).

Types are objects of \(\mathcal{E}\); terms \(t(x)\) with \(x : X\) of type \(Y\) are maps \(X \to Y\).
A formula \(\varphi(x)\) with \(x : X\) is interpreted as a part \(\{ x : \varphi \} \subseteq X\), or equivalently a map \(X \to \Omega\).
Connectives are interpreted by the Heyting operations of \(\operatorname{Sub}(X)\); quantifiers by \(\exists_\pi\) and \(\forall_\pi\) along projections; and \(\Omega\), \(Y^X\) give higher-order quantification (“for all subsets”, “for all functions”).
A sentence holds in \(\mathcal{E}\) if its interpretation is the top part, i.e. \(\mathrm{true}: 1 \to \Omega\).








Theorem 20.3 (Toposes model intuitionistic higher-order logic) 
Every statement provable in intuitionistic higher-order logic holds in every topos. Conversely, a statement holding in all toposes is intuitionistically provable: every theory has a “free” topos built from its syntax (Lambek–Scott).





Slogan. Toposes are to intuitionistic higher-order logic what Boolean-valued models are to classical logic. A mathematical argument that avoids excluded middle and choice is valid in every topos — for sheaves, \(G\)-sets, the effective topos, … all at once.


Local truth: Kripke–Joyal semantics
How do we actually compute whether a formula holds? For \(\mathrm{Sh}(X)\), write \(U \Vdash \varphi\) (“\(U\) forces \(\varphi\)”) for \(U \subseteq [\![\varphi]\!]\). Then:








\(U \Vdash \ldots\) iff




\(\varphi \wedge \psi\)
\(U \Vdash \varphi\) and \(U \Vdash \psi\)


\(\varphi \vee \psi\)
there is an open cover \(U = \bigcup_i U_i\) with each \(U_i \Vdash \varphi\) or \(U_i \Vdash \psi\)


\(\varphi \to \psi\)
for all open \(V \subseteq U\): if \(V \Vdash \varphi\) then \(V \Vdash \psi\)


\(\neg \varphi\)
the only open \(V \subseteq U\) with \(V \Vdash \varphi\) is \(V = \varnothing\)


\(\exists x\, \varphi(x)\)
there is a cover \(U = \bigcup_i U_i\) and sections \(a_i \in F(U_i)\) with \(U_i \Vdash \varphi(a_i)\)


\(\forall x\, \varphi(x)\)
for all open \(V \subseteq U\) and all \(a \in F(V)\): \(V \Vdash \varphi(a)\)



Two features stand out:

Disjunction and existence are local. A disjunction holds if it holds piece by piece; an existential statement holds if witnesses exist locally, which need not glue to a global one.
Implication and negation look ahead to all smaller open sets, exactly as in Kripke models (and in the Sierpiński topos, where “\(\neg\)” looks ahead to the later stage).

Example: square roots. In \(\mathrm{Sh}(\mathbb{C}\setminus \{0\})\), let \(z\) be the identity function, a global section of the sheaf of continuous complex-valued functions. Every point has a slit-plane neighborhood on which a continuous square root of \(z\) exists, so \[
\mathbb{C}\setminus \{0\} \;\Vdash\; \exists w\, (w \cdot w = z),
\] although there is no global square root (see the presheaves and sheaves handout). Internally, “\(z\) has a square root” is true; externally there is no element to point to. This is the intuitionistic meaning of \(\exists\), and it is why internal versions of the axiom of choice can fail even when every \(\forall\exists\) statement we care about holds.






TipConnection to Week 5



These clauses are the forcing clauses of Cohen’s method, with open sets in place of forcing conditions: a condition forces \(\varphi \vee \psi\) if densely many stronger conditions force one of them, and forces \(\neg\varphi\) if no stronger condition forces \(\varphi\). Forcing is sheaf semantics.

title: Toposes and Intuitionistic Logic
text:
Where classical logic lives







Theorem 20.4 (Classical toposes) 
For a topos \(\mathcal{E}\) the following are equivalent:

\(\mathcal{E}\) is Boolean: every \(\operatorname{Sub}(X)\) is a Boolean algebra;
\([\mathrm{true}, \mathrm{false}] : 1 + 1 \to \Omega\) is an isomorphism;
the internal language satisfies excluded middle, \(\forall p \in \Omega\,(p \vee \neg p)\).

Moreover (Diaconescu), the internal axiom of choice implies these.




Even in a non-Boolean topos, classical logic is not far away. Every topos \(\mathcal{E}\) contains a Boolean subtopos \(\mathrm{Sh}_{\neg\neg}(\mathcal{E})\) of “\(\neg\neg\)-sheaves”, where a statement holds iff it is not refuted. Applied to presheaves on a poset of forcing conditions, this is exactly how the Cohen topos is built — the categorical version of the passage from forcing to a Boolean-valued model. It mirrors the Gödel–Gentzen double negation translation, which embeds classical logic into intuitionistic logic.

Summary.

intuitionistic

In a topos, intuitionistic logic is not a philosophical restriction imposed from outside: it is forced by the fact that truth is local — it varies over stages, points, or conditions.


Outlook: Week 10
A Heyting algebra is a cartesian closed poset. Forgetting that the order is a preorder — keeping track of which proof shows \(a \le b\), not just that one exists — gives a cartesian closed category. This is the categorical side of the Curry–Howard correspondence: propositions are types, proofs are programs, and the BHK clauses above become the typing rules of the simply typed \(\lambda\)-calculus.

title: Toposes and Intuitionistic Logic
text:
Exercises







Exercise 20.1 In any Heyting algebra, prove: (a) \(a \le \neg\neg a\); (b) \(\neg\neg\neg a = \neg a\); (c) \(\neg(a \vee b) = \neg a \wedge \neg b\); (d) \(\neg\neg(a \vee \neg a) = 1\).











Exercise 20.2 In \(\mathcal{O}(\mathbb{R})\), find open sets \(U, V\) with \(\neg(U \cap V) \neq \neg U \cup \neg V\), and an open \(U\) with \(\neg\neg U \neq U\). Use your examples to show that the De Morgan law and double negation elimination from the right-hand column of the table of laws are not intuitionistically provable.











Exercise 20.3 Write out the truth tables of \(\wedge\), \(\vee\), \(\Rightarrow\), \(\neg\) on the three-element chain \(\{\bot, \tfrac12, \top\}\). Check that Peirce’s law fails for \(\varphi = \tfrac12\), \(\psi = \bot\).











Exercise 20.4 In \(\mathcal{S}\), verify \(\exists_f \dashv f^* \dashv \forall_f\) for \(f : Y \to X\), and check that for a projection \(\pi : X \times Y \to X\) they give the usual quantifiers.











Exercise 20.5 Using the Kripke–Joyal clauses, show that in \(\mathrm{Sh}(\mathbb{R})\), with \(x\) the identity function, \(\mathbb{R}\Vdash \neg\neg(x > 0 \vee x < 0)\) but not \(\mathbb{R}\Vdash x > 0 \vee x < 0\).

title: Topos Theory and ZFC
text:
Topos Theory and ZFC
Over the last weeks we developed category theory up to elementary toposes and met Lawvere’s Elementary Theory of the Category of Sets (\(\mathsf{ETCS}\)) as an alternative to \(\mathsf{ZFC}\). This lecture closes Part II by comparing the two on three fronts:
A preview of the answers: the difference in strength between \(\mathsf{ETCS}\) and \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) is not the difference between structural and material set theory — it is precisely the Axiom of Replacement. Size problems, on the other hand, are genuinely shared by both frameworks, and the standard fix (Grothendieck universes) is a large cardinal assumption you have already met. The debate is mostly about the third question.
